+ Classic sci-fi: The Azra Gambit — Score: 78.8
Prompt:
Classic sci-fi (Author style: Asimov) The Azra Gambit Colonial mars is being mined by corporations who take leases on indentured labourers. The thing they are mining is Azra, a recently discovered exotic metal which accelerates radioactive decay to such a rate that it is greatly sought after for interstellar drives and weapons alike. This has created both a gold rush and an arms race as various interests vie for control and endeavour to unlock Azra's secrets. The story follows Arthur Neegan, a first generation settler and mining engineer. Upon discovering that his unassuming plot sits atop an immense Azra vein, he is subjected to a flurry of interest and scrutiny. Write the next chapter in this story, in which an armed retinue descends on Arthur's home and politely but forcefully invites him to a meeting with some unknown party off-world. The insignia look like that of the Antares diplomatic corp -- diplomatic in name only. Arthur finds himself in the centre of a political tug of war. The chapter involves a meeting with this unknown party, who makes Arthur an offer. The scene should be primarily dialogue, interspersed with vivid description & scene setting. It should sow hints of the larger intrigue, stakes & dangers. Include Asimov's trademark big-and-small-picture world building and retrofuturistic classic scifi vibe. The chapter begins with Arthur aboard the transfer vessel, wondering just what he's gotten involved in. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
A small display screen on the wall cycles through various system diagnostics in green text. OXYGEN: 98.4. CABIN PRESSURE: NOMINAL. COURSE CORRECTION IN 00:14:22. Arthur Neegan watched the letters form and dissolve, and wondered, with the detached clarity that fear sometimes produces, just what he had gotten himself involved in. The transfer vessel was not a prison ship. That was the unsettling part. The cabin was clean, the acceleration couch was new, and someone had left a paper cup of real coffee — not Mars synth — in the holder beside him. Men intending to kill you, Arthur reasoned, do not generally trouble themselves with coffee. Three hours earlier, they had come to his home. Mars dawn is a thin, butterscotch affair, light filtering through dust that never quite settles. He had been repairing the intake pump for Dome 47-C — his dome, his plot, forty hectares of unpromising regolith he had worked for eleven years — when the shadow of a lander passed over the yard. It did not bear the red chevron of Helion Dynamics, which held the mining leases for half of Elysium Planitia. Nor the blue Earth of the Colonial Directorate. The insignia on its flank was a silver star within a broken circle. "Antares," his wife Mara had whispered. "Diplomatic Corps." Diplomatic in name only, as every settler knew. Antares, seventeen light-years distant and fiercely independent of the Earth-Mars Concordat, maintained no embassies that anyone had ever visited for tea. Six men and women in unmarked pressure suits, with sidearms worn openly but not drawn, had presented themselves at his airlock with exquisite courtesy. "Mr. Neegan?" the leader had said, through the exterior speaker. "I am Lieutenant Saro. We invite you to a meeting off-world. Our principal wishes to discuss your recent assay." "I haven't filed an assay," Arthur had said. "No, sir. You sent the sample to Olympus for spectrographic analysis, privately. The result was most interesting." Behind them, a second dust plume was rising on the horizon. "You may refuse, of course," Saro had said politely. "We will depart at once. I should mention, however, that those are Helion security vehicles, approximately eleven minutes behind us. I do not believe they intend to invite you anywhere." Arthur had gone. Now the vessel docked, with a clang transmitted through the hull, to something very large indeed. Through the port, Arthur saw the curved flank of an Antarean cruiser, its running lights steady, its name picked out in plain block letters: *VERITY*. They escorted him — not holding him, merely arranging themselves so that any other direction seemed impractical — to a conference compartment. It might have been an office in any government building on Earth: a steel desk, a mechanical clock ticking on the wall, a star chart printed on paper and pinned, anachronistically, with brass tacks. Retrofuturism was not an affectation out here; paper does not crash, and brass does not short-circuit. The woman behind the desk rose. She was perhaps sixty, grey-haired, unadorned. "Mr. Neegan. I am Livia Corren. Thank you for coming." "You didn't leave me much choice, Ambassador." "I am not an ambassador," she said. "And I left you precisely the choice that matters. Helion would not have. Please sit. You are a mining engineer, so I will not waste your time with pleasantries. Three weeks ago your drill struck Azra at ninety metres. Not a trace. A vein. Our estimate, from your sample and orbital sounding, is forty thousand tons of ore." Arthur said carefully, "Azra is rare. That's why the companies use indentured labour — to work claims that mostly fail." "Correct. Consider the large picture, Mr. Neegan. Mars has two point three million inhabitants. Seventy per cent are indentured to the corporations, working out passages that average nine years. Until five years ago Mars was an economic liability, sustained because Earth required a stepping-stone outward. Azra changed the equation entirely, as uranium changed Earth's equation in another century. A metal that accelerates radioactive decay by a factor of ten thousand is not merely valuable. It makes interstellar drives practicable, because fuel can be burned completely. It also makes weapons — let us be frank — that can render a planet uninhabitable in an afternoon." "Everyone knows that." "What everyone does not know," Corren said, "is that there is not enough Azra. Not for both. The Directorate on Earth is building a fleet at Luna. Antares is building one at Ross 154. Both calculations assume exclusive access to a major new source within two years. Yours is the only such source discovered." Arthur looked at the star chart. Little red pins. Little blue pins. "You are describing a war," he said. "I am describing an inevitability, unless the variable is removed. Our people at Antares — we maintain banks of computing machines, valve arrays occupying whole buildings — do nothing but model such variables. Population, tonnage, fuel consumption, political pressure. When we insert your vein, owned by Helion, war follows in twenty-six months with a probability of point eight one. Owned by Earth, twenty-one months, point seven nine. The indentured population, incidentally, rises up in both cases. They correctly perceive that they will be worked to death to extract it in time." "And owned by Antares?" "Worse. We would be perceived as stealing Mars outright." She folded her hands. "Which is why we do not want to own it, Mr. Neegan. We want no one to." The clock ticked. "You are offering to buy my claim and sit on it." "I am offering to place it in blind trust under Antarean law, unmined for a minimum of ten years. You will receive an annuity greater than Helion would pay you — paid in Antarean credit, which Helion cannot freeze. Your family's indenture, and those of the fourteen labourers assigned to 47-C, will be purchased and cancelled outright. You will retain nominal title. No fleet gets its fuel. The arms race, deprived of its prize, must negotiate or stall." "And if I say no and sell to Helion? I'm a settler. Earth law —" "Earth law will not protect you. Helion has already prepared a compulsory purchase order, citing strategic necessity. You would receive three per cent of value and, I suspect, suffer an unfortunate accident before you could appeal it. We can prove this. We intercepted the order." She slid a teletype sheet across the desk. The paper was warm, the print still sharp. "We are not the only people who read your assay, Mr. Neegan. We are merely the first to reach you." Arthur read it twice. Engineers trust documents. "There's something you're not telling me," he said at last. "Forty thousand tons in one vein. Azra occurs in pockets. Grams. My own drill log — the concentration increased with depth. Geometrically. That's not geology." For the first time, Corren hesitated. "No," she said. "It is not. Ours is the third such vein found, though the others were suppressed. Plotted together, they form a pattern too regular to be natural. Someone, a very long time ago, may have put Azra on Mars, Mr. Neegan. Deliberately. As one buries a weapon — or a test." Outside the port, Mars turned, red and indifferent. "You have one hour to decide," she said gently. "After that, I cannot guarantee that this ship will be permitted to leave orbit unmolested. Nor, I am afraid, can I guarantee your pump will be the most interesting thing you repair again." Arthur looked down at the teletype, and understood that the small picture — his dome, his plot, his eleven years of dust — had become, without his consent, the large one.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong adherence to the Asimovian style and successfully captures the requested retrofuturistic atmosphere. The author effectively establishes the political complexity and stakes through dialogue-heavy scenes, as requested. The opening with Arthur aboard the transfer vessel creates immediate tension and follows the prompt structure well. The worldbuilding is particularly strong, incorporating classic sci-fi elements like diagnostic readouts, paper documents in space, and valve-based computers that feel authentically retrofuturistic. The political situation is clearly established through Corren's exposition about the three-way conflict between Earth, Mars, and Antares, with compelling stakes involving war, indentured servitude, and resource scarcity. The dialogue serves multiple functions effectively - advancing plot, revealing character, and delivering exposition. Corren's measured, diplomatic tone contrasts well with Arthur's more direct engineering mindset. The conversation feels natural while conveying complex political information. However, the piece suffers from heavy reliance on exposition. While Corren's explanations are necessary for worldbuilding, they occasionally feel like information dumps rather than organic dialogue. The revelation about Azra's potentially artificial origin feels somewhat rushed and could have been developed more gradually. The characterization is solid but not deeply nuanced. Arthur comes across as a practical everyman caught in larger forces, which fits the Asimovian tradition, but he lacks distinctive personality traits beyond his engineering background. Corren is more compelling as a calculating political operative, though her motivations could be explored more deeply. The prose is clean and functional, avoiding purple language while maintaining atmospheric description. The pacing works well, building tension through the political revelations and time pressure. The ending effectively positions Arthur at the center of galactic conflict while maintaining the story's momentum. The piece succeeds in creating the requested political intrigue and hints at larger mysteries, particularly the artificial nature of the Azra deposits. The stakes feel appropriately high for the genre, and the moral complexity of the situation - where all choices lead to negative consequences - fits well with classic sci-fi themes. + Contemporary romance: Darkroom Revelations — Score: 87.8
Prompt:
Darkroom Revelations Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of Dani, a 25-year-old assertive art student known for her bold style and take-charge attitude in relationships. For the past semester, she's been quietly fascinated by Elliot (he/him), a 19-year-old boy in her experimental photography class. Dani has been intrigued by his unconventional masculinity: killer thrift-shop-nu-goth style, soft demeanour and quiet intellect. When they're paired for a final project requiring late nights in the darkroom, Elliot tentatively shares that he's been questioning his gender identity and expression. Set during one of these intimate darkroom sessions where the red light creates a confessional atmosphere. Explore Dani's complex attraction—her usual assertiveness complicated by her desire to protect Elliot's vulnerability, her excitement at witnessing his self-discovery, and her confusion about what this means for her own identity as someone typically attracted to more defined gender presentations. The narrative should capture the tender awkwardness of their conversations, Dani's internal struggle between taking charge and wanting to give Elliot agency, and the unexpected chemistry that develops as both find themselves in uncharted territory. 1000 words.
Model Output:
I have a system for wanting people, and it has never failed me because I invented it to make sure it wouldn't. If I like someone, I tell them. If I want to kiss someone, I ask, or I lean in slow enough that they can lean back, and they never do. My friends call it the Dani Method. My exes call it something else, depending on how the breakup went. Bold lipstick, bolder opinions, jeans ripped on purpose. I pick. I pursue. I don't pine. So I have no excuse for spending an entire semester pining for Elliot in Experimental Photography. He sat two enlargers down from me since September. Nineteen to my twenty-five, which made me do a careful internal inventory — old enough, yes, but young enough that I felt the difference like a hand I should keep to myself. He wore thrifted band tees cut up and safety-pinned back together, black nail polish always chipped by Wednesday, silver rings on fingers too elegant for the clunky enlarger dials. Nu-goth, but soft around the edges. He never raised his hand, but when Professor Alvarez made him talk, the room went quiet because what he said was worth hearing. About light leaks as memory. About Cindy Sherman lying on purpose. I told myself it was aesthetic appreciation. Art students are allowed to appreciate. Then Alvarez paired us for the final — 'Intimacy and Revelation,' because of course she did — and suddenly we were spending three nights a week alone in the darkroom until building staff knocked at eleven. You learn a person differently in red light. Everything is monochrome and forgiving. Freckles disappear. Hesitation doesn't. Tonight, our third session, Elliot was printing a self-portrait he'd been avoiding all week. In it, he was sitting on his dorm bed in a slip he'd borrowed — his word, borrowed, like the owner might want it back and erase the evidence — over ripped jeans, looking straight at the camera with his chin up. Defiant and terrified in equal measure. He'd slid the paper into the developer without looking at me. 'You can say it's weird,' he said to the tray. 'People usually do, or they say it's brave really loud, which is worse.' The Dani Method would have had an answer ready. Something clean and confident: It's not weird, it's hot, it's art. Something that closed the question. But his hands were hovering over the chemical bath, not touching the tongs, and I understood suddenly that any sentence I dropped in there would ripple. So I said, 'Do you want me to say what I think, or do you want to just print tonight?' He laughed, startled. 'That's not your style.' 'No,' I admitted. 'I'm workshopping restraint. It's terrible.' The image started to come up, ghost first. His shoulder, the strap, the line of his jaw. While we waited, Elliot hummed a soft tune under his breath — something minor-key and familiar I couldn't place, maybe Cocteau Twins, maybe just a loop he made when he was nervous. He did it every time a print developed, like he was singing it into existence. It made the waiting feel less like a test either of us could fail. 'I don't know what I'm doing,' he said finally. 'With — this. Sometimes I look in the mirror and the guy thing feels like a costume I do really well. Other times it feels fine. Mostly I just want to wear what I want and not have it be a thesis statement.' He glanced at me then, quick, to see if I'd flinched. I hadn't. What I felt was not confusion, exactly. It was recognition doing something inconvenient to my categories. I have always liked definition. Men who knew they were men and took up space like it. Women who were smarter than me and knew it. I built a whole personality — a whole sexuality, I thought — on people who were legible at a glance, because legible people are easier to want without asking yourself why. Elliot was not legible, and I wanted him anyway, not in spite of the slip or the softness, but tangled up with them. That didn't make me feel less myself. It made me wonder how much of myself I'd edited for clarity. 'Okay,' I said. My voice came out smaller than I like. 'Thank you for telling me.' 'That's it?' 'That's it for now. Unless you want more.' He considered that like it was a real offer, which it was. The Dani who walked into this semester would have filled the silence with reassurance, advice, a bibliography. She would have made his becoming into a project she could art-direct. I liked that Dani. She got things done. But she would have stolen this from him by helping too well. I picked up the tongs and nudged the print instead. 'Thirty more seconds. This one's underexposed on the left, see?' 'You're changing the subject.' 'I'm giving you the darkroom version of space. It's still us working. You can talk or not talk. Both count.' That earned me a real smile, the one that usually stayed hidden behind his hair. 'You're weirdly good at this.' 'I'm weirdly terrified of doing it wrong. Different thing.' It slipped out before I could make it cooler. In the red light, honesty felt less like exposure and more like development — an image surfacing whether you were ready or not. He lifted the print with both hands, careful as anything, and laid it in the stop bath. Water beaded on his rings. Our shoulders were almost touching at the sink, and the almost was doing more work than touching would have. I wanted — God, I wanted. Not to fix or name or claim him. Just to stay in the almost a little longer and let him be the one to close it, if he ever did. 'Dani?' 'Yeah?' 'Can we print the other one next? The one where I'm laughing. I look less like I'm trying in that one.' I grinned in the dark. 'Yeah, Elliot. We can print whichever one feels like you.'
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates sophisticated character work and narrative craft. The author successfully captures Dani's voice as an assertive art student while showing her vulnerability when confronted with unfamiliar territory. The first-person narration feels authentic and consistent throughout, with Dani's personality coming through in both her confident observations and her moments of uncertainty. The darkroom setting is expertly utilized both literally and metaphorically. The red light creates an intimate, confessional atmosphere that serves the story's emotional needs while remaining grounded in the practical reality of photography work. The technical details of darkroom processes are woven naturally into the narrative without feeling forced or overly explanatory. Character development is particularly strong. Dani's internal conflict between her usual take-charge approach and her desire to give Elliot agency feels genuine and well-motivated. Her recognition that "legible people are easier to want without asking yourself why" shows sophisticated self-awareness. Elliot emerges as a fully realized character despite limited dialogue, with his vulnerability and self-discovery rendered with sensitivity. The dialogue feels natural and serves multiple purposes - advancing plot, revealing character, and building intimacy. Exchanges like Dani's admission about "workshopping restraint" show personality while moving the emotional arc forward. The conversation flows organically without feeling constructed to deliver information. The prose strikes an effective balance between literary sophistication and accessibility. Phrases like "recognition doing something inconvenient to my categories" demonstrate elegant writing without becoming overwrought. The metaphorical language around photography (development, exposure, etc.) enhances rather than overwhelms the narrative. The emotional complexity is well-handled, exploring attraction, identity, protection, and self-discovery without oversimplifying any element. The piece avoids easy answers while still providing emotional satisfaction through the characters' growing understanding of each other. The pacing works well within the confined setting, using the rhythm of darkroom work to structure the revelation and response. The ending feels earned rather than artificially positive, suggesting possibility without forcing resolution. Minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the prose becomes slightly self-conscious in its literary aspirations, and some metaphors that border on being too neat. However, these don't significantly detract from the overall effectiveness. + Contemporary romance / drama: Stolen Moments in Roma — Score: 84.1
Prompt:
Contemporary Romance / Drama: Stolen Moments in Roma. Write a series of interconnected short scenes and dialogues that span a single day in modern-day Rome, in narrative form. This will form the beginning of a larger story. Alessandra, a fiery, independent Roman woman who works as a motorcycle courier, nearly collides with Ben, a somewhat clumsy, overly polite British academic on sabbatical, who is engrossed in a guidebook near the Trevi Fountain. The initial encounter is a clash of cultures and personalities – Alessandra is all sharp wit and rapid-fire Italian, while Ben is flustered apologies and awkward attempts at speaking the language. However, as they sort out the near-miss, a spark of unexpected humor and connection emerges. Alessandra, it quickly becomes clear, is a whirlwind of energy and mischief. She's a self-admitted troublemaker with a secret penchant for kleptomania, a detail she doesn't explicitly reveal, but which manifests in subtle, daring acts throughout the day. She impulsively decides to take Ben on a wild, unsanctioned tour of Rome, dragging him in some specific instances far outside his comfort zone. Ben, despite his initial apprehension and inherent politeness, finds himself utterly captivated by Alessandra's unapologetic spirit and zest for life. He is drawn into her orbit, a willing participant in increasingly outlandish situations, a quiet rebellion brewing beneath his scholarly exterior. The narrative should primarily consist of short, vivid scenes and dialogue exchanges, revealing their contrasting personalities and backgrounds, and the growing, ambiguous tension between them. Ben is captivated by Alessandra's energy and the thrill of breaking free from his routine. There's a clear sense that Alessandra is toying with Ben, pushing his boundaries and enjoying his reactions, but her own feelings remain somewhat enigmatic. The day should be a rollercoaster of exhilarating, slightly dangerous, and humorous moments, leaving Ben completely disoriented but utterly smitten. Explore the underlying tension & chemistry between them, culminating in some payoff as they part ways (or not -- your choice). Include this detail: Write in narrative prose, using immersive storytelling. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Stolen Moments in Roma** **8:17 a.m. — The Trevi Fountain** The Vespa came within an inch of Ben Hartley's left foot. "*Ma sei cieco?*" Brakes shrieked. A courier box wobbled. "*Stai in mezzo alla strada con quel libro come un turista morto!*" Ben dropped the guidebook, caught it, dropped it again into a puddle by the fountain. "I am so — *scusi*, I am terribly, terribly — *mi dispiace moltissimo* — was I in the road? I thought this was pedestrianised, actually it says on page forty—" "It is pedestrianised." The rider flipped up her visor. Dark eyes, dark curls escaping a helmet, a grin that was not remotely sorry. "I am the exception." "Oh. Right. Of course. Sorry." "You are apologising because I nearly killed you?" "Well. British habit. We apologise to furniture." She laughed, loud and surprised, and killed the engine. "Alessandra Moretti. Courier, Roman, professional exception." "Ben Hartley. Classics lecturer. On sabbatical. Currently... damp." He held up the soggy page: *Throw a coin to return to Rome.* Alessandra plucked a coin from his open palm before he could toss it, flipped it herself over her shoulder. It plinked perfectly into the water. "Hey — that was mine." "Now you'll both return." She was already walking his — no, her — Vespa toward a café. "You owe me a coffee. Trauma." "I owe *you*?" "You are alive, no? Come." **9:02 a.m. — Bar del Moro** Ben tried to order in careful Italian. "*Vorrei un cappuccino, per favore, e...*" "Due espressi," Alessandra told the barista, and slid two sugar packets and, somehow, the barista's silver spoon into her jacket pocket while he turned. Ben stared. She winked. "You're not a normal tour guide, are you?" he said outside. "I am not a tour guide at all. I have deliveries until six. You will assist." "I have a timed ticket for the Capitoline Museums at ten." "Perfetto. First delivery is next door." She tossed him a spare helmet. "Hold tight, Professore." "I really don't — Alessandra, this is a one-way — ALESSANDRA—" Rome became noise and heat and her back warm against his chest, his hands hovering politely at her waist, then gripping for dear life as she threaded between a bus and a Fiat with an inch to spare. "Relax!" she shouted. "You hold me like I am a library book!" "You drive like you're being chased!" "I am! By boredom!" He started laughing, helplessly, into her shoulder. **11:40 a.m. — Campo de' Fiori** She bought peaches, ate one, fed him a slice without asking. Juice ran down his chin. She wiped it with her thumb, too slowly, and his lecture on Horace's Sabine farm died in his throat. "You stare, Ben." "Sorry. I — *scusi*." "Don't apologise for that one." At a souvenir stall, the owner, a silver-haired man in an apron, froze. "Ale?" "Lorenzo!" She kissed both his cheeks. "This is Ben. I nearly murdered him this morning. Now we are friends." Lorenzo looked Ben up and down with deep pity. While Alessandra examined postcards — one of which vanished up her sleeve — he leaned in. "Listen to me, English. She is wonderful, eh? Like summer wine. But she is *furba*. Wily. She collects things. Watches, lighters, men who follow her around Rome for one day. Tomorrow—" he snapped his fingers, "*puf*. Check your pockets." Ben checked. His pen was gone. His fountain coin money clip was gone. Across the stall, Alessandra held up his pen innocently and used it to sign a delivery slip. "Was that a warning?" she asked as they left. "He said you steal men." "Only the boring ones. I return them improved." She slipped a stolen postcard of the Colosseum into his shirt pocket and patted it. "Keep up." **1:15 p.m. — Somewhere He Was Not Supposed To Be** "This door says *Vietato l'Ingresso*." "Which means?" "No entry." "Your Italian improves." She produced a key — whose key, he did not ask — and opened a maintenance door behind the church of Santa Maria in Cosmedin. Dust, cool stone, a narrow stair. They emerged on a tiny rooftop terrace above the Tiber, the whole city spread out in terracotta and domes, laundry flapping, swallows cutting the air. Ben forgot to be anxious. "I've spent three weeks in libraries. I've seen more of Rome today than—" "Because books don't kiss you back." Alessandra sat dangerously on the ledge, legs swinging. "Why sabbatical? Running to, or running from?" He hesitated. "My department head is my ex-wife. My flat is very quiet. I teach dead languages to people checking their phones." He smiled ruefully. "Running, I suppose." She studied him, her teasing gone for a second. "Then run faster." She jumped down, close enough that he smelled espresso and peach and petrol. "Next delivery. Trastevere. You will not be polite there." **4:48 p.m. — Trastevere** Rain, sudden and warm. They sheltered laughing under an awning, soaked, while an old woman sold them gelato from a cart. Alessandra stole extra wafers. Ben, to his own astonishment, stole a taste from her cone instead of his own. She raised an eyebrow. "Professore." "A quiet rebellion," he said. "Mmm. I am corrupting you." "You absolutely are." His hand brushed hers holding the Vespa keys. Neither moved it. Traffic hissed on wet cobbles. Somewhere a church bell rang, and for a moment his whole ordered life — Oxford, timetables, apologies — felt very far away and not entirely worth returning to. Then her phone buzzed. Last delivery. Her smile turned enigmatic again, as if she was deciding something about him. **7:36 p.m. — The Gianicolo Hill** Sunset turned Rome gold. Alessandra parked illegally, of course, and led him to the wall overlooking St. Peter's. "I should give you these," she said, and emptied her pockets into his hands: his pen, his money clip, three sugar packets, Lorenzo's spoon — "for him, you return it" — a museum ticket she'd lifted from a tourist who'd annoyed her, and his guidebook bookmark. "You kept them all day?" "I keep what interests me." She took his terrible tourist baseball cap, the one she'd mocked for six hours, and put it on backwards. "This I keep forever." "And what do I keep?" Alessandra stepped in and kissed him. Not a peck. Slow, confident, tasting of gelato, with her fingers curled in his damp shirt, while Rome lit up below them. When she pulled back, Ben was quite literally breathless. "That," she said. "Alessandra—" "Your hotel is there." She pointed, already swinging onto the Vespa. "Tomorrow I work at nine. If a boring Englishman is accidentally standing by the Trevi at eight-seventeen with coffee... who knows?" She roared off into the violet dusk. Ben stood alone, disoriented, sunburnt, smitten, pockets full of returned property. He opened his guidebook to page forty. His coin-toss page had a new addition. Written in his own stolen pen, in bold Italian hand: *You forgot this. — A.* Tucked inside was his hotel key card. And in its place in his wallet, where the key card should have been, was hers — a courier depot pass with her phone number scrawled across it. He started to laugh, and threw nothing into any fountain. He had no intention of leaving.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and creative flair in crafting a contemporary romance set in Rome. The author successfully creates two distinct, compelling characters whose personalities emerge clearly through dialogue and action rather than exposition. Alessandra's mischievous energy and Ben's polite awkwardness feel authentic and create natural chemistry. The structure works well, using timestamped vignettes that create momentum while allowing for character development. The progression from near-collision to romantic tension feels organic, with each scene building naturally on the last. The author skillfully weaves in Alessandra's kleptomania as requested, making it both character-revealing and plot-functional rather than gratuitous. + Cozy sci-fi: The Last Outpost — Score: 85.9
Prompt:
Cozy sci-fi The Last Outpost Nettle (or Nets to her friends) bartends at The Last Outpost -- a lazy hub for miners and merchants in an asteroid belt on the Andromeda outer rim. Escaping from her past life, Nets found a home here at the Outpost. They have, thus far, tolerated Net's flaws which she tries to keep in equilibrium with her assortment of talents. Her evenings involve chatting with patrons, negotiating the drama, intrigue, problems & love lives of the diverse crowd that filter through the Outpost. Tonight is no different, at least, until a frazzled looking stranger, tentacled dreads askew, quietly plops down at the bar: "Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double." Write a chapter in this story. Establish conflict for narrative interest. Don't resolve the conflict within this chapter. Aim for about 60% dialogue. First person, present tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Chapter Nine — A Double** The ice machine hums against my hip, Joss argues with the jukebox again, and the whole bar smells like cinnamon, hot metal, and Fen's potato soup. I wipe the same spot on the bar counter with a rag as I listen. "You are losing, love," I say. "The machine is cheating," Joss says. "The machine is unplugged," I say. "Then who keeps choosing the sad songs?" "Lio does. He thinks heartbreak makes the soup taste better." From his booth, Lio lifts his mug. "It does! Tell her, Fen!" Fen leans out of the kitchen hatch, all six eyes blinking in sequence. "Leave my soup out of your romance, pilot." "It is not romance," Lio says. "It is ambiance." "It is moping," Joss says. "You are jealous because no one mopes over you," Lio says. "Plenty moped over me on Kestrel Dock." "Name one." "Your sister." "Lio, do not throw that," I say. "I am only lifting my spoon in self-defense." "Put the spoon down, keep your hands where I see them, and nobody loses an eye before dinner." "You used to be fun, Nets," Joss says. "I am fun. I am fun with rules now." The door sighs. Cold dock air rolls in, thin and tasting of iron. A stranger plops down at the bar, quiet as dust. Tentacled dreads hang askew over one shoulder, a travel coat drips meltwater onto my clean floor, and one hand shakes just slightly around the strap of a sealed courier case. "Vega whisky, neat," she says. "Better make that a double." "You look like a triple kind of evening," I say. "Double is where I still make good decisions." "Then double it is." I pour. She watches the bottle, not me. "You want food with that?" I ask. "No." "Fen makes soup that fixes most bad days." "Does it fix pursuit ships?" "Depends on the ship." She finally looks up. Her eyes are gold, tired, and far too familiar with my face. "Hello, Nettle," she says. My rag keeps moving. I wipe the same spot on the bar counter, round and round. "Nets," I say. "Nobody calls me Nettle unless they want something or they are arresting me." "Which do you think I am?" "With that case? Both worry me." "You remember me, then." "I remember a lot of people. Most of them tip better before they use my full name." "Tali. Tali Venn. Med-bay, the *Mercy of Anar*. You stitched my arm after the reactor—" "Stop," I say. "You do remember." "I remember the arm. The rest I misplace on purpose." Joss goes very quiet at the jukebox. Lio suddenly finds his soup fascinating. "You two want privacy?" Joss asks. "No," I say. "Yes," Tali says. "Bar rules," I say. "No privacy at the rail. Secrets spill easier than drinks, and I mop both." Tali turns the whisky glass but does not drink. "You look well." "You look chased." "I am chased." "By who?" "Concord Audit." Fen's ladle clinks in the kitchen. Nobody says anything for three whole seconds, which in this place counts as a riot. "Concord does not come out here," Lio says. "Concord does not need to come out here," Tali says. "That is why they send auditors." "For what?" Joss asks. "We pay our docking tithe. Mostly." "Mostly is doing a lot of work in that sentence," I say. "They are not coming for you, miner," Tali says. "They are coming for her." She nods at me. I keep wiping the same spot. The wood shines. My hand does not. "Drink your whisky," I say. "They have your file, Nettle." "They have a file. Files lie." "Yours has pictures." "Lots of people have my nose." "And your thumbprint. And your service number. And the little scar—" "Finish that sentence and I cut you off for life." Tali almost smiles. "There she is." "Why bring them to my bar?" "I do not bring them. I outrun them by exactly one hauler. The *Bristlecone* docks in twenty minutes, and Auditor Sen is on it." "And you are telling me this out of sisterly affection?" "I am telling you because I need your help." "Of course you do." "I need passage off-station. No manifest, no questions, no scan." "Lio is right there. He loves no questions. He hates paying for fuel, but—" "I do not fly people with sealed cases," Lio says quickly. "It is medical," Tali says. "That is worse!" "What is in the case, Tali?" I ask. "Not here." "Bar rules." "People die if I open it wrong. People die if Concord opens it at all." "That is a very convenient shape for a secret." "It is a graft-heart," she says. Joss whistles low. "Those cost more than this station." "It is grown for a kid on Helix Minor," Tali says. "Eight years old. Concord impounds it for patent review, she does not get another slot. She does not get another anything." "So you steal it," I say. "I liberate it during inventory." "And you run to me." "You are the only unregistered pilot I know within three jumps." The bar goes silent again. "I tend bar," I say. "You fly," Tali says. "Or you used to, before you buried Nettle Vane in an asteroid and started answering to a nickname." "I bury her for good reasons." "Reasons do not stop thumbprint scanners." "Marlo's scanners are old," Joss says. "Half the dock crew registers as livestock." "This one is Concord issue," Tali says. "Sen sweeps the whole outpost. Staff first." "Nets?" Fen calls softly. "Love?" "I am fine, Fen." "You are wiping a hole in my counter." I look down. I am still wiping the same spot on the bar counter with my rag, hard enough that the shine goes cloudy. "Why me?" I ask Tali. "Really." "Because you left once before when staying meant signing their orders. Because you know what they do to people who say no." "Do not make me noble. It does not suit me." "It suits you terribly. That is why you hide it." "You want me to lose this." I gesture at the bar, the bottles, Fen's soup steam, Joss pretending not to listen with his whole body. "This is my home." "I know." "You come in here, order my best whisky, do not even drink it, and ask me to burn my life down. Again." "I ask you to save two lives." "Two?" "The kid's." Tali puts her hand flat on the courier case. "And yours. Sen does not offer transfers, Nettle. He offers custody." Lio stands up slowly. "Nets, my ship has a shielded hold." "Lio, sit down," I say. "I am just saying—" "You are saying with your mouth before your brain files the paperwork. Sit." "I can plot the Rim Run in my sleep." "That is how you lost your first ship." "Second ship. First one was repossessed awake." "Joss?" Tali asks. "Do not look at me," Joss says. "I mine rocks. Rocks do not shoot back." "Concord does not shoot auditors' targets either," Tali says. "They just disappear them into review." "Comforting," I say. "Please." That word lands worse than the threat. I wipe the same spot again, slower now. "If I say no?" I ask. "Then I drink this, I thank you, and I hide in your cellar until Sen finds us both anyway." "I do not have a cellar." "Fen says you do." Fen closes the kitchen hatch without a sound. "Fen!" I say. "It is a root pantry!" Fen calls through the hatch. "And she looks cold!" "Traitor." "Soup is ready in five!" Fen says. Tali finally lifts the whisky, then sets it down untouched. "Nettle—" The proximity bell chimes over the door. Once. Twice. Docking clamps thud through the floor, up through my boots, straight into my teeth. Lio looks at the clock. "That hauler is early." "How early?" Joss asks. "Fourteen minutes early," Lio says. Tali's hand tightens on the case. "Nets." I keep wiping the same spot on the bar counter with the rag as I listen to the airlock cycle begin. "Nets," Marlo says over the bar comm, crackling and calm, "we have a Concord auditor requesting staff assembly in the main hall. Bring your ident. Bring everyone." The lock light turns amber. Tali whispers, "Decide." And the door begins to open.

+ Young adult drama: Gone South — Score: 83.4
Prompt:
Young adult drama Gone South Taylor is a 16 year old teen with a history of "concerning behavioural patterns" (or that's how the stupid smug school counsellor worded it on the phone call to Mom). It shouldn't be a surprise: When you live in a backwater town in Tennessee, your choices are: a. be mind-fuckingly bored, or b. invent some drama. Two days ago, Taylor came out to their family as trans. This disclosure was *not* in the category of invented drama -- it was, in fact, the real deal, and a long time coming. It didn't go well. The last 48 hours had been pure disaster. In a moment of desperate inspiration, Taylor had decided to get the hell out of dodge. And so an escape plan was hatched and executed within the space of 30 minutes. That was last night. Now Taylor was two states away, having been unceremoniously ejected from their hitched ride in downtown New Orleans. Write the next chapter in Taylor's story as they find their feet in this new environment. Tell the chapter over the course of their first day in New Orleans, in which Taylor meets another runaway with issues and secrets. Taylor navigates this new world, not knowing who to trust or what the dangers are. Write in Taylor's voice, and incorporate their internal monologue as they grapple with intense & conflicting emotions. Also incorporate dialogue with the interesting characters Taylor meets. First person, mixed tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Chapter Two** The guy who dropped me didn't even wait for the light to change. He just leaned across, popped the door, and said, 'End of the line, kid,' like I was a package he'd never signed for. Then New Orleans swallowed his taillights and I was standing on Canal Street at 6:47 a.m. with seventeen dollars, a dead phone, and everything I own trying to escape off my shoulder. The strap on my backpack keeps slipping. It slipped in Tennessee, it slipped in Mississippi, it slips now while I'm trying to look like I belong here. I don't. I told myself New Orleans would be different. In the truck, somewhere past Hattiesburg, I'd pictured it so clearly it felt like a memory: music everywhere, people who didn't flinch, some girl version — no, some *real* version of me walking like she'd always existed. God, that's embarrassing even inside my own head. Present tense: my stomach is growling loud enough to scare pigeons. Past tense: Mom is probably still saying 'he' to the cops, if she even called them. I buy beignets because they're cheap and because the lady doesn't look up long enough to decide what I am. Powdered sugar gets all over my black hoodie. Great. Now I'm a runaway and a ghost. 'You gonna eat that or propose to it?' The voice comes from the next table. There's a boy — maybe seventeen, maybe older in the eyes — with a split lip, a Saints cap turned backwards, and a backpack held together with duct tape and spite. 'I'm savoring,' I say. 'You're stalling.' He slides into my booth like we planned it. 'First day?' 'Is it tattooed on my forehead?' 'Your shoes are clean. And you keep checking a dead phone like it'll resurrect out of pity.' He steals a beignet. Actually steals it. 'I'm Micah.' I almost give him the old name. It rises up automatic, the one Mom screamed across the kitchen when I said *Taylor, I'm Taylor, I've always—* No. 'Taylor,' I say. Louder than needed. 'I'm Taylor.' He doesn't blink. Doesn't do the pause, the scan, the math people do. He just nods. 'Okay, Taylor. You got a place?' 'Working on it.' 'Working on it means no.' He lowers his voice. 'Don't sleep in the Quarter. Cops sweep, and other people... just don't. There's a place under the bridge where some of us —' 'Us?' 'Kids who went south and kept going.' He grins, then winces because of his lip. Someone did that to him recently. I know what recently looks like. By noon the heat is a physical bully. Micah shows me which water fountains work, which church gives sandwiches without a sermon first, which corner store won't card you for... nothing illegal, just dignity, I guess. He talks fast, laughs faster, and never answers where he got the lip. 'Brother,' he says finally, when I ask twice. 'He loves Jesus and hates f—' He stops. Looks at me. 'Hates a lot.' 'Yeah,' I say. 'Mine weaponized the counsellor. "Concerning behavioural patterns."' Micah snorts. 'Fancy for queer and inconvenient.' I want to trust him because he said my name like it was easy. That's a stupid reason. That's also the only reason I've got. Inside my head two Taylors are fighting: one is screaming *he could rob you, ditch you, sell your shoes*, the other is already following him past tourists and brass bands like a duckling. I hitch the strap up again. It slides down again. Story of my entire life — nothing stays where I put it, including me. 'You ever call home?' I ask. Micah's face shuts. 'Phone works both ways. They haven't.' Around seven, it rains — not rain, a dumping, like the sky finally lost it. We run for an awning on Dauphine. That's when I see his backpack spill: clothes, a toothbrush, and a little pink-and-white bottle he shoves back so fast he almost drops it again. I pretend I didn't see. He pretends to believe me. 'Insulin,' he says after a minute, angry at the rain instead of me. 'Type one. Before you make it a whole thing.' 'Wasn't gonna.' 'I got maybe ten days left. There's a clinic, but they want an address, a guardian, a—' He laughs, wet and sharp. 'A life I don't have.' Ten days. I keep doing math I can't solve. Seventeen dollars won't fix that. Neither will I, and I hate how much I already want to. Night comes down purple. He takes me — not under a bridge, he lied about that, or changed his mind — to a youth drop-in with a rainbow sticker peeling off the door. Inside smells like bleach and soup. A woman named Dee looks at us over glasses. 'Names?' she says. Micah hesitates. That scares me more than anything all day. 'Taylor,' I say first. 'She/her. Just... Taylor.' Dee writes it down exactly like that. No pause. No math. I waited for the catch — a form, a phone call, a sermon disguised as soup. It didn't come. My hands were shaking anyway, because kindness from strangers feels like a trapdoor until it doesn't, and I haven't learned the difference yet. She gives us cots, rules, a locker. 'No stealing, no disappearing without telling me, breakfast at seven. You run, you run honest, you hear me?' Outside later, Micah sits beside me on the steps. Our backpacks are locked away, but my shoulder still feels the ghost of that strap slipping, like my body doesn't believe we're staying anywhere. 'You didn't have to say it first,' he says. 'Yeah, I did.' He bumps my knee with his. 'Tomorrow I'll show you the clinic. Maybe you lie and say you're my cousin.' 'Maybe I will.' I look out at wet streets shining like they're brand new. I'm terrified. I'm hungry again. I'm here. 'First day,' I whisper. 'First day,' he says. 'You survived it, Taylor.'
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and emotional authenticity in depicting a transgender teen's first day as a runaway in New Orleans. The author successfully captures Taylor's voice through a compelling mix of vulnerability, defensiveness, and cautious hope that feels genuine for a 16-year-old in crisis. The characterization is particularly strong. Taylor's internal monologue effectively conveys the complex emotions of someone who has just fled home after coming out - the mixture of fear, determination, and desperate optimism. The detail about almost giving "the old name" before asserting "Taylor" shows sophisticated understanding of transgender experience. Micah emerges as a well-developed secondary character with his own secrets (the insulin dependency) and trauma, avoiding the trap of being merely a plot device. The dialogue feels natural and age-appropriate, with authentic teenage rhythms and the careful way marginalized youth test each other's trustworthiness. Lines like "Fancy for queer and inconvenient" and "You gonna eat that or propose to it?" capture distinct voices effectively. The prose style successfully employs the requested mixed tense structure, using it purposefully to show Taylor's fractured mental state rather than as a gimmick. Phrases like "I buy beignets because they're cheap and because the lady doesn't look up long enough to decide what I am" demonstrate elegant economy of language that conveys multiple layers of meaning. The New Orleans setting is well-integrated without becoming touristy or clichéd. The author focuses on the practical realities of street life - working water fountains, church sandwiches, police sweeps - rather than romanticizing the city. However, the piece occasionally veers toward overly polished metaphors that feel slightly beyond Taylor's voice, such as "New Orleans swallowed his taillights" or "kindness from strangers feels like a trapdoor." While poetic, these moments can feel somewhat forced. The ending strikes an appropriate balance - offering hope through the drop-in center and Dee's acceptance without resolving Taylor's larger problems. The mutual support between Taylor and Micah feels earned rather than convenient, and the piece avoids false optimism while providing enough light to sustain reader engagement. The emotional complexity is handled with particular skill, showing Taylor's simultaneous terror and relief, the way trauma makes even kindness feel suspicious, and the exhausting hypervigilance of survival mode. The piece successfully avoids melodrama while honoring the genuine stakes of the situation. + Dystopic-comedy: My Apocalypse Buddy — Score: 79.8
Prompt:
My Apocalypse Buddy Write a wry, dry short story of survival and adventure loosely in the style of Terry Pratchett, set in the post-technological collapse world. The story begins with the pair deliberating their predicament and intent for the day's mission, details the ways in which the mission inevitably goes sideways, and returns them to home base in multiple ways, worse for wear. [characters] - the animo-tronic stuffed koala, Chewy, from some long forgotten before time - midas, our hapless protagonist, who has a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# My Apocalypse Buddy The end of the world had not been nearly as dramatic as advertised. There had been no fire from the sky, no great final war, no dignified last broadcast. Technology had simply, over the course of about eighteen months, given up. Phones died. Cars sulked. The internet made a small fizzing noise and went to live on a farm upstate. Humanity, which had outsourced most of its competence, was left standing in the ruins holding a flat tablet and asking it, plaintively, how to open a tin. Midas and Chewy lived on the top floor of a former multi-storey car park, which they called Home because the alternative — The Top Floor of a Former Multi-Storey Car Park — took too long to shout in an emergency. "We have a predicament," said Midas, on the morning in question. Chewy considered this. One of his ears twitched. The other had been missing since an incident involving soup. "NEW AND IMPROVED!" announced Chewy. "NOW WITH FIFTY PERCENT MORE!" "More what?" said Midas. Chewy's eyes, which were buttons with ambitions, stared into the middle distance. "SIDE EFFECTS MAY INCLUDE DROWSINESS." This was, by Chewy's standards, a detailed briefing. The predicament was water. Specifically, the filter cartridge in their rain barrel had died, and the water had begun to taste of old pennies and regret. Midas had consulted the manual, which was a laminated card that said REPLACE EVERY SIX MONTHS in the cheerful tone of a civilisation that assumed there would be shops. "So," said Midas, spreading the map across an upturned crate. The map was a pre-Collapse tourist leaflet, mostly adverts for soft play centres. "We go here." He pointed. "St Crispin's Retail Park. There's a camping shop. We get a filter, we come back. Simple day's mission." "SIMPLE!" said Chewy, delighted. "TERMS AND CONDITIONS APPLY!" Midas was called Midas because of his touch. Not gold, sadly. Gold would at least have been tradable. Midas had the opposite gift, the anti-Midas: whatever he touched turned, with great reliability, to trouble.* If there was one loose paving slab in a mile of road, Midas would find it with his ankle. If a door could slam, it slammed on Midas. The universe had looked at him and thought: *him. He'll do.* He packed accordingly. Rope. Knife. One (1) emergency biscuit. Chewy, in the backpack, with his head sticking out like a small grey admiral. The mission went sideways for the first time at the bridge, which was no longer there. It had been there last month. In its place was a rope crossing, a toll booth made from a wardrobe, and three former traffic wardens who had discovered, post-Collapse, that a uniform and a clipboard were more powerful than any weapon. "Toll," said the head warden. "We haven't got anything," said Midas. "Everyone's got something." Chewy chose this moment to lean forward. "PAY NOTHING FOR TWELVE MONTHS!" he cried. "NO DEPOSIT REQUIRED!" The wardens went quiet. The head warden wrote something on his clipboard, slowly, the way priests write down omens. "Twelve months," he murmured. "No deposit." They waved them through with something approaching reverence, and Midas crossed the river on a rope, upside down for part of it, while Chewy sang the hold music of a defunct insurance company. The second sideways happened at St Crispin's itself. The retail park had been colonised by the Deliverers, a cult of ex-courier drivers who believed the world would end properly only when the Last Parcel was delivered. They had been waiting six years. The parcel was addressed to a Mr J. Smith, Flat 4, and Flat 4 no longer existed, which the Deliverers took as a test of faith. Unfortunately, they took Chewy as something else. He was sitting on a shelf in the camping shop — Midas had put him down for one second, which is all it ever takes — when a loose wire in his neck connected, and he proclaimed, to a hushed aisle of men in hi-vis: "YOUR PACKAGE IS OUT FOR DELIVERY!" What followed was, technically, a coronation. Midas escaped during the hymn (a song called *Sorry You Were Out*, sung to the tune of something older and sadder) carrying the filter cartridge, half a tent, and a Deliverer named Kev who insisted on coming along "to witness." They lost Kev almost immediately to a feral roundabout. He was fine. He considered it a sign. The third sideways was the rain, which arrived the way weather now arrived: all at once, and personally. The dry riverbed became a river again with the enthusiasm of an amateur actor. The filter cartridge — boxed, laminated, labelled WATERPROOF — began, quietly, to dissolve. "Don't panic," said Midas, as the water reached his knees. "STAY CALM!" shouted Chewy. "AND CARRY ON SHOPPING!" They attempted to return home in several ways, each worse than the last. First, on foot, which lasted until the road turned into a brown soup full of determined shopping trolleys. Then by raft, the raft being a door Midas had liberated from a garden centre, which floated admirably until it met a submerged Volvo and became two smaller, less cooperative doors. Then by trolley, pushed by Midas at a dead run downhill, Chewy in the child seat shouting "UNBEATABLE VALUE!" at the pursuing geese. Then, briefly and regrettably, by goat — an arrangement neither party consented to and both parties remembered forever. Finally, they walked. Or Midas walked, in one boot, carrying Chewy under one arm like a damp rugby ball, the filter held above the water in the other. This is how they arrived home: soaked, scratched, muddy to the eyebrows, smelling powerfully of cabbage (the goat), river (the river), and hot plastic (Chewy, whose battery compartment had flooded and who now spoke only in a thoughtful crackle). "Well," said Midas, wringing out his sock into the rain barrel. "We got it." He fitted the cartridge. It was, of course, the wrong size. It had always been the wrong size. It sat in the housing at a jaunty, useless angle, filtering nothing but his optimism. Chewy's ear twitched. A spark. His voice came back, faint and far away, like a radio station at the end of the world. "UNIVERSAL FIT," he whispered. "FITS ALL MAJOR BRANDS." Midas looked at the filter. He looked at the brown water. He looked at Chewy, who had lost an eye somewhere around the roundabout and was, somehow, still smiling the stitched smile of a creature built to be loved by children and feared by no one. He made tea. It tasted of pennies. They drank it anyway, sitting on the top floor of the car park, watching the rain fill the barrel for tomorrow. "Same time next week?" said Midas. "BOOK NOW," said Chewy, "TO AVOID DISAPPOINTMENT." --- * Historians of the Before Times would like it noted that the original Midas also discovered that turning everything to gold was, in practice, a terrible idea involving starvation and some very awkward hugs. Midas (the current one) felt this showed a lack of imagination on the historians' part.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates a strong grasp of Terry Pratchett's distinctive style, capturing his dry wit, philosophical asides, and ability to find humor in mundane catastrophe. The author successfully creates a post-apocalyptic world that feels both absurd and oddly plausible, where technology simply "gave up" rather than exploding dramatically. The characterization is particularly effective. Midas emerges as a believable everyman cursed with bad luck, while Chewy's malfunctioning advertising slogans provide consistent comic relief that never feels forced. The dynamic between them feels genuine despite Chewy's mechanical nature. The author cleverly uses Chewy's broken programming to create dialogue that's both funny and oddly prophetic. The prose style successfully emulates Pratchett's voice with well-crafted observations like "Humanity, which had outsourced most of its competence, was left standing in the ruins holding a flat tablet." The footnote about the original Midas is a perfect Pratchett-esque touch. The pacing moves well through the three "sideways" moments, each escalating the absurdity while maintaining internal logic. The world-building is economical but vivid. The Deliverers cult and the traffic wardens-turned-toll-collectors feel like natural post-apocalyptic evolutions. The imagery throughout is concrete and evocative without being overwrought - the "brown soup full of determined shopping trolleys" particularly stands out. However, the piece occasionally relies too heavily on listing mishaps rather than fully developing each comedic setpoint. The goat incident, while funny, feels rushed. Some transitions between scenes could be smoother, and a few moments veer toward telling rather than showing, particularly in explaining Midas's curse. The ending strikes the right tone - neither falsely optimistic nor gratuitously dark. The characters accept their failure with resigned humor, which feels earned given their personalities and circumstances. The circular structure, ending where it began with planning the next doomed mission, provides satisfying closure while suggesting the endless cycle of their existence. The dialogue generally works well, though Midas's lines occasionally feel slightly flat compared to Chewy's memorable malfunctions. The piece maintains coherence throughout and delivers genuine laughs while creating characters the reader cares about despite their absurd circumstances. + Romance: Love in the Limelight — Score: 78.8
Prompt:
Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write one scene within a larger story set in Wales. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. The scene takes us through the characters meeting in this odd circumstance. Over the course of the scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. Write the actor as somewhat of a rogue with a fragile ego, which needs to be fed by having everyone like him. He is thoroughly charming, but the bookstore owner seems (at least superficially) immune to this; which paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive. The bookstore owner, despite the superficial rebuffs of the actor's charm, is inwardly more than a little charmed and flustered despite themselves. Write primarily in dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The bell over the door of Vaughan's Books in Hay-on-Wye did not so much ring as panic. Elin Vaughan looked up from the counter. A man had come in backwards, at speed, in wet sunglasses, and was now pressed flat against the door as if holding back a siege. Outside, in the rain on Castle Street, three men with cameras were doing the same to her window. "Don't mind me," the man said, flashing a smile that had clearly worked on continents. "Just a normal customer. Browsing. Invisibly." "Right," Elin said. "We do a lot of invisible browsing on Tuesdays." "Perfect. I love Tuesdays. And bookshops. Especially this one. It's — what's the word — atmospheric." "It's damp." "Atmospheric damp. Very Welsh. Very..." He lowered the sunglasses. "You don't know who I am, do you?" Elin stacked a pile of paperbacks with more force than necessary. She knew exactly who he was. Kit Avery. Thirty-six. Star of *The Last Prince*, *London in Flames*, and a aftershave advert involving a horse that every woman in her book club had discussed at length. She had seen *The Last Prince* three times. Once, admittedly, because of the flu. "Should I?" she said. His smile faltered, just a fraction. "No! God, no. Lovely. Refreshing. I adore being anonymous. It's why I came to Hay. For the anonymity. And the books." "And the three photographers?" "Fans of literature. Ruthless ones." "They're fogging my window." "I'll pay for the fog." "That's very generous. Are you actually going to buy a book, Mr Anonymous?" "Kit," he said quickly. "Kit Avery. Since we're... I mean, not that it matters." "It doesn't, bach." "Bach," he repeated, delighted. "See, that's charming. Nobody calls me bach in London. They call me 'talent' and feed me tiny sandwiches." "Poor you." "I know. Tragic. I should write a memoir." He wandered, dripping, toward Biography, picked up the first book he saw and held it upside down. "So. What do you recommend for a man hiding from the press, mildly wet, universally beloved —" "Universally?" "— broadly beloved, then. Regionally beloved. Beloved in this room, potentially, if given a chance?" Elin felt her ears go hot and hated them for it. "Try Crime. Back corner. Very secluded. People have hidden from spouses in there for hours." "Are you trying to get rid of me, Elin?" She stopped. "How do you know my name?" "It's on the sign above the door, on your apron, and on that certificate for Best Independent Bookseller, Powys, 2022. I'm observant. It's an actor thing. Also a stalker thing, but let's go with actor." "Let's go with you dripping on Dylan Thomas." He looked down. "Oh, Christ. Sorry. Sorry, Dylan." He stepped sideways and knocked a display of bookmarks clean off the table. "I meant to do that. Casual. Humanising. The public love it when I'm clumsy." "Do they?" "They used to." He crouched to pick them up, suddenly less performed. "Sorry. Genuinely. I'm making a mess of your shop." "You are a bit." "Only a bit? Earlier I was tragic and universally beloved. I'm losing you, aren't I?" "You never had me, Mr Avery." "Kit." "Mr Avery." He grinned then — a different grin, unpractised, pleased despite himself. "Wow. Okay. This is new." "What is?" "Working for it." He stood, bookmarks in both hands like an offering. "Usually people ask for a selfie and tell me their cousin went to school with me in Cardiff. You haven't asked me anything." "I asked if you were going to buy a book." "Brutal. Fair, but brutal." His eyes drifted past her to the back table, and the grin vanished into real interest. "Is that a binding press?" Elin blinked. "Yes." "And you're — is that *The Mabinogion*? You're rebacking it?" "It's a 1912 Everyman. Spine's gone. Lady from Cusop found it in her father's attic." "Can I—" He was already there, sleeves pushed up, careful in a way she hadn't expected. "You've sewn new tapes. Japanese tissue on the joints?" Now she was staring. "How do you know that?" "I played a bookbinder. *The Binder's Daughter*, 2019. Filmed in Monmouth. Three months with a wonderful woman called Priya who told me I had pianist's fingers and the patience of a spaniel." "It flopped, that film." "It absolutely flopped. Devastating reviews. My ego still writes me letters about it." He touched the edge of the cloth, reverent. "But I kept it up. Binding. At home. I've got a press in my flat in London that my cleaner thinks is for paninis. I restore things. Badly, mostly. Maps, mainly. Old Ordnance Survey maps of Wales that people have folded wrong for fifty years. I flatten them, mend the tears. It's the only time my head shuts up." Elin became very aware of her hands. She put them on the book, took them off, put them in her apron pocket where they immediately found a pencil, a receipt, and no dignity whatsoever. "I do maps too," she said, before she could make it sound cooler. "Found in books, mostly. People leave things in books. Train tickets, pressed flowers, love letters, once a very angry note about a borrowed lawnmower. I keep them. In that box. I mend the books and I — this is pathetic — I try to guess who left what." "That's not pathetic. That's the whole point." "Of what?" "Of books. Other people's fingerprints." He looked up. "Sorry. That sounded like a line. It wasn't a line. I actually meant it, which is inconvenient, because now I don't know what to say next and normally I always know what to say next." "Try nothing. It's underrated." "Is it working?" "What?" "Nothing. Me, saying nothing, holding your bookmarks, dripping less than I was." Outside, miraculously, the photographers had drifted away toward the castle, distracted by someone getting out of a Range Rover. The street was clear. The rain had thinned to that fine Welsh mist that wasn't quite weather, just atmosphere with opinions. Elin saw it at the same time he did. "You're free to go," she said. "Am I?" "Door's there. Paparazzi's gone. Anonymity restored." He didn't move. "What if I wanted to stay and be told off a bit more? I could buy that Dylan Thomas I baptised. And you could tell me I'm holding this book wrong too." He picked up *Under Milk Wood*, correctly this time. "And maybe — if you're not busy guessing about lawnmowers — you could show me how you got that tissue so neat. Mine always bubbles. Like pastry." "You bind like pastry and act like—" She stopped. "Go on." "No." "Please. My fragile ego. It needs feeding, remember? Everyone has to like me or I perish dramatically, probably in Biography." Despite herself — despite three-times-seeing-*The-Last-Prince* and the hot ears and the hands that would not behave — Elin laughed. Out loud. In her own shop. "There it is," Kit said softly, as if he'd won something he hadn't expected to want. "Knew I'd get you eventually." "You haven't got me." "No," he said, and put the book down very gently, and stayed exactly where he was. "But I'm not leaving yet, either." "Tea, then," she said, far too quickly. "Kettle's on. Only because you're wet. And because if you bubble Japanese tissue, someone has to intervene." "Elin Vaughan," he said, following her to the counter with the bookmarks still in his hands, "that is the nicest thing anyone has said to me all year." "That's very sad, Kit Avery." "I know," he said. "Stay tragic with me a minute."

[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and adherence to the prompt requirements. The author successfully creates a meet-cute scenario in a Welsh bookstore with well-defined character archetypes - the charming but insecure actor and the seemingly immune but inwardly affected bookstore owner. The Welsh setting is authentically rendered through specific details like Hay-on-Wye, Castle Street, and natural use of "bach." The dialogue carries the scene effectively, with distinct voices for each character. Kit's performative charm gradually giving way to genuine vulnerability is well-executed, particularly in moments like his knowledge of bookbinding and his admission about restoring maps. Elin's resistance coupled with her internal attraction creates appropriate romantic tension. The author skillfully shows her growing interest through physical reactions (hot ears, fidgeting hands) rather than stating it directly. The pacing builds naturally from Kit's dramatic entrance to the quieter, more intimate moments over the bookbinding discussion. The chemistry develops organically through shared interests rather than forced attraction. The ending strikes an appropriate note - suggestive of possibility without rushing into romance. However, some elements feel slightly calculated. Kit's convenient expertise in bookbinding, while serving the plot, stretches credibility somewhat. Certain phrases like "smiled that had clearly worked on continents" border on trying too hard for cleverness. The piece occasionally indulges in overly precious observations that call attention to the writing itself. The emotional complexity is present but not deeply explored - we see the surface of Kit's fragile ego and Elin's conflicted attraction, but don't delve into the psychological depths that would elevate this from competent to exceptional. The transformation from mutual wariness to tentative connection, while believable, happens somewhat predictably. The prose is generally elegant with good rhythm and flow, though it sometimes prioritizes wit over naturalism. The author demonstrates strong control over tone and maintains consistency throughout.
