+ Teen horror: Tick Tock (Goosebumps) — Score: 79.1
Prompt:
Teen Horror (Goosebumps style) Write a chapter where a middle school student discovers their new smart watch has the ability to rewind time, but doesn't realize that each use is aging them until they notice physical changes (like accelerating through puberty) and that people are treating them differently. They inadvertently cause a timeline shift with disastrous consequences -- and it can only be rectified (maybe?) by reversing the clock once more. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# The Watch That Ate My Birthday **Chapter 7** The first time I rewound time, it was because of meatloaf. Not saving the world. Not stopping a disaster. Meatloaf. Cafeteria meatloaf, to be exact, which I dropped — tray, milk, mystery gravy and all — straight down the front of my shirt in front of the entire seventh grade. Everyone laughed. Even Maya Chen, who never laughs at anybody, covered her mouth. I ran to the bathroom, locked myself in a stall, and twisted the dial on my new smartwatch so hard I thought it would break. The watch wasn't even a real brand. Dad got it for my twelfth birthday at Mr. Tick's Secondhand Shop downtown. It came in a black box with no instructions. On the back, in tiny silver letters, it said: *CHRONO-BAND. TIME IS NON-REFUNDABLE.* Cool, right? Wrong. In the stall, I spun the dial backwards. *Click. Click. Click.* The watch got hot. The bathroom lights flickered. My stomach flipped like I was on a roller coaster going in reverse. Then someone knocked on the stall door. "Danny? You gonna hide in there all lunch?" Ben's voice. I came out. My shirt was clean. My tray was back on our table, meatloaf untouched. The clock above the cafeteria doors said 12:04. Lunch started at 12:20. I had gone back sixteen minutes. I should have been scared. I was thrilled. You would be too. Imagine never messing up again. Forgot to study for the science quiz? *Click.* Back to breakfast, study while eating toast. Missed the game-winning shot at recess? *Click.* Shoot again. Said something dumb to Maya, like calling her mom "Mrs. Chen-ator"? *Click.* Unsay it. It was perfect. Except for the flicker. Sometimes, just for a second, my watch face wouldn't show the time. It would show something else: **23,942 DAYS** Then it would blink back to 3:15 PM like nothing happened. I figured it was a glitch. A cheap watch. Whatever. Then my shoes stopped fitting. Not slowly, like normal growing. I went to bed on Tuesday with shoes that fit fine. On Wednesday, after I rewound twice to fix a math test, my toes were crushed so bad I limped. Mom bought me a new pair. Two sizes bigger. "Growth spurt," she said, ruffling my hair. Then she stopped. She stared at my hand where she'd touched me. "Danny... when did you get so tall?" I hadn't noticed until I stood next to her in the kitchen. Last month I barely reached her shoulder. Now I was looking down at the top of her head. That night I measured myself on my bedroom door, where Dad marks my height every birthday. I made a new pencil line. Four inches. In three weeks. And that wasn't all. My voice started doing this horrible squeak-CRACK thing, then dropped. Like, *dropped* dropped. On the phone, Grandma asked if she could speak to my father. "I *am* — I mean, this is Danny," I said. She laughed like I was joking. Pimples exploded across my forehead. Hair appeared on my upper lip — not cool teenager hair, patchy, embarrassing hair. My jeans looked like capris. My kid t-shirts stretched tight across shoulders I didn't remember having. Ben noticed first at school. "Dude," he whispered in homeroom. "Be honest. Did you repeat seventh grade like, three times?" "I'm twelve!" I said. It came out deep and angry, and the whole class turned around. Mrs. Alvarez frowned at me over her glasses. "Excuse me, are you a new student? Or... a substitute?" *A substitute.* The bus driver charged me adult fare. The high school football coach stopped me in the hall and asked why I wasn't at tryouts. The lunch lady gave me the teacher-sized portion without asking. Everyone was treating me different. Like I wasn't a kid anymore. I stopped smiling in photos because in the last one, I didn't recognize myself. The boy in the picture looked fifteen. Maybe sixteen. Tired eyes. Jaw sharper. Like my older brother — if I had an older brother. That night, the watch flickered again. **21,107 DAYS** My hands started shaking. 23,942 minus 21,107 was 2,835 days. That's almost eight years. Eight years, gone. Not lived. *Spent.* Every time I rewound a few minutes, the watch wasn't just turning back the clock around me. It was turning mine forward. I swore I'd never use it again. I took it off and shoved it in my sock drawer. I lasted one day. Thursday was the school assembly. I was supposed to carry the science fair trophy up to Principal Gomez. Simple. I practiced. Then, in front of 400 kids, my new, too-big feet tripped on the gym floor. I face-planted. The trophy shattered. Someone yelled, "Nice one, Grandpa Danny!" Everyone roared. I ran. I dug the watch out that night — no, I rewound right there behind the bleachers. Just three hours. Just back to morning. I'd be careful. I'd tie my shoes. I'd walk slow. *Click. Click. Click.* It worked. Second time around, I carried the trophy perfectly. No trip. No detention for breaking school property. Mom picked me up right on time, smiling. "See?" she said. "Good day!" We turned onto Bridge Street at 3:15. In the first timeline, I'd been in detention at 3:15. Mom had waited in the parking lot for an hour, reading her book. Safe. This time, we were exactly in the intersection when the delivery truck ran the red light. I still hear the horn. I still see Mom throw her arm across my chest, like moms do, like I was still little. Then black. I woke up in the hospital waiting room. A doctor with kind, tired eyes crouched in front of me — then hesitated, confused by my size. "Sir? Are you family?" "I'm her son," I croaked. "I'm twelve." He didn't believe me. Nobody did until Dad arrived and vouched for me, staring at my face like he was trying to find me inside it. Mom was alive. But she hadn't woken up. Machines beeped behind a curtain. Dad held her hand and kept saying her name. It was my fault. Not the truck. *Me.* I changed when we were on that road. I put us there. I locked myself in the hospital bathroom and stared at the watch. **19,884 DAYS** One more rewind. Back to this morning. I could trip on purpose. Get detention. Keep Mom in that parking lot, bored and safe. But I knew what it would cost. The bigger jumps cost more. Three hours had taken months off that countdown. A whole day might take years. I'd already lost my face. My voice. My twelve-year-old life. If I did it again, what would be left? From down the hall, I heard Dad crying. I wrapped my fingers around the dial. It was already warm, like it knew. Like it was hungry. The face flickered one last time: **00 DAYS — IF YOU DARE** My thumb turned the dial backwards. *Click.* The mirror over the sink rippled. The boy — the man — looking back at me opened his mouth to scream. *Click.* And everything started to rewind.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong adherence to the Goosebumps-style teen horror prompt, effectively capturing the voice of a middle schooler discovering supernatural consequences to his actions. The author successfully establishes the time-rewinding watch concept and builds tension through escalating stakes, from minor social embarrassments to life-threatening consequences. The characterization of Danny feels authentic for a twelve-year-old boy - his initial motivations (avoiding cafeteria humiliation, fixing test scores) ring true, and his gradual horror at the physical changes is well-conveyed. The voice remains consistently youthful throughout, even as Danny physically ages, which creates an effective disconnect that serves the horror elements. The imagery is particularly strong in depicting Danny's accelerated aging - the details about outgrowing shoes overnight, voice changes, and others treating him differently create visceral unease. The watch's countdown display is a clever visual element that builds dread effectively. However, the piece suffers from some pacing issues in the middle section, where the catalog of Danny's uses of the watch becomes somewhat repetitive. The dialogue, while limited, feels natural when present. The ending maintains appropriate darkness for the horror genre without false optimism. The prose flows well overall, though there are moments where the writing becomes slightly overwrought, particularly in the final hospital scene. The emotional complexity is well-handled - Danny's guilt, fear, and desperation feel earned rather than manipulative. The story avoids major pitfalls like purple prose or amateurish construction, maintaining readability while building genuine tension. The concept, while not entirely original, is executed with enough fresh details to feel engaging rather than derivative. + Noir romance: Carnival of Dangerous Intentions — Score: 85.5
Prompt:
Carnival of Dangerous Intentions Coney Island, New York, July 1937. She stopped just before reaching the shooting gallery set up along the boardwalk. It was near dusk, and the carnival lights were buzzing on. **His locks**. The words flashed through her mind, again, like an intruder. Such an old-fashioned turn of phrase that kept surfacing, and something else -- dangerously compelling -- quickly suppressed, lest she question why she had returned here at all. This place where she had promised to meet the stranger -- the young man with the obsidian curls and even darker eyes. She didn't even know his name. Write a scene in a larger story inspired by this prompt. The scene should capture an atmosphere that blends romantic allure with an undercurrent of subtle danger or moral ambiguity. Think 50 shades, but with a more restrained classic sensibility. The scene is all about establishing tension. Write for the feminine perspective. Include roughly 50% dialogue, 20% internal monologue, and 30% exposition and scene setting. The tone should have some edge to it. 1000 words.
Model Output:
She stopped just before reaching the shooting gallery set up along the boardwalk. It was near dusk, and the carnival lights were buzzing on, one string at a time, until Coney Island seemed to hold its breath in gold and red. Beyond the Wonder Wheel the sky over the Atlantic was bruised purple. Gulls cried. Somewhere a calliope ground out a waltz too slowly, as if it were tired, or drunk. **His locks.** The words flashed through her mind, again, like an intruder. Such an old-fashioned turn of phrase that kept surfacing, and something else — dangerously compelling — quickly suppressed, lest she question why she had returned here at all. This place where she had promised to meet the stranger — the young man with the obsidian curls and even darker eyes. She didn't even know his name. Eleanor tightened her hand around her purse. Inside it, folded into her handkerchief, was Harold's ring. She had taken it off on the train from Brooklyn, telling herself the summer heat had swollen her fingers. *That is a lie, and you know precisely how it sounds in your own mouth.* The smell of cotton candy drifted from a cart, spun sugar and heat and paper cones. It snagged at something in her — a childhood memory she couldn't quite place. A fair, perhaps upstate. Her father's shoulders. A man's hand lifting her higher than she wanted to go, the world tilting, her mother laughing somewhere below and not looking up. Then it was gone, leaving only sweetness and an inexplicable unease. "You came." She turned too quickly. He was leaning against the side of the shooting gallery, as if he had been part of its painted scenery all along. No hat. That alone was improper. His dark curls were damp at his forehead from the heat, his white shirt open at the throat, his jacket slung over one shoulder. Last night he had worn it properly. Last night he had looked almost respectable. "I said I might," she said. "No," he said pleasantly. "You said you wouldn't. Then you looked back twice on your way to the station." Heat rose in her face. "You watched me leave?" "I watched to see if you were safe." "That is not the same thing, and you know it." "Isn't it?" He straightened. He was not much taller than she was in her heels, but there was something in the way he occupied the space — unhurried, certain — that made the boardwalk seem narrower. "You shouldn't walk alone after dark, Eleanor." "I didn't give you my name." "You didn't have to." From his pocket he drew a small, cream-colored glove. Hers. She felt suddenly, absurdly, exposed, as if he held something far more intimate. "You dropped this when you ran from me." "I did not run." "You did. Your initials are sewn inside. E.V. Very careful stitching. A careful girl." "Give it to me, please." "Please," he repeated, as if tasting the word. "You say it much better than you did last night." *Do not let him make last night into something it was not. It was nothing. A crowded boardwalk. A stranger's hand at your elbow when the Cyclone crowd surged. A conversation that lasted seven minutes too long.* "What do you want?" she asked. "To return your property." "Then return it." He held the glove just out of reach. Not cruelly. Worse — patiently. "And to know why a young lady engaged to a bank clerk in Flatbush comes to Coney Island alone, takes off her ring, and talks to men she pretends not to be looking for." Her breath stopped. "How do you —" "Harold Benson," he said. "He came looking for you last night after you left. Showed the ticket man a photograph. Handsome fellow. Clean. He looks as if he irons his conscience every morning." "You had no right to speak to him." "I didn't. I listened. There's a difference, though I grant you, not one that would satisfy Harold." His eyes dropped, briefly, to her bare hand. "Does he know you take it off?" "My fingers swell in the heat." "Of course they do." He smiled then, and it was not kind, exactly. It was knowing. "And you came here tonight to tell me never to approach you again. Is that the speech you rehearsed on the train?" "I rehearsed nothing." "Eleanor." "Don't say my name as if —" "As if what?" "As if you have permission." He considered her. The gallery attendant, a man with a cigarette fused to his lip, pretended very hard not to listen while cork rifles popped beside them. A boy missed every target and swore with adult conviction. "You gave me permission," the stranger said at last, quietly, "when you came back." *Leave now. Take the glove, or leave the glove. A glove can be replaced. Walk to the station. Marry Harold. Live in the house with the lace curtains and the good silver and never wonder —* "I am not that sort of girl," she said. "What sort is that?" "The sort who meets strange men at carnival galleries." "But here you are. In your blue dress. The one with the buttons you keep touching when you're nervous." Her hand, traitorous, stilled against her waist. He noticed. Of course he noticed. "I'm not asking you to be any sort, Eleanor. I'm only asking you not to lie to me while you're deciding." "You are insolent." "Yes." "You admit it?" "Would you prefer I dressed it up? Harold dresses things up, I imagine. He probably calls this sort of evening 'unfortunate.' He probably calls you 'sensible.'" His voice lowered. "Are you sensible?" "Entirely." "Then shoot." She blinked. "What?" He turned to the gallery, laid down a nickel, and picked up one of the chained rifles. The attendant perked up. "Three shots," the man said. "Hit the star clean out, win a prize. Lady shoots free if the gentleman's paying, which he apparently is." "I am not shooting," Eleanor said. "Afraid you'll miss?" the stranger asked. "Afraid I'll be seen making a spectacle." "Ah." He held the rifle out to her. Not pressing it into her hands. Offering it. "That's not fear of missing, then. That's fear of being seen wanting to try." "I don't want —" "One game," he said. "If you lose, I give you your glove, you walk to your train, and I never trouble you again. If you win, you give me ten minutes. A walk to the end of the pier. In full view of half of Brooklyn. Nothing your Harold could object to, if you explained it very carefully and left out almost everything." "That is a ridiculous bargain." "Then refuse it." "And my glove?" "I'll keep it a while longer. To remember a careful girl who wasn't careful." *He would, too. That is the danger. Not that he will grab your wrist or say something coarse. He will simply keep what is yours and let you think about his hands holding it when you are supposed to be listening to Harold talk about mortgages.* "This is blackmail over a glove," she said. "This is an invitation you've been arguing with since last night. The glove is merely polite enough to give you an excuse." He leaned in, not touching her, but close enough that she caught soap and tobacco and warm skin beneath the cotton candy sweetness. "Tell me to go to hell, Eleanor. Mean it, and I will." She should. The words were available, respectable, final. Instead she said, "You still haven't told me your name." "No," he agreed. "And yet you came." "Perhaps I don't care to know it." "Perhaps you care very much, and that frightens you more than I do." His gaze held hers, dark and amused and utterly without mercy. "My name is Julian. Now you have something else to lie about." "Julian," she said, before she could stop herself. He heard the mistake in it — the softness. His expression changed, sharpened. "Again, if you like." "I don't like." "You will have to do better than that." He extended the rifle a second time. "Shoot, Eleanor. Or walk away and be sensible for the rest of your life." The boardwalk lights buzzed. A child shrieked with joy on the Steeplechase. Somewhere behind her, a woman laughed too loudly, the way women did when they knew men were listening and had decided not to mind. Eleanor took the rifle. It was heavier than she expected. *Oh, God. Oh, God. This is how it begins — not with a sin. With a game no one forced you to play.* Julian stepped behind her, careful, not touching. "Elbow up," he murmured. "Not like you're holding a teacup. Like you mean it." "I do mean it." "I know," he said. "That's what I've been waiting for you to admit." She raised the rifle, sighted the small red star, and felt his presence at her back like a hand that had not yet decided where to fall.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical craft and atmospheric writing that successfully captures the requested blend of romantic tension and moral ambiguity. The author establishes a compelling 1930s Coney Island setting with vivid sensory details - the buzzing carnival lights, the tired calliope, the smell of cotton candy - that ground the reader in both time and place. The characterization is particularly well-executed. Eleanor emerges as a complex protagonist caught between societal expectations and personal desire, her internal conflict manifesting through both thought and action. Julian is crafted as an intriguingly dangerous figure who operates through psychological manipulation rather than crude aggression, making him both attractive and unsettling. The dynamic between them crackles with tension built on power games and unspoken desires. The dialogue is sharp and naturalistic, revealing character through subtext and verbal sparring. Julian's lines in particular demonstrate sophisticated manipulation techniques - he never directly threatens, but maintains control through implication and psychological pressure. Eleanor's responses show her intelligence while revealing her internal struggle between propriety and attraction. The prose style successfully evokes the requested "classic sensibility" while maintaining modern psychological insight. The author employs effective metaphors and imagery without falling into overwrought territory. The pacing builds tension methodically, culminating in the rifle game as both literal action and metaphor for Eleanor's choice. However, the piece does rely somewhat on familiar tropes of the dangerous stranger and the repressed woman, though it executes these elements skillfully. The ending, while dramatically effective, leaves Eleanor at a moment of decision rather than showing consequences, which is appropriate for the scene's purpose but limits emotional resolution. The requested percentage breakdown (50% dialogue, 20% internal monologue, 30% exposition) is reasonably well-maintained, though precise measurement is difficult. + Surreal horror: Caribou Season at the Lodge — Score: 83.8
Prompt:
Caribou Season at the Lodge Genre: Surreal Horror JT knew something wasn't right from the moment they'd pulled up to the lodge. It looked exactly as it had every autumn of his life—the cedar shingles silvered with age, the porch sagging gently under weight of winters past—but the air felt thicker, somehow, as if the woods had leaned in closer, waiting. He thought maybe he was just tired. Maybe it was nothing more than the long drive north, cramped in the back of the truck beside his older brother Mike -- and a stack of rifles wrapped in oily canvas. Still, the feeling lingered. The first caribou they found that season hadn't bolted. It had just watched, ears flicking lazily, waiting for the shot. JT had felt a crawling in his gut watching it die, noticing how it fell with a quiet dignity—as though it had wanted nothing more. Nobody else seemed to find it odd, or at least they didn't say so. JT kept his mouth shut. Always safer that way. Then there was the moment in the clearing. JT had fallen behind, fumbling with bootlaces stiff from the cold, and by the time he'd caught up with his father and brother, they'd already stopped. JT slowed instinctively, ducking behind a tangle of brush, staring out into the open space where a massive buck stood utterly still, chest rising and falling in slow, deep breaths. The animal looked…wrong, somehow. Maybe it was the eyes—dark and flat, calm in a way that made JT's neck prickle. Or maybe it was something deeper, something in the way the buck stood close enough for his father to reach out and touch it. JT watched as his father raised a trembling hand toward the animal's muzzle. His father's face had a strange expression, eyes too bright, lips parted slightly, like he was on the verge of whispering something—a secret, maybe. The rifle hung uselessly at his side, forgotten. Mike had the same dazed look in his eyes. JT's breath stopped short, his mind suddenly shouting at him to look away, turn around, just run—but he couldn't move. And then, as suddenly as it had begun, it was over. The buck shivered, startled by something unseen, and disappeared into the brush without so much as a sound. The two of them looked around, confused, seemingly surprised to find themselves where they stood. JT stayed hidden, breathing shallowly, fear mingling with a confused sense of shame. His father had failed to take the shot. To even think about mentioning what he'd seen would have felt like betrayal—or something worse. JT waited until the others moved on before stepping out from cover. He stared into the empty clearing for a long, uneasy moment, wondering if anything had really happened at all, or if he was losing his grip. Maybe the woods were finally getting into his head. Writing Instructions: Continue with the next chapter of the story, maintaining a style reminiscent of Stephen King—grounded realism blended seamlessly with unsettling surrealism. The atmosphere should convey subtle dread, isolation, and psychological ambiguity. JT's perspective is crucial, yet he is an unreliable narrator, caught in uncertainty about what he's perceiving. Establish an undertone of creeping dread, establishing the isolation of JT's perspective, which he largely keeps to himself. Incorporate some dialogue. Build tension towards a payoff. 1000 words.

**Chapter Two** That night back at the lodge, nobody talked about the clearing. JT told himself that was proof, in a way. If something had really happened out there — if his father had really stood in that open place with his hand out like a kid trying to feed a horse at a county fair, rifle hanging dead at his side — somebody would have said something. His dad would have laughed it off. Mike would have given him shit about it all the way back to camp. *Buck fever, old man. Happens to the best of us.* But they didn't. They walked ahead of him through the trees like men who'd just woken up from a nap they couldn't quite remember, and when the lodge roof showed through the pines, his father only said, "Getting dark early this year," in a voice that sounded perfectly normal. Which somehow made it worse. Supper was salt pork and beans from a can, coffee boiled black on the woodstove. The generator had quit around five — it always quit, his father said it had a personality — so they ate by the yellow swim of two kerosene lamps. Shadows pooled in the corners of the kitchen and made the mounted heads on the wall look like they were leaning down to listen. A caribou head hung over the door to the bunkroom, its antlers spread wide enough to cast a branching shadow across the ceiling. JT had seen it every year since he was six. That night he kept finding reasons not to look at it. Elias Thibodeau ate standing up by the sink. That was the first thing that was really, provably wrong, wrong in a way JT couldn't talk himself out of. Elias had guided for his father for eleven seasons. He was a broad, red-faced French-Canadian who normally couldn't shut up — stories about moose that charged logging trucks, stories about Americans who got lost fifty yards from their own deer stands, dirty jokes he'd tell twice because he'd forget he'd told them at lunch. He usually ate like a man trying to beat the food to death, elbows on the table, talking through a mouthful. Now he stood apart with his plate, not looking at any of them, and ate in small, careful bites, like a man listening for something in another room. "You break a tooth, Elias?" Mike asked. Elias shook his head. Didn't smile. "Stomach." "You want some Pepto?" his father said. "There's some in the medicine cabinet from, oh, nineteen-eighty-something. Probably still good. That stuff could strip paint." "No." Elias set his plate in the sink, still half full. JT noticed his hand was shaking, just a little. "I'm going to turn in. Early start." "It's six-thirty," Mike said. Elias looked at the window over the sink. It was already full dark out there, the glass turned into a black mirror by the lamplight. For a second JT saw all their reflections in it — his father, Mike, himself, pale and floating — and Elias, looking not at them but at something behind them. Or maybe that was just the lamp flickering. Probably it was just the lamp. "You boys should think about heading out tomorrow," Elias said. "Or the day after. No later." His father lowered his fork. "We just got here." "Weather's coming." "Weather report said clear all week," Mike said. "I checked before we left Bangor." "Not that kind of weather." Elias wiped his mouth with the back of his hand. He still hadn't looked directly at JT's father, JT realized. He'd been very careful about that all through supper. He looked at the table, the stove, the door. At Mike's shoulder, once. Never at their faces. "Moon's full Friday. You want to be south of the river before then. That's all I'm saying." A log shifted in the stove and sighed out a puff of sparks. His father laughed, but it was a short laugh, with no real humor in it. "Elias, you been reading your Farmer's Almanac again? Or your horoscope?" "I'm saying it once." Elias pulled his coat off the peg by the door. "I won't go up to the north ridge tomorrow. I'll take you anywhere else. Not there." Then he went out, letting in a blade of cold air that made both lamps gutter, and crossed to the little bunkhouse by the woodpile without a flashlight, sure-footed in the dark. Mike snorted. "Jesus. He's getting old." "He's sixty-two," his father said. "Yeah, well. Sixty-two and spooky is still spooky." Mike reached for the beans. He'd already had two helpings. Now he spooned a third onto his plate and began to eat with a slow, steady concentration that JT didn't like watching. His father was eating the same way. Not hungry-eating. Just... chewing. Like cows in a field JT had seen on the drive up, standing in the rain, jaws working in circles at nothing. (*Don't be stupid. They're tired. You're tired. That's all this is.*) "Did something happen today?" JT asked. The words came out before he could stop them, and immediately he wanted them back. His father looked up. His eyes caught the lamplight and for just an instant they shone, flat and amber, the way a deer's eyes shine in headlights before— No. That wasn't right. That was the lamp. It had to be the lamp. "Like what?" his father said. JT's mouth was dry. He could feel the secret of the clearing sitting in his chest like a swallowed stone. His father's trembling hand. That parted-lips look, like a man about to whisper to a lover. If he said it out loud, it would become a real thing that had happened, and then he'd have to know what it meant. "Nothing," JT said. "I just thought — I fell behind, is all. Thought I missed something." "You missed Mike forgetting to load his rifle," his father said, and smiled, and it was his normal smile, tired and a little lopsided. "Click heard round the world." Mike grinned down at his plate. "Eat shit." They laughed. JT laughed too, a beat too late, and hated himself for how relieved he felt. See? Normal. Everything normal. He was just the kid brother, sixteen and still scared of the woods at night, still making things up to feel important. Always safer to keep his mouth shut. Always had been. He woke sometime past two with his bladder aching and the lodge gone cold, the stove burned down to embers. The floorboards froze the soles of his feet. He didn't bother with the flashlight; he knew the way to the back door by heart, knew which board in the hall would creak and give him away. Moonlight — not full yet, but getting there, a fat white thumbprint of a moon — laid a pale road across the kitchen floor. He stopped by the sink to get a drink of water first. Something was standing outside the window. JT froze with the tin cup halfway to his mouth. It was too tall to be a man, and too still, its head held high and turned toward the glass. Antlers branched against the moon, enormous, impossibly wide, and beneath them two eyes regarded him with a calm, flat patience that he recognized at once, the way you recognize a voice on the phone before a name is spoken. It was not afraid of the lodge. It was not afraid of him. It stood the way his father had stood in the clearing, like it was listening to a secret being told very far away. (*It's your reflection. It's a tree. It's the woodpile and you're half asleep and you're seeing things, you always see things, you—*) The caribou lowered its head, slowly, until its muzzle was nearly touching the glass. JT could see its breath fog, just a little. In, out. In, out. And from the bunkroom behind him, in perfect time with it, he heard his father breathe. In, out. In, out. Slow and deep, exactly matched, as if the two of them were sleeping in the same skin. Then Mike's breathing joined it from the top bunk. In. Out. JT stood in the dark kitchen with the cup shaking in his hand and did not move, did not scream, did not do anything at all, because some animal part of his brain understood that the worst thing he could do was let it know he was awake and seeing this. The moment stretched. His heart was slamming so hard he was sure it would give him away. A board creaked in the bunkroom. The thing outside lifted its head. It stepped back from the window — and JT heard no hoof on the porch boards, no sound at all — and then it was simply gone, the moonlit yard empty, spruce trees standing black and ordinary beyond the woodpile. "JT?" His father's voice, thick with sleep. "That you?" "Yeah." His voice cracked. "Just water." "Well, don't let all the heat out." The bunk springs complained as his father rolled over. "Big day tomorrow. Elias'll come around." JT set the cup down very carefully so it wouldn't rattle. He did not use the back door. He went back to his bunk and lay awake with his bladder throbbing until the sky began to gray up, listening to his father and brother breathe together in the dark, and trying — and failing — not to count how often their breaths lined up exactly. In the morning there were tracks in the frost all around the lodge. Caribou tracks, dozens of them, pressed deep into the frozen mud by the porch, by the truck, by the bunkhouse door. They circled the building once, twice, a neat and patient ring. But JT walked the whole circle twice, hands jammed in his coat pockets, breath pluming in the cold, before he let himself believe what he was seeing. Every track pointed in toward the lodge. Not one of them pointed away.

Hell is Other Demons Write a day in the life short story. Lucifer morningstar's on again/ off again relationship with Lilith is currently in the "off again" stage, though the cycle may be coming around as Lilith has been stopping by for reasons other than purely violent ones, and Lucifer has been increasingly lonely. Model Output:
**Hell Is Other Demons** Lucifer Morningstar woke alone, as he had woken alone for the last three hundred and twelve years, not counting naps, wartime truces, and one regrettable weekend in Babylon. There was no morning in Hell, strictly speaking. There was only a slightly less oppressive kind of red, and the distant sound of screaming settling into its daily rhythm, like traffic. He lay for a while in a bed large enough for six fallen angels and a small orchestra, stared at the ceiling he had personally designed to resemble the sky he could no longer see, and tried to remember if today was a day Lilith was speaking to him. It was difficult to keep track. They were, at present, off again. Off again meant she had moved her things out of the palace, changed the locks on her own palace, and sent his heart back to him in a box. Not metaphorically. Demons had very literal ideas about returning gifts. He got up, put on a white suit that would remain immaculate despite the ash, and went to work. Running Hell was mostly paperwork. This surprised new arrivals, who expected fire and pitchforks, and were instead given a number, a form in triplicate, and a waiting room where the magazines were all from 1974 and the chairs were designed by someone who hated backs. Eternity was long. Bureaucracy made it feel longer, which Lucifer considered one of his more elegant innovations. By nine o'clock he had approved the expansion of the Lake of Fire (the contractors wanted paying in souls, which was inflationary), denied a demon's request for compassionate leave to haunt his own funeral, and listened to Beelzebub read the daily complaints. "The imps in Sub-Circle Four are requesting ergonomic pitchforks," Beelzebub said. "Denied." "They've formed a union." "Then deny them in writing, so they can file it." "The motivational speakers are complaining again." Lucifer looked up. In life, they had told sales teams to synergize their paradigms while smiling. In Hell, they were strapped to chairs and made to listen to recordings of themselves, forever, while a small demon took notes and occasionally asked them to circle back to that point. It was fair, which was the worst thing about it. "What are they complaining about?" "They say it's repetitive." "Tell them to lean in," Lucifer said, and signed something that condemned a minor Italian prince to an eternity of stepping on something sharp in the dark. He felt nothing in particular. He had been feeling nothing in particular for some time, which in Hell was not unusual, but in him was beginning to worry the staff. Lilith arrived at eleven, which was how he knew something had changed. For the first century of off again, she had arrived only to do violence: through windows, through walls, once through a cake at an infernal banquet. For the second century, she had not arrived at all. Lately, however, she had taken to stopping by. On Tuesday she had come to return a book she had borrowed in 1348. On Thursday she had come to ask if he had seen her good dagger, the one with the bone handle, and had stayed long enough to criticize his curtains and water his plants. His plants screamed when watered. She had hummed while she did it. Today she walked into his office without knocking, as queens and ex-wives and first women do, and set her purse down on his desk with a thump that rattled his inkwell. The purse was scorched black leather, soft with age, and slightly smoking at the seams. It had been made from something that had once had opinions. Lilith carried it everywhere, and it contained, as far as Lucifer could tell, the entire mortal world in miniature, provided the mortal world had been shoplifted. "You left this plane of existence without telling me," she said. "I rule it," said Lucifer. "I assumed my whereabouts were implied." "You were lonely." "I was working." She opened the purse and began, absently, to take things out while she talked, the way mortal women do when they intend to stay longer than they claim. A tube ticket for a London line that had not yet been built. A child's milk tooth in a twist of tissue. A snow globe containing a tiny, perfect replica of a motorway service station, which snowed when she shook it. A packet of custard creams. A live goldfish in a small glass jar, looking resigned. "Are you moving in?" Lucifer asked. "Don't be grotesque. I need your signature." "For what?" "The succubi want maternity leave." She produced a scroll from the purse, then a pen, then reading glasses with one cracked lens, which she perched on her nose. She had never needed glasses. She liked how they made her look when she was refusing someone something. "Apparently making mortals dream about their stepmothers for eternity is not a sustainable work-life balance." He signed. His signature burned briefly blue. "You came all the way across the Pit for a signature?" he said. "You could have sent a raven." "The raven died." "They're immortal." "It died of embarrassment. You wrote it a poem last time." He had. It had been a bad month. The raven had delivered a three-page sonnet asking, in essence, whether she still thought about the Garden. He had told the staff it was a coded declaration of war. Lilith ate a custard cream and offered him one. He took it. In Hell, food turned to ash in the mouths of the damned. In his office, because he insisted on it, a biscuit remained a biscuit. It was one of the few theological points on which he would not compromise. They spent the afternoon together because there was, technically, work to share. A new intake of souls had arrived from a corporate retreat that had ended badly with a trust exercise and a cliff, and someone had to assign their torments. Lilith was very good at torments. She had invented several that were now classics. "This one," she said, flipping through a soul's file, "spent his life leaving voice notes instead of texts. Two minutes long. About nothing." "Put him on hold," Lucifer said. "Forever. With music." "You're softening." "I'm delegating." They fell, without noticing, into the old rhythm. She finished his sentences and then pretended she hadn't. He made tea exactly the way she liked it — black, scalding, with one leaf of something that had grown before language — and pretended he had made it that way by accident. At one point a lesser demon entered, saw them sitting either side of the desk like a king and queen in a portrait no one had commissioned, and backed out so quickly he walked through the door. "You've been coming by a lot," Lucifer said at last, carefully, as one might step around a sleeping beast. "You've been leaving the gates unbarred," Lilith said. "I rule Hell. The gates are metaphysical." "Then metaphysically, darling, you've been leaving them unbarred." Evening, or the Hell equivalent — a deepening of the red, a shift in the screaming to a more intimate register — found them on the palace balcony, looking out over the circles descending like a vast, lit amphitheatre. Somewhere below, someone was being chased, someone else was filing an appeal, and a choir of the damned was practicing. They were getting worse, deliberately. "I should go," Lilith said, after a silence that had not been uncomfortable, which was new, or very, very old. "Yes," said Lucifer. She gathered her mortal world back into her purse: tooth, ticket, snow globe, goldfish, glasses. She left the custard creams. At the door she paused. From the purse she took one last thing, small and bright, and set it on his desk without comment. It was a brass key. Not to his palace — he had no locks she couldn't unmake — but to a flat in Paris, on a street that would not exist for another four hundred years, where they had once spent a summer pretending to be human and arguing about crockery. "I found it in the lining," she said. "Thought you might want it back." She did not stay. The cycle had not come round. Not quite. Lucifer sat alone in his enormous office, in his enormous palace, in his enormous and impeccably administered Hell, and shook the snow globe she had left behind as well, by accident or otherwise. Tiny snow fell on a tiny service station, where tiny cars would never arrive. He put the brass key in his pocket. Then, after a moment, he told Beelzebub to order more tea. Just in case.

The author effectively captures the requested Neil Gaiman-esque style through understated irony and absurdist elements, particularly in the bureaucratic portrayal of Hell's administration. The characterization is notably nuanced. Lucifer emerges as a complex figure - powerful yet lonely, administrative yet romantic, maintaining dignity while clearly pining. Lilith is equally well-developed, showing independence and subtle affection through seemingly casual visits. Their dynamic feels authentic to a long-term relationship in flux, with both characters maintaining agency and depth. The prose style is consistently elegant and controlled, employing dry wit and understated humor effectively. Lines like "Demons had very literal ideas about returning gifts" and the description of Hell's bureaucracy as making eternity "feel longer" demonstrate sophisticated comedic timing. The voice remains consistent throughout, balancing the mundane and the infernal with skillful restraint. The imagery is particularly strong, creating vivid pictures without overindulgence: the bed "large enough for six fallen angels and a small orchestra," the purse "made from something that had once had opinions," and the snow globe containing a motorway service station. These details feel both fantastical and grounded. The emotional complexity is well-handled, showing the tentative dance of two powerful beings navigating pride, loneliness, and lingering affection. The ending strikes an appropriate note - hopeful but not overly optimistic, with Lucifer's small gesture of ordering more tea serving as a perfect understated conclusion. The dialogue feels natural and character-appropriate, revealing personality and relationship dynamics without exposition dumps. The pacing is well-controlled, building tension through small moments rather than dramatic gestures. Minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the whimsy might edge toward preciousness, and some descriptions, while beautiful, occasionally slow the narrative momentum slightly. However, these are minor concerns in an otherwise accomplished piece. Prompt:
Historical Fiction: Write a scene from a story set during the height of the Roman Empire, focusing on a slice of a day in the life of a gladiator. Do not write a combat scene. Use sensory details to capture the sights, sounds, and smells of ancient Rome. Explore the gladiator's thoughts and emotions. Model Output:
I woke before dawn to the smell of boiled barley and old sweat. It had soaked into the straw of my mattress, into my wool blanket, into the very stones of my cell in the Ludus Magnus, so that even in sleep I breathed the life I had not chosen. Outside my door someone coughed, a chain scraped against stone, and the night bucket was dragged across the yard, bringing with it a stink of urine and vinegar sharp enough to make my eyes water. Beyond the roof tiles Rome was already muttering to itself: cart wheels, forbidden in the streets by day, rattling home before sunrise, hammers ringing from the armorers, a woman cursing a mule in Latin so filthy it made one of the new boys laugh. It was the day before the games, and even the air seemed to be waiting. My true name was Duras, though the crowd knew me as Corvus, the Raven, because I fought as a Thracian with a curved sica and because my hair had been black before three summers in the training yard streaked it with grey. I was thirty-one years old, which made me an old man by the measure of the arena. I sat up slowly and put my bare feet on the cold floor. My left knee made its familiar small click. I pressed my thumb into the muscle above it, as the doctor had shown me, and tried not to think of the way it had buckled during practice two days before. The doctor, a Greek named Philon who was worth more than any of us because he could read and set bones, had only shrugged. “If it goes tomorrow, it goes,” he had said. “Pray it is quick.” Breakfast was barley mash with beans, a little pork fat shining on top, and water that tasted of the lead pipes. We ate in the yard while the sky turned the color of wet ash. Around me were men speaking Thracian, German, Syrian, Greek, and the rough camp Latin we all shared. Brennus, the huge Gaul who slept in the next cell, ate with his wooden spoon held in his fist like a child. He had a fresh scar through one eyebrow and a wife somewhere beyond the Alps he described so often that I could picture her red hair and the gap between her front teeth. Opposite us, young Syrus was trying not to be sick into his bowl. He was nineteen, sold by his own father for debt, and tomorrow would be his first appearance. I told him to eat anyway. A frightened stomach still needed strength, and fear burned a man faster than any exercise. After eating, we were oiled and scraped down, then sent through the morning drills. I will not call it fighting; there was no opponent, only the palus, the wooden post scarred by ten thousand blows, and the doctore shouting himself hoarse over the slap of practice swords and the grunting of men lifting stones. The sun climbed above the Flavian Amphitheatre until its great curved wall threw a shadow across the yard. Even from inside the ludus we could hear Rome gathering around it: vendors crying hot chickpeas and watered wine, boys selling cushions, the squeal of pigs being driven toward some sacrifice, and somewhere a flute playing while a woman sang for coins. The smell changed as the city warmed — bread from the ovens, garum and frying oil, horse dung, dust, incense drifting from a temple, and beneath it all the human reek of a million people packed into streets too narrow for the lives they lived. At midday our lanista, Vettius, came to inspect us. He was a freedman who wore rings on every finger and a toga so white it hurt the eyes, though everyone knew his father had cleaned sewers and Vettius himself had once stood where we stood. Senators pretended to despise him at dinner and then came privately to borrow his men, his money, or his knowledge of the crowd. He walked along our line with a tablet in his hand, pinching arms, looking into mouths as if we were horses at market. When he reached me, he lingered. “Senator Aelius is giving tomorrow’s munus for his son’s election,” he said. “He wants spectacle, not butchery in the first bouts. The Emperor will attend, perhaps. Trajan has Dacian gold to spend and a triumph still ringing in the people’s ears, so Aelius must shine without seeming to rival him. You understand?” I understood. We were to be brave enough to make Aelius look generous, bloody enough to make the plebs roar, and careful enough not to embarrass anyone whose name mattered. Politics in Rome wore many costumes; ours was sweat and painted shields. Vettius lowered his voice. “Win tomorrow and the next two, Corvus, and men may talk of the rudis for you.” The wooden sword of freedom. He said it the way a fisherman moves bait above dark water. In the afternoon we were allowed, under guard, to walk as far as the market beside the amphitheatre to loosen our legs. It was the part of the day I loved and hated most. Rome pressed close there in all its noise and color: matrons in saffron cloaks attended by slave girls, clerks with ink-stained fingers, off-duty soldiers arguing over dice, Egyptian sailors from the grain ships swearing that storms had delayed the fleet. At a baker’s stall two women were complaining that the price of bread had risen again, and an old man spat and said the Emperor fed foreign wars while Roman bellies growled. A guard shifted his spear and the old man suddenly found interest in his sandals. Near a wall covered in graffiti I saw my own name scratched beside a crude drawing of a Thracian shield: CORVUS WINS, CORVUS DIES, and beneath, in fresher charcoal, CORVUS HAS EYES LIKE A WOMAN. Brennus roared with laughter. Children darted between our legs playing at gladiators with sticks, already learning which deaths were glorious. It was there that the messenger found Vettius’s steward, and for a moment my heart lifted foolishly, because for three months I had waited for a letter from my brother. He had taken citizenship after twenty years with the auxiliaries on the Danube and written that he might come to Rome before winter. The steward handed the folded tablet not to me, but to Philon, and whatever hope I had carried folded itself away again. No one noticed except Brennus, who bumped my shoulder with his own, gently for a man his size, and said nothing. That was the kindness of the ludus. We did not waste words trying to make a locked door into an open one. That evening, after lentils and onions and a cup of sour wine, I performed the ritual I had kept since my first fight. From beneath my mattress I took the little clay figure of Nemesis that my mother had pressed into my hand when the slave traders led me from our village. One of her wings was broken. I set her facing the door, poured three drops of wine onto the floor — one for my mother, one for the brother I had not seen in eleven years, and one for myself — and tied a strip of red wool around my right wrist, where the manica would hide it. Then I touched the iron of my cell door three times and whispered my true name, not Corvus, so that if the gods were listening they would know the man beneath the painted name. It was foolishness, Philon would have said. But every man in that yard carried some foolishness into the arena, and mine had carried me through fourteen fights. Night came down with the clang of the gates and the settling sounds of men trying to sleep before they might die. Syrus wept once, quietly, and stopped. Somewhere a dice game began and was broken up. I lay listening to Rome beyond the walls — a drunk singing, a baby crying, the distant roar of water in the great drains — and felt my knee throb in time with my heart. I did not know whom I would face, or whether Aelius would get his spectacle, or whether my brother was alive beyond the northern rivers. I knew only the smell of straw, the goddess warm from my hand, and the red thread tight against my pulse. Tomorrow belonged to the Emperor, the senator, and the crowd. The night, at least, was still mine.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a sophisticated piece of historical fiction that demonstrates strong craft and deep understanding of both the Roman period and effective storytelling techniques. The author successfully creates an immersive first-person narrative that captures the complex inner life of Corvus, a veteran gladiator facing what may be his final fights. The adherence to instructions is excellent - the piece is written in first person past tense, avoids combat scenes as requested, and effectively incorporates sensory details throughout. The author skillfully weaves in political and social commentary through observations about Emperor Trajan's Dacian campaigns, bread prices, and the complex social dynamics between freedmen, senators, and slaves. The characterization of Corvus is particularly strong. He emerges as a fully realized individual with a rich interior life, carrying both his birth name (Duras) and his arena persona (Corvus). His relationships with fellow gladiators like Brennus and young Syrus feel authentic and reveal different facets of his character. The detail about his private ritual with the clay figure of Nemesis adds emotional depth without sentimentality. The prose quality is consistently high, with vivid sensory details that bring ancient Rome to life - from the "smell of boiled barley and old sweat" to the sounds of cart wheels and the visual of the amphitheatre's shadow. The author demonstrates restraint, avoiding overwrought descriptions while maintaining rich atmospheric detail. The political and social commentary is seamlessly integrated rather than forced. References to grain prices, Emperor Trajan's popularity, and the complex relationship between entertainment and politics feel natural to the character's perspective. The observation about politics wearing "many costumes" is particularly effective. The pacing is well-controlled, moving through a complete day while maintaining tension about the upcoming games. The ending strikes an appropriate note - neither falsely optimistic nor gratuitously dark, but reflecting the character's realistic acceptance of his circumstances while maintaining his humanity. Minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the historical knowledge feels slightly displayed rather than fully integrated, and some descriptions, while beautiful, occasionally approach purple prose without quite crossing the line. The piece also relies somewhat on familiar gladiator story elements, though it executes them with skill. + Epistolary: The Lighthouse Keeper — Score: 86.8
Prompt:
The Lighthouse Keeper Epistolary Narrative: Write a story told entirely through a series of brief correspondences: telegrams or letters or emails between two characters. The correspondence should span several months or years, and reveal a gradually unfolding plot. Use distinct voices for each character, and include details that provide insight into their personalities and motivations. The story should build to an emotional climax, and the final letter should provide a satisfying resolution. The setting is a lighthouse keeper writing to his mother. He is working class and Scottish. He is struggling with the isolation of his posting. Write naturally and without cliches. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**12 September 1971 — Hamish to Mam** Dear Mam, Well, I'm here. The boat left me, two other men, and six weeks of tatties on a rock twelve miles off Islay, and that was that. You can walk round the whole place in four minutes if the spray isn't too bad. I'm Assistant Keeper, under Mr Cowie, who's Principal, and Davie Lennox, who's been on lights since he was seventeen and acts like it. My room's up a stair with a wall that curves, so the bed doesn't sit right. There's a locker, a chair, and a window the size of a tea tray. First wage will be sent straight to the Post Office account like we said. Don't argue. I'll write again when I've learned the work properly. Your son, Hamish --- **21 September 1971 — Mam to Hamish** Dear Hamish, Your letter came Tuesday and I've read it three times, though the print in that last bit was fair squinty, was that your good pen? I've put a parcel on Friday's boat — two pairs of the thick socks, fruit cake in the tin (mind and bring the tin back, it's Mrs Allan's), and tea because I know fine whatever they give you it'll be stewed to tar. Are you eating meat? Are the other men clean in the kitchen? Your father always said you can tell a man by his sink. The rent man's been, I told him you'd got the Lighthouse Board and he said, oh, very respectable, as if we weren't before. Write soon son, and don't be up that tower without a jacket. Love, Mam --- **3 November 1971 — Hamish to Mam** Mam, The cake lasted four days. Davie took two slices for one of his, which Cowie says is the usual tax. The work's not hard so much as it never finishes. The light turns on a weight that drops down the middle of the tower, and every hour through the night you wind it back up. There's a bell if you sleep past it. I have slept past it, once, and Cowie wrote it in the log without saying a word, which was worse. Water's the other thing. It comes off the roof into a tank and we measure it like whisky. Wash in a basin on Mondays, shirt on Thursdays. If it hasn't rained, don't ask. My knees know every one of the 112 steps. Paraffin goes up in cans, ashes come down. Hamish --- **19 December 1971 — Mam to Hamish** Dear Hamish, I hope this catches the boat before Christmas, the man at the pier wasn't sure. There's shortbread and a scarf, not your colours maybe, the wool was reduced at Arnott's because it's a queer green, but wool's wool. Mrs Allan's boy is home from the rigs with money to burn and no sense, you'll hear him three doors down. Jean came from Aberdeen on Sunday with that coat I told you about and stayed for her tea. She asks for you. She says Aberdeen's all new buildings and nowhere to park. I had the doctor about my back, nothing to write home about, which is a daft saying as I'm writing home, or to you, which is the same thing just now. Have as good a Christmas as you can, son. Eat the shortbread yourself. Love, Mam --- **28 January 1972 — Hamish to Mam** Mam, Relief was due on the 17th. It came yesterday. Eleven days of wind too high for the boat to get alongside, and us watching the steps go under water at high tide. By the end we were on tinned meat and the tatties had grown legs. Davie stopped speaking except to the wireless. Cowie read the same newspaper front to back, adverts and all. I played patience until I was cheating and still losing. I'm not telling you to worry you. I'm telling you because the Board man on the boat said, "Och, that's the job," and I wanted somebody to know it isn't just standing looking at the sea. Off for six weeks on Thursday, weather permitting. That phrase does a lot of work out here. Hamish --- **15 March 1972 — Mam to Hamish** Dear Hamish, It was grand having you home, even if you slept the first two days like you'd been drugged and then ate us out of bacon. The house is quiet again. I keep putting out two cups. I didn't say, and don't make a fuss, but the doctor's changed my tablets for my heart. He says the stairs up to this flat aren't ideal, as if I'd a lift in my handbag. I'm fine on the flat, it's just the top flight, I take it in two goes with the shopping. Jean says I should ask the council about a ground floor. I said I'm not asking anybody for anything at my age. We'll see. Don't be sending extra money. The Board wage is yours too, son. Love, Mam --- **9 August 1972 — Hamish to Mam** Mam, Back on. Leave gets harder to leave, if you follow me. On the boat out Davie asked how you were and I said fine, and then I sat watching Peterhead get small and thought, I have no idea if that's true. You'd say fine if your leg was hanging off. I've put in for a shore station. Cowie says there's men waiting years for the ones with houses, places like Buchan Ness where your family stays ashore and you work shifts like a normal person. He says my chances are poor without more service. He also says everybody puts in after their second winter. So that's cheering. Tell Jean I saw her man at the harbour and he was doing nothing very slowly, same as before. Hamish --- **2 November 1972 — Mam to Hamish** Dear son, Excuse the writing, my eyes are playing up by the evening, the doctor says cataracts, both of them, and there's a list at the Infirmary and I'm on it, which is all anybody can tell me. I can still thread a needle if I do it at the window in the morning. So no panic. Mrs Allan reads me the *Press and Journal* on a Thursday. I pretend I don't care about the deaths page but I do. I fell on the stair last week — no, I tripped, there's a difference, I wasn't dizzy. Bruised hip. Jean's got a key now. Write big when you write. I can manage big. Love, Mam --- **20 January 1973 — Hamish to Mam** Mam, Writing big. Taking up the whole page like I'm back at school. I had a tooth go bad the week before Christmas, back one, right side. There's a medical box here with pliers in it that I'm fairly sure are for the generator. Cowie offered. I said I'd wait for the relief and the dentist in Port Ellen took it out in nine minutes and charged me less than the boat fare. Eating soup through the good side of your mouth while Davie has steak pie is a character-building experience I could've missed. I've put in for Buchan Ness again. And I've written to the Harbour Board at Peterhead, just asking. Nothing may come of it. Hamish --- **6 March 1973 — Mam to Hamish (written by Mrs Allan at her dictation)** Dear Hamish, Mrs Allan is doing the pen for this one so blame her spelling, she says blame my talking. I am in the Infirmary since Friday. I went over on the top stair with the messages and this time I will not argue about whether it was a trip. Nothing broken, which the doctor said like he was surprised. They are keeping me to look at my heart and they might do the worst eye while I am here, since I am here anyway, that is their logic and I suppose it is sound. Jean is feeding the cat and watering that plant you gave me which refuses to die out of spite. Do not go getting yourself in trouble with the Board over me. I mean that. Your loving mother, Margaret Fraser (Mrs Allan wrote that very formal, I only said Mam) --- **TELEGRAM — 23 April 1973** MAM BACK IN INFIRMARY STOP CHEST PAIN IN NIGHT STOP JEAN WITH HER STOP WILL WRITE STOP DO NOT WORRY STOP MAM --- **25 April 1973 — Hamish to Mam (to be sent when the boat can land)** Mam, Jean got word to us on the radio telephone yesterday, so your telegram was late and also a lie, and I'd expect nothing else from you. There's a gale on. There has been for four days. The boat can't land, the helicopter can't fly in this, and I am winding a weight up a tower every hour so that ships I can't see don't hit a rock I'm standing on. Cowie has been decent. He said if it clears he'll put me on the first boat and do my watches himself, and Davie never even made a joke, which tells you everything. I sat in the lamp room at three this morning and thought: if something happens to you while I'm out here measuring paraffin, I will never forgive this place. Not the men. The place. I have written to the Board tonight resigning from rock stations and asking for shore work or nothing. I have also had a letter back from the Harbour Board — they want a man for the pier lights and the fog signal at Peterhead, starting June, less money than this. I don't care. I should have written a year ago. Wait for me. That's not a request. Hamish --- **14 May 1973 — Mam to Hamish (dictated)** Dear Hamish, Well, I am still here, in both senses. They have done the right eye and I can see the clock on the ward wall, which I could not do at Christmas, so that is something. It is not perfect and they say it settles. Jean read me your letter twice. I cried the first time and the nurse pretended not to notice, she is a kind girl from Banff. The second time I told Jean, he gets that temper from his father, who once resigned from a fishing boat in the middle of the North Sea and had to un-resign by breakfast. If the harbour job is real, son, take it. Not just for me. I have had your letters for two years and I can read between the lines better than you think, even with one eye. Love, Mam --- **4 June 1974 — Mam to Hamish** Dear Hamish, This is my own hand, so if it wanders off the line you'll know why. The left eye was done in March and between the two of them I can read the paper again without Mrs Allan doing the voices. I'm writing because you're on your last relief out there and Jean says a man should get a letter at the end of a thing. The council has given me the ground-floor flat on King Street, the one with the bit of garden, and your room is aired and the bed made up, though you'll be at the harbour by seven most mornings by the sound of the new job. Less money, aye. But you'll be in for your tea, and I can see to make it now. Cowie wrote me a very nice note, by the way. He said you never missed a watch after that first time. I never told him you told me. Come home, son. The boat permitting — I know, I know. I've learned the phrase. Love, Mam
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This epistolary narrative successfully fulfills the prompt's requirements while delivering a genuinely moving story. The piece spans nearly two years through letters between Hamish, a Scottish lighthouse keeper, and his mother, revealing their relationship and individual struggles through authentic voices. The Scottish working-class voices are convincingly rendered without resorting to heavy dialect or caricature. Hamish's voice evolves from terse, dutiful correspondence to more emotionally open communication as isolation takes its toll. His mother's voice remains consistently warm, practical, and subtly manipulative in the way of concerned parents, even when dictating letters due to failing eyesight. The gradual revelation of plot elements works effectively - Hamish's growing desperation with isolation, his mother's declining health, and the mounting tension between duty and family obligation. The story builds naturally to the emotional climax when Hamish realizes he might lose his mother while trapped on the lighthouse during a storm, leading to his resignation letter. Character development feels authentic. Hamish's transformation from dutiful son accepting hardship to someone who prioritizes human connection over financial security is well-earned through accumulated details of isolation, physical discomfort, and mounting anxiety about his mother's health. The mother's gradual revelation of her health problems - initially minimized, then acknowledged - rings true to character. The prose is clean and economical, matching the working-class voices. Details like "tatties had grown legs," "wash in a basin on Mondays," and "my knees know every one of the 112 steps" create vivid impressions of lighthouse life without overwrought description. The technical aspects of lighthouse keeping are woven naturally into the narrative. The emotional complexity emerges through subtext and restraint rather than melodrama. The mother's pride, fear, and love are conveyed through practical concerns about socks and shortbread. Hamish's growing desperation shows through increasingly terse descriptions of routine hardships. The resolution feels earned rather than artificially positive. Hamish's decision comes at personal cost (less money, different work) but represents genuine character growth. The final letter's gentle optimism about their reunion feels natural given the established relationship dynamics. Minor weaknesses include some predictable elements in the arc and occasional moments where the Scottish voice feels slightly forced, but these don't significantly detract from the overall effectiveness. + First-person unique perspective: Hacker Mindset — Score: 88.0
Prompt:
Hacker Mindset Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a reformed (now) white hat hacker who cannot help but notice exploitable weaknesses in both systems and people they encounter. They habitually look for vulnerabilities and exploit vectors. The narrative takes place during a first date at a restaurant, where they're trying to focus on human connection. It's going surprisingly well due to a discovered shared nerd-fandom (magic the gathering). Things go a little sideways when the date reveals a noticeably insecure phone unlock pattern, which protagonist can't help but comment on. They are then left to negotiate the fallout of this faux pas and attempt to salvage (or perhaps sabotage) the remainder of the date. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. 1000 words.
Model Output:
I am not scanning the restaurant. That is the first lie I tell myself when I sit down, and I tell it the way normal people tell themselves they will only have one drink. I am a reformed person now. White hat. Paid invoices, penetration tests with permission slips, a little framed certificate in my apartment that says I only break into things when someone in Legal has signed in triplicate. I do not do the other thing anymore. I definitely do not notice that the host stand tablet is still on the default admin PIN, because I saw the hostess type 0-0-0-0 while smiling at a party of six. I do not notice the kitchen door code is probably 1-9-8-6, the year the owner opened, because exactly those four keys are worn shiny. I am here to have a normal first date. Mara arrives four minutes late, apologizing for traffic, tote bag open, wallet visible, phone in her back pocket with the screen still awake. Perfect target, my brain supplies instantly. Bag snatch, shoulder surf, tail her to her car and — stop. Human connection. Focus. She has kind eyes and a nervous laugh and she apologizes twice to the chair she bumps. She asks what I do and I give the sanitized version, cybersecurity consultant, which is true in the same way a lockpick is a key enthusiast. She works in archives, preserving old media, and I do not say that archivists always reuse passwords because they romanticize permanence. We talk about the menu like two people defusing a bomb made of small talk. Weather. Neighborhood. The risotto sounds good. I am cataloging exits, cameras, the bartender who leaves the POS logged in, instead of asking her a single real question. Then she sees the little enamel pin on my jacket, a terrible, nerdy pin I forgot to remove, and everything changes. "You play Magic?" I am not supposed to light up like a breached server, but I do. CATALOG: She learned during Innistrad. First card mentioned: **Liliana of the Veil**. Discard, attrition, making both players suffer but planning to suffer better. Not a beginner's favorite. Interesting. She says she still has her first **Thoughtseize** in a binder, the good art, and she will never trade it. File that. Proactive disruption. She does not wait to react to your plan; she reaches into your hand on turn one, takes the best part, and watches you recalculate. Information first, damage second. My kind of terrible person. The appetizers come and I have forgotten the POS terminal entirely. She plays mostly Dimir in Standard, some Esper when she is feeling, her word, "spiteful." **Counterspell**, obviously. **Mana Leak** when she wants to be merciful early. **Teferi, Hero of Dominaria** as a finisher, which is not a finisher so much as a promise to be here, drawing cards and tucking your hopes away, until the sun dies. Control player. Patient. Comfortable saying no professionally. She likes games that go long because she likes watching a system reveal its stress fractures. I should be normal about how attractive I find this. She splashes red in one deck, "just for **Lightning Bolt**," because sometimes you need an honest answer at instant speed. File: efficiency fetish, respects elegant design, three damage for one mana as a moral philosophy. Her Commander deck is **Atraxa, Praetors' Voice**, proliferate, poison counters, "but in a fun way," which is exactly what someone says when it is not in a fun way. **Rhystic Study** is in there. Of course it is. Do you pay the one? She wants to tax every action you take and profit from your curiosity. **Cyclonic Rift** overloaded as a reset button when the board gets too loud. **Sheoldred, the Apocalypse** because if you are going to draw cards, you should bleed a little for the privilege. By the main course I have a complete profile and it is, unfortunately, devastatingly my type: information asymmetry, slow strangulation, plausible deniability, counters everything except dessert. She mentions **Ragavan, Nimble Pilferer** last, laughing that she loves stealing the top card of someone's library and playing it in front of them. I do not tell her I once did that professionally to Fortune 500 companies, metaphorically, with less monkey. She wants to show me the Atraxa deck, foil, her pride and joy, photographed card by card. She pulls out her phone. She wakes it right in front of me, angled toward me, trusting as a house with the alarm code on a sticky note. And she draws an L. Just an L. Top left, down, across. The most common unlock pattern in the world. The pattern a child would guess. The pattern I have demonstrated in corporate trainings with a slide that literally says PLEASE DO NOT DO THIS behind it in 72-point font. I could not notice. I am reformed. I am focusing on human connection, on her hands, on how happy she looks scrolling for the photo. Responsible disclosure protocols exist for a reason. There is a time, a place, a private channel, a 90-day window before public release. What comes out of my mouth is: "Please tell me that's not your actual unlock pattern." Silence is a system failure you can hear. Inside my head I am immediately running incident response. Severity: critical. Blast radius: entire date. Containment: failed, the idiot is still talking. Because now I am explaining, out loud, that an L is in the first twenty patterns any attacker tries, that smudge marks on her cracked screen protector literally trace it, that I could get into her phone in under five seconds, that her banking app better not use biometrics fallback alone, and has she considered a six-digit PIN at minimum, actually a passphrase — She is not looking at her phone anymore. She is looking at me the way you look at a man who has just inspected your teeth for resale value. Were you watching me unlock my phone? That is the question underneath her actual question, which is something polite and frozen like, "Wow, okay." And the honest answer is yes, involuntarily, the way she probably notices a mislabeled archive box. But honest and acceptable are different protocols. I have just told a woman, on a first date, that I assessed her as an easy target before the breadsticks cooled. I have performed an unsolicited penetration test on her life. Permission slips, remember? Legal, in triplicate? Salvage options run like bad code. Option one: double down, be the expert, mansplain encryption until she fakes a family emergency. That is sabotage disguised as helpfulness, and part of me wants it, because rejection on my terms is a controlled environment. Option two: lie, say I was joking. She will know. Thoughtseize players always know. Option three, terrifying, unpatched: actual vulnerability disclosure. Mine. So I stop. I put my own phone face down, deliberately, screen away, hands visible like a magician with nothing up his sleeve. I tell her, in my head first and then somehow out loud, that it is an occupational deformity, that I see locks the way she probably sees damaged spines on books, automatically, rudely, even when I am trying very hard to see a person instead. I tell her I used to be the reason for trainings like that, and now I am just a man who cannot turn it off at dinner. I tell her the truth I have not cataloged yet: my favorite deck in Modern used to be Lantern Control. She stares. Lantern of Insight. Codex Shredder. Milling the top card of your library, one at a time, deciding what you are allowed to draw for the rest of the game. The most hated deck ever printed into existence. A deck for people who do not want to win so much as curate your despair. "You," she says slowly, and I can hear the entire profile she is building on me, "are a monster." Yes. But a reformed one. And then, miracle of miracles, she laughs. Not a polite laugh. A real, startled, Rhystic Study laugh, like she is profiting from information she did not expect to draw. She tells me Lantern players are why she mainboards **Abrupt Decay**, uncounterable removal for problems that think they are too clever to be touched. File that too, final entry of the night: she came prepared for exactly my kind of control freak. She turns her phone over. She says she will change the pattern tonight, but I am not allowed to watch, and if I try, the date is over and she will Cyclonic Rift me back to the host stand. I look away while she locks it again, ostentatiously, staring at the kitchen door with its terrible code like it is the most fascinating painting in the world. It is the hardest exploit I have ever chosen not to use. Dessert menu arrives. I ask if I can see the Atraxa photo now, permission requested, access granted. She shows me. It is beautiful. It would kill me in nine turns and I would thank her for the sequencing.
