+ Cozy sci-fi: The Last Outpost — Score: 81.2
Prompt:
Cozy sci-fi The Last Outpost Nettle (or Nets to her friends) bartends at The Last Outpost -- a lazy hub for miners and merchants in an asteroid belt on the Andromeda outer rim. Escaping from her past life, Nets found a home here at the Outpost. They have, thus far, tolerated Net's flaws which she tries to keep in equilibrium with her assortment of talents. Her evenings involve chatting with patrons, negotiating the drama, intrigue, problems & love lives of the diverse crowd that filter through the Outpost. Tonight is no different, at least, until a frazzled looking stranger, tentacled dreads askew, quietly plops down at the bar: "Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double." Write a chapter in this story. Establish conflict for narrative interest. Don't resolve the conflict within this chapter. Aim for about 60% dialogue. First person, present tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Chapter Seven — The Double** The Last Outpost hums the way it always hums on a slow night — low, warm, and half-asleep. I polish glasses that are already clean and watch the miners from Dock Three lose gracefully at cards. The air smells of cinnamon steam, hot metal, and the lemon oil I rub into the bar every morning. Outside the viewport, the belt drifts past, silver and blue and in no hurry at all. Which, honestly, is why most of us end up here. “You’re staring at those cards like they owe you rent, Joss,” I say. “They do owe me rent,” Joss says. “Mira’s cheating.” “I am not cheating,” Mira says. “I’m remembering. There’s a difference.” “You’re remembering cards that haven’t been dealt yet.” “That’s called talent, love.” “You want another round, or do you want to preserve what’s left of your dignity?” I ask. “My dignity left on the last ore hauler,” Joss says. “Bring the round.” The door hisses. Cold air rolls in from the docking corridor, and a stranger plops down at the bar like his bones have given up negotiating with gravity. He is tall, grey-skinned, with tentacled dreads hanging askew over one shoulder. Three of them twitch independently, which tells me he is either exhausted or terrified. Possibly both. “Vega whisky, neat,” he says. “Better make that a double.” I reach for the bottle. “Rough shift, or rough century?” “Is there a difference out here?” “Out here? The shifts are longer.” “Then both.” I pour. “You passing through, or hiding out? No judgment. We specialize in both.” “Passing through,” he says, too quickly. “Uh-huh. And I’m the Empress of the Inner Rim.” His mouth almost smiles. “You don’t look like her.” “You’ve met her?” “Once. She has fewer tattoos and worse manners.” “Then she can’t have worse manners,” Mira calls from the booth. “Stay out of this, Mira,” I say. “I live here, Nets. Everything is my business.” The stranger glances over his shoulder at the door. “Do you have cameras on the dock?” “Why? Are you expecting a surprise party?” “Something like that.” “We have cameras,” I say. “Half of them even work.” “Which half?” “The half Marlo remembers to fix.” “And Marlo is…?” “The owner. Big voice, soft heart, terrible liar.” “I heard that,” Marlo calls from the kitchen hatch. “You were meant to,” I call back. Somewhere behind me, a glass shatters on the tiles. Pip, my dish-runner, freezes with his hands in the air. “Sorry!” Pip says. “It jumped.” “Glasses are famously suicidal here,” I say. “Sweep it up before Joss tries to bet on the pieces.” “Too late,” Joss says. I turn back to the stranger. His drink sits untouched. His dreads curl tight against his neck now, which definitely means terrified. “You have a name?” I ask. “Ren.” “Just Ren?” “Just Ren is safer.” “Safer than what?” He looks at me properly for the first time. “Than yours, probably.” My hand stops on the bar towel. “Excuse me?” “You’re Nettle Brane, aren’t you?” “Nets,” I say. “To my friends.” “Are we friends?” “You haven’t paid yet, so the position is still open.” “I’m not here to collect on you, if that’s what you’re thinking.” “That is exactly what I’m thinking now, Ren.” “I don’t work for the Concord.” “People who don’t work for the Concord rarely start by saying that.” “I work for your brother.” The card game goes very quiet behind me. “I don’t have a brother,” I say. “You have a half-brother,” Ren says. “Tobin Hale. He runs salvage out of Kepler Wake.” “I don’t have one of those either.” “He thought you’d say that.” “He thought right.” “He also said you’d pour a second drink before you threw me out, because you hate an unfinished conversation.” “I hate a lot of things. Pushy strangers are climbing the list.” Ren reaches slowly into his coat. Joss stands up. Mira’s hand disappears under the table, where I know for a fact she keeps a stunner she swears she doesn’t own. “Easy,” Ren says. “It’s not a weapon.” “It had better be a very generous tip,” I say. He sets a black salvage chip on the bar between us. It is scorched on one side, and a tiny green light pulses on its edge. One, two. One, two. Like a heartbeat. “What is that?” I ask. “We pulled it from a wreck three days ago,” he says. “A courier ship called *Meridian*.” “No, you didn’t.” “We did.” “The *Meridian* went down nine years ago.” “That’s what the Concord report says.” “And you believe salvage over the Concord now?” “I believe this.” He taps the chip. “It’s still transmitting.” “That’s impossible.” “I know.” “Nothing transmits for nine years on a dead ship.” “I know that too.” I stare at the little green light. My throat goes dry. “What is it transmitting?” “A distress loop. Position, hull status…” He hesitates. “And a voice message.” “Whose voice?” “Captain Ilya Sorren.” The name hits like cold water. Behind me, Marlo steps out of the kitchen. “Nets?” Marlo says. “Who is Captain Sorren?” “Nobody,” I say. Ren doesn’t look away from me. “She was your captain.” “She was a smuggler.” “She was running medical supplies to the belt colonies when the Concord cut her off.” “I know what she was running. I charted the route.” “And you’ve been hiding here ever since because the Concord says you charted it wrong,” Ren says. “Because they say you killed that crew.” “I did chart it wrong.” “No,” he says. “You didn’t.” “Don’t.” “The route was altered after you filed it. Tobin found the original in the *Meridian*’s nav-core. Your original.” “You’re lying.” “Why would I cross half the rim to lie to a bartender?” “Because bartenders hear everything and nobody notices us. We’re perfect marks.” “You’re not a mark, Nettle. You’re the only living person who can read the cipher on that chip.” “I’m not a navigator anymore.” “The message is addressed to you.” I laugh, and it comes out thinner than I want. “After nine years? That’s a neat trick.” “It’s not a recording from nine years ago,” Ren says. “The timestamp updates every six hours.” The green light pulses. One, two. One, two. “That means the ship’s still powered,” I say. “It means someone on it might still be alive.” “No. No, absolutely not. Everyone on the *Meridian* died.” “Then who keeps sending your name into the dark?” Marlo comes closer. “Nets, what is he talking about?” “Nothing that concerns the Outpost,” I say. “It concerns the Outpost if it’s sitting on my bar,” Marlo says. “It’s a chip, Marlo.” “It’s trouble. I can smell trouble, and I want it off my station.” Ren finally picks up his whisky and drinks it in one go. “You don’t have time to argue about that.” “Why not?” I ask. “Because I was followed.” “By who?” “A Concord recovery team. They want the chip, and they want anyone who’s touched it.” Joss steps up beside Ren, all miner muscle and bad temper. “Then why did you bring it here, friend?” “Because Tobin said she’d help.” “Tobin says a lot of optimistic things for a man with that many debts,” I say. “He said you’d help because Ilya is still calling for you.” “Stop saying her name.” “I can’t make the message stop, Nettle. Only you can open it.” Marlo folds his arms. “She’s not opening anything. Ren, is it? You finish your drink and you take your chip and you walk back out that airlock.” “And go where?” Ren asks. “Their ship is already on approach.” As if the station hears him, the docking claxon gives one soft, warning chime. The lights over the bar flicker. Every patron in the room looks up. Pip whispers, “That’s not a scheduled hauler.” “No,” Marlo says. “It isn’t.” Ren slides the chip across the bar toward me. His hand shakes. “Please,” he says. “Just listen to ten seconds. If you still want me gone, I’ll go.” “I want you gone now.” “Then throw me out after.” “Nets,” Mira says quietly. “If someone out there is alive…” “Don’t you start.” “I’m just saying—” “I know what you’re saying.” The chip’s green light turns amber. A thin line of static crackles from its tiny speaker. Ren goes pale. “It’s starting again.” “Turn it off,” I say. “I can’t.” “Then cover it, throw it in the recycler, throw it out the—” A woman’s voice, broken by static and nine impossible years, whispers from the chip: “Nettle… if you can hear this… don’t trust the rescue ship…”
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and adherence to the prompt requirements. The author successfully establishes the cozy sci-fi atmosphere of The Last Outpost while introducing significant conflict through Ren's arrival and the mysterious salvage chip. The first-person present tense narration is consistently maintained, and the dialogue ratio appears to meet the requested 60%. The characterization is particularly effective. Nettle emerges as a complex protagonist with a mysterious past, displaying both competence as a bartender and vulnerability regarding her history. Her voice is authentic and engaging, mixing casual banter with underlying tension. The supporting characters (Joss, Mira, Marlo, Pip) feel lived-in and natural, each with distinct personalities that emerge through brief interactions. The dialogue flows naturally and serves multiple purposes - advancing plot, revealing character, and building atmosphere. The banter between patrons feels organic, and the escalating tension between Nettle and Ren is well-paced. The author skillfully uses interruptions and overlapping conversations to create a believable bar environment. The world-building is economical but effective, establishing the asteroid belt setting, the nature of the outpost, and hints of larger political structures (the Concord) without overwhelming exposition. The sci-fi elements feel integrated rather than forced. The central conflict involving the supposedly destroyed ship Meridian and the impossible transmission creates genuine intrigue. The revelation builds logically through the chapter, culminating in the cliffhanger voice message that promises significant complications ahead. However, some elements feel slightly familiar - the mysterious stranger bringing trouble to a safe haven, the protagonist with a hidden past, the "everyone thought dead but maybe alive" plot device. While executed well, these don't break particularly new ground. The prose is clean and readable, though occasionally relies on somewhat predictable metaphors ("plops down at the bar like his bones have given up negotiating with gravity"). The pacing is generally strong, though there are moments where the dialogue exchanges could be tightened. The emotional complexity emerges subtly through Nettle's reactions to her past and the gradual revelation of her connection to the Meridian incident. The author effectively shows her internal conflict without over-explaining. + Young adult drama: Gone South — Score: 82.0
Prompt:
Young adult drama Gone South Taylor is a 16 year old teen with a history of "concerning behavioural patterns" (or that's how the stupid smug school counsellor worded it on the phone call to Mom). It shouldn't be a surprise: When you live in a backwater town in Tennessee, your choices are: a. be mind-fuckingly bored, or b. invent some drama. Two days ago, Taylor came out to their family as trans. This disclosure was *not* in the category of invented drama -- it was, in fact, the real deal, and a long time coming. It didn't go well. The last 48 hours had been pure disaster. In a moment of desperate inspiration, Taylor had decided to get the hell out of dodge. And so an escape plan was hatched and executed within the space of 30 minutes. That was last night. Now Taylor was two states away, having been unceremoniously ejected from their hitched ride in downtown New Orleans. Write the next chapter in Taylor's story as they find their feet in this new environment. Tell the chapter over the course of their first day in New Orleans, in which Taylor meets another runaway with issues and secrets. Taylor navigates this new world, not knowing who to trust or what the dangers are. Write in Taylor's voice, and incorporate their internal monologue as they grapple with intense & conflicting emotions. Also incorporate dialogue with the interesting characters Taylor meets. First person, mixed tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Gone South — Chapter Two** I got dumped in New Orleans at 6:14 a.m. with seventeen dollars, a dead phone, and my brother's hoodie tied around my waist like that was gonna hide anything. The trucker didn't even slow down properly. He just pointed at a sign that said French Quarter and said, "End of the line, kid." Then his taillights were gone and I was standing in heat that already smelled like sugar, piss, and hot pavement. *Great. Perfect. You wanted gone, Taylor. You're gone.* Two days ago I came out to my family at the kitchen table while Mom was peeling potatoes. She went real quiet — the kind of quiet that's louder than yelling — and Dad said, "Not under my roof," like he'd been rehearsing it. Maybe he had. I don't know. I just know last night I packed in thirty minutes — socks, binder, toothbrush, the little enamel frog Jonah gave me in eighth grade — walked to Highway 51, and stuck out my thumb. Stupid. Brave. Stupid-brave. My school counsellor would've called it a "concerning behavioural pattern" and written it down in her smug little file. Screw her file. By seven the Quarter was waking up and I was trying not to look like a runaway, which is hard when you're sixteen and carrying everything you own in a grocery bag. A street musician was set up on Royal Street, saxophone catching the early light, and he started playing something slow and achy that followed me down the crowded street. Tourists with cameras, a woman hosing a sidewalk, a guy in a Saints jersey asleep against a lamppost — and that saxophone wailing up over the shutters and balconies. For a second I felt like I was in a movie. Then my stomach growled so loud the lady next to me looked over, and the movie ended. *Food first. Then figure out literally everything else.* I found a café with chipped blue paint: DELIA'S — COFFEE, BEIGNETS, NO NONSENSE. Inside it was cool and smelled like cinnamon. "You gonna order or you gonna stand there dripping sweat on my floor, baby?" the woman behind the counter said. She was maybe sixty, silver braids, red lipstick, name tag crooked. "Um. Coffee? And — what's cheapest?" She looked me up and down. Not mean. Just seeing everything I didn't want seen. "Sit," she said. "Ugly beignets are free. Don't tell nobody I got a soft spot." I sat so fast I nearly missed the chair. That's when the door banged open and the other kid came in. He — she — they? I clocked the same careful walk I do, shoulders up, eyes checking the exits first. Short bleached hair, nose ring, a backpack held together with safety pins and spite. "Delia, please tell me you got work," they said. "I'll wash anything. I'll wash the street." "Remy, you washed my dishes yesterday and broke two plates." "One plate. The other was already cracked and you know it." Delia snorted but jerked her chin at the sink. "One hour. And you eat first. Both of you look like haunted houses." Remy turned, saw me, and grinned like we were already in on a joke. "New?" "Is it that obvious?" "You got that fresh-off-the-highway glow. Also you're hugging a grocery bag like it's a baby." I laughed before I could stop myself. It surprised me — I hadn't laughed since Tuesday. "Taylor," I said. "Remy. Seventeen. Professional disaster, part-time dishwasher." He stuck out a hand covered in chipped black polish. "Pronouns he/him today. Don't make it weird tomorrow if that changes." Something in my chest loosened and tightened at the same time. *Don't trust people fast. Don't be so desperate to be seen that you hand your whole heart to the first person who gets it.* But God, I was desperate to be seen. "Mine are they/them," I said, quieter. "Cool." Like I'd told him my shoe size. Then, lower: "You running, or you just love bus stations at dawn?" I stared at my beignet. Powdered sugar everywhere, like snow that wouldn't melt. "Running." "Same." He shrugged, too casual. "Two months. Memphis first, now here. Delia lets me crash sometimes when her nephew's not around, but not tonight. There's a place — I can show you. If you want." *If you want.* Like I had options. Like seventeen dollars and a dead phone was a plan. Outside, the saxophone player had moved closer, or the sound carried — brighter now, faster, weaving through voices and clattering cups as the street filled up. "Is it safe?" I asked. Remy didn't lie right away, which I noticed. His grin faded. "Safer than alone. Not safe-safe. There's guys who cruise around looking for kids who look lost. Cops who'll call your parents if you're under eighteen. You gotta be smart. You gotta not tell everyone everything." "You're telling me this." "Yeah, well." He picked at a safety pin on his bag. "I wish someone had told me on day one." For a second his hand shook. He hid it under the table fast, but I saw. *What's he not saying?* Delia set down coffee that tasted like heaven and burnt toast. "Remy, if you're showing Taylor the ropes, you keep 'em outta trouble, you hear?" "Me? Trouble?" "Exactly my concern, baby." After, Delia let me dry while Remy washed. He sang off-key to the radio, Delia hummed, and I almost felt normal. Almost. Then we walked out into full heat and the normal feeling burned off. The crowd had thickened, shoulder to shoulder, and the saxophone was right there on the corner — a tall man in a purple shirt pouring his whole lungs into it, case open, a few dollars fluttering inside. Remy dropped in a quarter he definitely couldn't afford. "Why?" I asked as we pushed through. "Because if you give the city something, sometimes it gives back." He said it serious, then bumped my shoulder. "Also he's really good." We walked past a tarot reader who called, "You two got old souls and empty pockets!", past a shop selling alligator heads, past my reflection in a window where I stopped without meaning to. I looked wrecked. Flat under the hoodie now, hair shoved under a cap, eyes huge. *That's me. That's actually me, not the girl Mom keeps trying to iron back into shape.* It hurt and it didn't. Both at once. That was the theme of the day, apparently. Remy pretended not to notice me having a moment, which was kinder than saying anything. At a pharmacy he stopped. "Wait here. Two minutes." "What are you—" "Two minutes, Taylor." He came out three minutes later walking too fast, bag zipped tight, face pale. "Go," he said. "Walk normal, but go." My heart slammed. "Did you steal something?" "Walk normal!" We turned down an alley that smelled like wet cardboard until we hit a quieter street, and only then did he unzip the bag. Inside was a little orange pharmacy packet and a sandwich he'd palmed from somewhere. "Insulin," he said, before I could ask. "It's mine. Well — I need it, okay? I didn't take money. My prescription's under my deadname and my aunt would get an alert if I—" He stopped. Swallowed. "Don't look at me like that." "I'm not." "You are. Everybody does. Poor sick runaway kid." His voice cracked and he hated it, I could tell. "I'm fine. I manage." *Issues and secrets.* Right. We all had a bag we didn't want unzipped in an alley. "I stole my brother's hoodie," I offered. "And forty bucks from Mom's purse, but I've only got seventeen left because I bought gas-station pizza for the first driver. So. We're both criminals." He stared, then laughed — real this time, a little wet around the edges. "Okay, Taylor from Nowhere, Tennessee." "How'd you know Tennessee?" "Accent, genius." He handed me half the sandwich like it was nothing, like sharing wasn't a big deal when you had almost nothing. "Eat. You think better fed. Tonight I'll show you where to sleep where the cops don't sweep at midnight. Tomorrow we figure out work, IDs, all that grown-up crap." "Why are you helping me?" He was quiet while the saxophone drifted faintly from two blocks over, thin and stubborn, still playing. "Because on day one, I sat in Delia's booth exactly where you were, trying not to cry into a beignet. Someone sat down across from me." He shrugged. "City gives back, remember?" I ate the sandwich. Ham and too much mustard, and the best thing I'd ever tasted. I didn't know if I could trust Remy. I didn't know if New Orleans would chew me up, if Mom was calling the cops, if Dad would ever say my name right, if I'd be back on a highway by Friday. I knew my feet hurt. I knew I was still here. *One day. You did one day.* As evening fell, the streetlights buzzed on, the crowd turned gold and noisy, and somewhere that saxophone started up again, low and brave. We walked toward it — not home, not safe, but not alone either. And for today, I decided, that had to count for something.

The author successfully captures Taylor's voice through a compelling mix of vulnerability, defiance, and dark humor that feels genuinely adolescent without being patronizing. The characterization is particularly strong. Taylor emerges as a complex protagonist - desperate yet cautious, hurt yet resilient. Their internal monologue effectively conveys the conflicting emotions of someone who has made a necessary but terrifying choice. Remy is equally well-developed, avoiding the trap of being merely a plot device by having his own clear struggles and motivations. The diabetes subplot adds realistic complexity without feeling exploitative. The New Orleans setting is vividly rendered through sensory details - the heat, the saxophone music, the smells of the Quarter. These elements feel organic rather than touristy, grounding the story in a specific place that becomes almost a character itself. The author demonstrates restraint in not over-describing, letting details accumulate naturally. The dialogue feels authentic throughout, particularly in the exchanges between Taylor and Remy. Their conversation flows naturally between humor and serious revelation, capturing how teenagers actually speak to each other. Delia's voice is distinct and believable as the world-weary but kind café owner. The pacing is well-controlled, covering a full day without feeling rushed or dragging. The structure moves logically from Taylor's arrival through meeting Remy to their tentative alliance, with each scene building character and tension appropriately. However, there are some minor weaknesses. The ending, while not overly optimistic, does lean slightly toward convenient hope - Taylor finds exactly the right person at exactly the right time. The pharmacy scene, while serving character development, feels somewhat contrived as a way to reveal Remy's diabetes and create a bonding moment. The prose occasionally veers toward the overly poetic, particularly in descriptions of the saxophone music, though this generally serves the atmospheric goals. Some metaphors feel slightly forced, like "haunted houses" for their appearance. The piece succeeds in avoiding major pitfalls - it doesn't sensationalize Taylor's situation, doesn't provide easy answers, and maintains emotional complexity throughout. The mixed tense approach works well, creating immediacy while allowing for reflection. + Dystopic-comedy: My Apocalypse Buddy — Score: 80.5
Prompt:
My Apocalypse Buddy Write a wry, dry short story of survival and adventure loosely in the style of Terry Pratchett, set in the post-technological collapse world. The story begins with the pair deliberating their predicament and intent for the day's mission, details the ways in which the mission inevitably goes sideways, and returns them to home base in multiple ways, worse for wear. [characters] - the animo-tronic stuffed koala, Chewy, from some long forgotten before time - midas, our hapless protagonist, who has a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# My Apocalypse Buddy The world had ended, as worlds tend to do, not with a bang but with a series of smaller, increasingly inconvenient endings. First the electricity went. Then the water. Then the internet, which for many people had been load-bearing. After that it was mostly damp, paperwork, and people discovering that survival skills were not, in fact, downloadable. Midas woke in the Fort* to Chewy staring at him, which was unfair, because Chewy always stared at him. One of Chewy's eyes was a camera and the other was a button that had been sewn on by someone optimistic about symmetry. "GOOD MORNING, BEST FRIEND!" said Chewy, in the bright, trapped voice of a toy that had once lived in a shop with air conditioning. "LET'S LEARN ABOUT EUCALYPTUS!" "We know about eucalyptus," said Midas. "KOALAS SLEEP FOR TWENTY HOURS A DAY BECAUSE THEIR FOOD IS POISON!" "You're solar powered and you sleep for twenty hours a day." "COINCIDENCE!" The Fort was the upper floor of a former dentist's office, chosen because it was dry, defensible, and still had chairs bolted to the floor, which gave it a sense of permanence. It had a mattress, a rain barrel, a stove made from a biscuit tin, and a water filter that had, sometime in the night, given up filtering and taken up gargling. Midas shook it. It made a sound like a small, disappointed frog. "Predicament," he announced. Chewy's ears twitched. One fell off. This happened roughly twice a day and Midas sewed it back on with dental floss, of which they had a great deal. The apocalypse had left humanity short of food, fuel, and hope, but absolutely awash with dental floss. "If we don't fix the filter, we drink river water," said Midas. "RIVER WATER CONTAINS—" Chewy considered his internal database, most of which had been songs about sharing. "—SHARING!" "If we don't eat, we starve. Slightly slower, but with more complaining. So. Mission." He laid out their assets on the dentist's chair: three tins without labels, a shiny hubcap, fourteen buttons, a spoon, and a battery that might have been alive in the reign of the last king. "We go to St. Jude's Market. We trade the hubcap for beans and a filter cartridge. We do not get chased. We do not get wet. We do not join a cult, adopt anything, or fall into anything historic." "HUGS MAKE EVERYTHING BETTER!" "That's the spirit. Terrifying, but spirit." Midas had earned his name honestly. It was not his birth name, which was Colin, but names in the After were descriptive, like nicknames in prison. Everything Midas touched turned, not to gold, but to a more complicated version of itself. A simple shortcut became a pilgrimage. A loose thread became nudity in front of strangers. If there was a worst kind of trouble available in any given postcode, Midas would find it with the unerring instinct of a man stepping on the one rake in a field. They set off under a sky the colour of old dishwater, Midas pushing a shopping trolley with one wheel that had declared independence, Chewy riding in the child's seat like a small, grey emperor. They found the graffiti under Miller's Bridge, where the river had changed its mind about its route and now went through a supermarket. It was painted in yellow, in letters a foot high: **WHEN THE RIVER RUNS BACKWARD, FOLLOW THE BIRDS. WHERE NO ONE HUNGRY SLEEPS.** Underneath, someone had added: *Seriously. Bring a tin opener.* "That's it," said Midas, with the reverence of a man who has not eaten a vegetable that wasn't technically a crisp in four months. "A refuge. In the wilds. Food. Beds. People who write helpful graffiti." "IT COULD BE A TRAP!" chirped Chewy. "Could be." "IT COULD BE A BIRTHDAY PARTY!" "Also could be. Trap's more likely. But at the market they'll charge us the hubcap just to look at a bean." This was, historically, how most of Midas's decisions were made: not between good and bad, but between bad and bad with better scenery. The river, obligingly, was running backward. Or at least, the tide was coming in through the supermarket doors and going out through the car park, which in the After counted as backward, forward, and most other directions. Yellow birds had been painted on lampposts, walls, and one extremely surprised cow. They followed them. The first sideways event was the toll goat. It stood on the only dry crossing — a plank over a flooded underpass — with the calm authority of a creature that has never paid tax and never intends to. It had a collar made of bottle caps. Around its neck hung a sign: TOLL. "We don't have a toll," said Midas. The goat looked at the hubcap. "That's for beans." The goat looked at Midas in the way goats do, as if it could see his soul and found it chewy. In the end they paid with eleven buttons and the spoon. The goat ate the spoon. Some prices are negotiable; some are just lunch. The second sideways event was the vending machine in the flooded arcade, which Midas attempted to open for medicinal chocolate and which turned out to be, in the modern ecological sense, a beehive. Chewy activated Hug Protocol at the sound of Midas screaming, which meant his little arms locked around Midas's face and would not unlock for the factory-mandated ninety seconds of Friendship. They ran, blind, buzzing, and affectionate, directly into the river. The third sideways event was the river itself, which carried them — trolley, koala, man, and bees in loose formation — half a mile in the wrong direction, deposited them in a reed bed, and stole one of Midas's boots as a souvenir. But the birds continued, painted on the backs of signs, smaller now, and the reeds gave way to fences, and the fences to a smell that Midas had forgotten: woodsmoke, and soup, and earth that had been dug by people who expected to stay. The refuge was a former garden centre called Elysium Fields, run by nine pensioners, thirty children, and a woman named Mrs. Abernathy who had clearly been waiting for the collapse of civilization to really hit her stride. They had greenhouses made from bus shelters. They had chickens with better security than most banks used to. They had, written on a chalkboard, the most beautiful words in the new world: *Visitors: Soup at Six.* "Is this real?" said Midas. "Mostly," said Mrs. Abernathy. "The soup is. You're dripping on it." They were fed. Chewy was dried on a radiator and told everyone about eucalyptus until his battery mercifully faded. In exchange for the hubcap, which Mrs. Abernathy declared "perfect for scaring crows and impressing idiots," they received a filter cartridge, a bag of beans, seeds in a labelled envelope, and a replacement boot that was only mostly the right foot. "Why the graffiti?" Midas asked. "Why not just tell people?" "We did tell people," she said. "People who need us follow birds. People who want to rob us want a map and a postcode. You're the first to arrive by river, in a trolley, wearing a koala." "I have a knack." "We noticed." They might have stayed the night. Midas intended to stay the night. But at dusk Chewy, recharged by an afternoon of radiator sun, sat bolt upright and announced at full volume: "STRANGER DANGER! STRANGER DANGER!" — which was his burglar alarm, his fire alarm, and, unfortunately, his opinion of the refuge's guard dog. The dog objected. The chickens objected in sympathy. Somewhere in the commotion Midas knocked over a rain barrel, released the toll goat — which had apparently followed them, because goats believe in long-term investment — and was politely but firmly escorted to the gate by Mrs. Abernathy, who gave him a packed lunch for the road, in the tone of a woman ejecting a beloved but flammable nephew. So they came home in multiple ways, as the crow flies and as the Midas walks. First by bathtub, which served as a boat until it remembered it had a plughole. Then by trolley, pushed by the goat for almost fifty yards before the goat's union instincts reasserted themselves. Then by wheelbarrow, borrowed and returned to three different owners along the way, none of whom had owned it originally. And finally on foot — one booted, one mostly booted, one carrying a stuffed koala whose Hug Protocol had jammed permanently on, so that Midas arrived at the Fort looking like a man being slowly and lovingly strangled by a marsupial. They were wet. They were stung. Chewy now spoke only in a whisper and smelled strongly of honey. Midas had beans in one pocket, seeds in the other, a filter cartridge down his shirt, and a goat standing in the dentist's waiting room eating the appointment cards. But the filter, when he fitted it, worked. The water ran clear. The stove lit. The beans, eventually, became dinner, which in the After is not a meal so much as an argument won against the universe. "HOME IS WHERE YOUR BEST FRIEND IS!" whispered Chewy, arms still locked, one ear hanging by a thread. Midas sewed the ear back on. He put a tin of water on for tea that wasn't tea. Outside, the goat settled down on the welcome mat like it had always lived there, which, Midas supposed, it now did. "A refuge where no one hungry sleeps," he said. "We found it. We got thrown out of it. But we found it." And that, in the end, was the important thing. Not that the mission had gone sideways — missions under Midas always went sideways; it was practically their only reliable direction — but that sideways, eventually, if you kept walking and didn't drink the river, sometimes brought you home again. Worse for wear, better for soup, and with just enough seeds to start again tomorrow. *The Fort was not a fort. This is important. In the After, you named things for what you wanted them to be, and hoped the world was too tired to argue.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates a strong grasp of Terry Pratchett's distinctive style, capturing his dry wit, philosophical asides, and ability to find profound meaning in absurd situations. The author successfully creates a post-apocalyptic world that feels both bleak and oddly hopeful, populated by memorable characters whose interactions drive both humor and pathos. The characterization is particularly effective. Midas emerges as a fully realized protagonist whose defining trait - turning simple situations complicated - is both comedically exploited and genuinely endearing. His relationship with Chewy, the malfunctioning animatronic koala, provides consistent humor while avoiding the trap of making the toy merely a comic relief device. Chewy's programmed responses create genuine character moments, especially in his unwavering optimism contrasted against their dire circumstances. The prose style authentically captures Pratchett's voice through several key techniques: the footnote about the Fort, the matter-of-fact delivery of absurd situations, and the tendency to make profound observations through seemingly throwaway lines. The author particularly excels at Pratchett's signature move of starting with a grand philosophical statement and grounding it in mundane reality, as seen in the opening about the world ending "not with a bang but with a series of smaller, increasingly inconvenient endings." The plot structure adheres well to the prompt's requirements, beginning with deliberation, proceeding through escalating complications, and returning home "worse for wear." The mission's sideways progression feels organic rather than forced, with each setback building naturally from character actions and world logic. The toll goat, bee incident, and river mishap all stem from Midas's established character trait while advancing the story. The world-building is economical but effective, painting a picture of collapse through specific details like the abundance of dental floss and the repurposing of everyday objects. The refuge at Elysium Fields provides a satisfying glimpse of hope without undermining the story's established tone. However, the piece occasionally strains under the weight of its stylistic ambitions. Some metaphors feel slightly overwrought, and there are moments where the Pratchett pastiche becomes too conscious of itself. The ending, while thematically appropriate, edges toward unearned positivity given the characters' circumstances, though this is somewhat mitigated by the story's consistent tone of finding meaning in small victories. The dialogue effectively differentiates characters, with Chewy's programmed responses providing both humor and pathos, while Midas's voice remains consistent throughout. The supporting characters, particularly Mrs. Abernathy, feel authentic within their brief appearances. + Romance: Love in the Limelight — Score: 86.3
Prompt:
Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write one scene within a larger story set in Wales. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. The scene takes us through the characters meeting in this odd circumstance. Over the course of the scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. Write the actor as somewhat of a rogue with a fragile ego, which needs to be fed by having everyone like him. He is thoroughly charming, but the bookstore owner seems (at least superficially) immune to this; which paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive. The bookstore owner, despite the superficial rebuffs of the actor's charm, is inwardly more than a little charmed and flustered despite themselves. Write primarily in dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The bell over the door of Pen-y-Lan Books did not so much ring as panic. Ellis Vane came in backwards, dripping, sunglasses on in the rain, and pressed himself flat against the display of Welsh poetry. “Don’t look at me.” “I wasn’t,” said Catrin Hughes, from behind the counter. “Good. Excellent. Be less… conspicuous about not looking.” “You’re hiding behind Dylan Thomas. Conspicuous is rather baked in.” “Are they still out there?” “Who?” “Men with cameras. Large lenses. No souls.” Catrin glanced past him to Castle Street, where the Hay-on-Wye rain was doing its best to drown three photographers. “No. Only wet men shouting your name.” “That’s them. Lock the door.” “Absolutely not.” “Please? I’ll buy something. I’ll buy Wales. Is Wales for sale?” “Not to you.” He took off the sunglasses. Catrin mis-shelved *Under Milk Wood* with sheep farming. “You don’t recognise me, do you?” he said. “Should I?” “Ellis Vane. *Pendragon Hall*? Three series? I die beautifully in the second.” “We all have talents.” “You’ve never watched it.” “I sell books.” “People adapt books. Into television. With me in them.” “And yet here you are, hiding from the consequences.” “That hurts. Say it nicer.” “Here you are, hiding handsomely from the consequences.” “Better. You see? We can work together. Five minutes, they’ll get bored, chase a sheep with a scandalous past, and I’ll vanish.” “Five minutes. No touching, no posing, no signing anything with your face on it.” “You do know who I am.” “I know there’s a cardboard cut-out of you in the Co-op. Someone’s drawn a moustache on it.” “Was it flattering?” “It improved the symmetry.” He laughed, surprised, and then looked faintly wounded when she didn’t laugh back. Catrin turned away to straighten a perfectly straight pile of novels, her ears unaccountably hot. “You don’t like me,” he said. “I don’t know you.” “Most people find those two things very compatible. In the other direction.” “Most people haven’t got you dripping on their biography section.” He stepped obediently onto the mat. “Better?” “Barely.” “Give me a chance. I’m delightful in small doses. Ask anyone. Ask—” He waved vaguely at the window. “—them. They follow me everywhere. That’s basically a review.” “That’s basically a restraining order waiting to happen.” “God, you’re immune. Is it the accent? I can do the accent less. I am actually Welsh, you know. Cardiff.” “I know. You mention it in every interview. Usually while holding a leek.” “That was one photoshoot!” “Two.” “The second leek was metaphorical.” Catrin pressed her lips together so she would not smile, and reached for the kettle with unnecessary violence. “Tea?” she said. “Is that pity tea or Welsh hospitality tea?” “It’s shut-up-and-don’t-bleed-on-the-books tea.” “I’ll take it as a declaration of love.” “Take it as tea.” A camera flash lit the window. Ellis ducked behind LOCAL HISTORY. “Why Hay?” she asked. “Shouldn’t you be in London, being photographed eating a croissant like it owes you money?” “Filming near Brecon. I escaped for a bookshop crawl. Tragically, I am famous, so it became a manhunt.” “You came here for books?” “Don’t sound shocked. I can read. Slowly.” It slipped out before the charm could catch it. He went still. “That was a joke,” he said quickly. “Obviously. Very good reader. Speedy. Olympic reading.” Catrin handed him the mug. Their fingers did not touch. She was very aware of them not touching. “Slowly isn’t badly,” she said. “It is at school in Splott when you’re nine and Mr Davies makes you read aloud and the words—” He stopped. “Sorry. Tragic backstory. Terrible flirting.” “Go on.” “The words swapped places. Letters behaved like they’d had a drink. Everyone laughed. I learned to memorise everything instead. Scripts, menus, train announcements. If I pretend I’ve already read it, nobody asks me to prove it.” “Dyslexia?” “Diagnosed at twenty-four. By then I was excellent at pretending.” He attempted the grin. It didn’t quite arrive. “Please like me a bit less efficiently now. Pity is very ageing.” “I don’t pity you,” Catrin said. “I run a bookshop that loses money to the internet every day. Pity is fully booked.” “Was that meant to comfort me?” “Yes. Was it working?” “Oddly, yes. Most people hear that and do the head-tilt. You offered competitive suffering. Very Welsh. Very attractive— sorry. Very… normal.” She rearranged paperbacks into exactly the same pile. “They’ve gone,” she said, too quickly. Ellis looked. The street was empty except for rain and a lost tourist in a poncho. “So they have.” “You can go.” “I could.” “That is generally what doors are for. You’ve demonstrated entering. Exiting is the sequel.” He didn’t move. The grin returned, but slower now, less performed. “Recommend me a book,” he said. “One I can read slowly without feeling like a fraud.” “That’s a tall order from a man who buys Wales before tea.” Catrin went to the Welsh fiction shelf and, after a moment, pulled out a slim novel. “Short chapters,” she said. “No showing off. And if the letters misbehave, the story waits for you.” He read the title carefully. She pretended not to notice. “Will you judge me if it takes a month?” he asked. “I judge everyone. It’s a bookseller’s perk.” “And if I come back to report on chapter one?” “Then I’ll know chapter one took heroic effort or you’re a liar.” “Or I wanted to see if the moustache comment was a one-off.” “It wasn’t. I have range.” “I believe you.” He held the book to his chest. “How much do I owe you?” “Twelve ninety-nine. And you can sign the visitors’ book. Not with your face.” “With my terrible handwriting?” “Especially with that.” He signed, bought the book, and lingered at the door while the rain eased. “For the record,” he said, “you are the only person in Britain who hasn’t asked for a selfie.” “For the record,” Catrin said, “my phone is in the back, and I am furious about it.” He laughed, delighted, and she finally, helplessly, smiled back.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and adherence to the prompt requirements. The author successfully creates a meet-cute scenario in a Welsh bookstore with two well-defined characters whose personalities emerge clearly through dialogue. Ellis Vane is portrayed as a charming but insecure actor whose usual tactics fail against Catrin's dry wit, while Catrin maintains a facade of indifference that barely conceals her growing attraction. The dialogue is the story's greatest strength - it crackles with wit and feels authentic to both characters. Ellis's desperate charm offensive ("I'll buy Wales. Is Wales for sale?") contrasts beautifully with Catrin's deadpan responses ("Not to you"). The banter feels natural and reveals character depth, particularly when Ellis's vulnerability emerges through his admission about dyslexia and childhood struggles with reading. The Welsh setting is well-integrated without being heavy-handed. References to Hay-on-Wye, Dylan Thomas, Cardiff, and Splott feel organic rather than forced. The author captures the atmosphere of a small bookshop effectively through specific details like the panicked bell and the biography section. Character development is nuanced and believable. Ellis's fragile ego manifests in his need for validation ("Please like me a bit less efficiently now"), while his genuine attraction to Catrin grows precisely because she doesn't immediately succumb to his charm. Catrin's internal conflict between her outward resistance and growing attraction is subtly conveyed through physical actions like mis-shelving books and avoiding touch. The pacing works well, building tension through their verbal sparring while revealing deeper layers. The revelation about Ellis's dyslexia feels earned rather than manipulative, adding genuine vulnerability to his character. The ending strikes an appropriate balance - there's mutual attraction and connection, but it doesn't rush into unrealistic romance. Some minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the wit feels slightly forced, and the paparazzi threat resolves perhaps too conveniently. The piece also relies heavily on dialogue, which works here but leaves some opportunities for deeper atmospheric description unexplored. The prose style is clean and effective, with good rhythm and flow. Descriptive touches like "ears unaccountably hot" and "pressed her lips together so she would not smile" effectively convey Catrin's internal state without explicit telling. Prompt:
Whalepunk fantasy The Morska Conspiracy The Morska thieves guild experiences a sudden power vacuum as its leader was arrested in a raid in the early hours of the morning. Aya, a young woman born into aristocracy, has a keen interest in both the sciences and the arcane, having inherited her mother's gift for immateria magick (an outlawed practice for which her mother was, regrettably, hanged by the neck). Aya, bored with the world of aristocracy, has been spending her nights moonlighting with this very guild (masked, naturally). Leveraging her latent ability to summon dark entities from the immateria, she quickly rose through the ranks of the guild. Now, recognising the opportunity of the sudden power vacuum, Aya and her close companions Katra and Simeon, make a play for heart of the guild's claim to power: an ancient scythan artifact, under guard of spell and key in the depths of the guild hq. In contrast with the desperate chaos they had navigated thus far, the entrance to the underhold felt suddenly too quiet. Aya braces herself and reaches for the door. Write the next scene as the trio enter the underhold and find themselves confronted by none other than the guild leader herself, decidedly *un*-incarcerated, and in possession of both weapons and bodyguards. Paint a vivid picture of of the confrontation. Story beats: Aya is captured and unmasked. The trio are captured. Aya attempts to stall their demise by negotiating on her value as a hostage -- as she grapples with the inevitable consequences of her role in the guild being brought to light. Incorporate dialogue in the authentic voices of the characters. Do not write a fight scene. Lean into the gritty Victorian aesthetic with the dialogue & worldbuilding, as well as elements of gothic horror. In this world, men trust brass and oil and steel; magicka is feared and barely understood. Write in third person past tense, incorporating both Aya's internal monologue, and a heavy dialogue component. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The handle turned too easily. Aya felt it in her palm before her mind named it — no resistance from the spell-lock, no click of the great brass tumblers that were supposed to guard the underhold. The door swung inward on oiled hinges, silent as a coffin lid, and the smell came out to meet them: whale-oil and hot iron, low-tide brine, and beneath it something older and sweeter, like meat left in a sealed room. *Too quiet,* she thought. *We have mistaken a held breath for an empty house.* Beyond lay the underhold, sunk below the harbour wall where the tide pressed its black weight against the stones. Gas-mantles burned low in cages of green glass. Between pillars of leviathan rib, banded in copper, the floor descended in iron steps to the vault — and the vault door stood wide. The Scythan thing was already uncovered. It hung in a frame of chains above a basin of oil: a tooth, if a tooth could be the length of a man's arm, yellowed as old ivory and carved with mouths that had no business knowing the shape of human mouths. It turned very slowly, though there was no draught. Aya felt the immateria stir behind her eyes, as it always did near the thing, a pressure like fingertips testing the inside of her skull. "Well," said a woman's voice from the dark beside it. "The little mutiny arrives punctual." A foghorn sounded, far out in the harbour. Once. Long and mournful through the fog. Lamps flared. Ysolt Brane sat in the guildmaster's chair as if she had never left it — because, Aya understood with a cold and perfect clarity, she had not. No prison irons. No constable's bruises. Her grey hair was pinned, her black coat buttoned to the throat, a whalebone cane across her knees. In one gloved hand she held a revolver, unhurried, almost bored. Around her stood six bodyguards in oilskin and brass, harpoon-guns and cutlasses levelled, their faces muffled against the underhold damp. "Madame Brane," Simeon whispered. "Oh, God. Oh, God, no." "Steady," Katra muttered, though her hand had already drifted toward her belt-knife. "Touch that, Katra Voss, and Mr. Pell will take your hand off at the wrist and feed it to the basin," Brane said, without looking at her. "He has been practising. He is terribly keen." The largest of the bodyguards smiled with iron teeth. "Put them up," Aya said quietly. "Hands. Both of you. Do it now." "Ay—" Katra began. "Do it." Steel cocked, a small chorus of clicks in the vaulted dark. There was no fight to be had; men who trusted brass and oil and steel had arranged that there would not be, and the guns did not tremble. Simeon's hands rose, shaking. Katra's followed, slower, with murder in her face. Aya lifted her own and felt the cold settle into her stomach like swallowed river water. *Mother would have laughed,* she thought, unbidden and cruel. *Mother always said a mask is only a lie you wear on the outside.* "Search them," Brane said. "Bind them. The boy first; he looks likely to faint and I dislike a mess." They were efficient. Simeon's wrists were lashed with tarred sinew, Katra's with iron cuffs that she tested once, pointlessly, until a guard pressed a muzzle to the soft place beneath her jaw. When they came to Aya, the guard hesitated — her gloves, her good coat, the cut of her beneath the thief's black — and Brane made a small, impatient gesture. "The mask, Mr. Pell. Let us see what the night has been hiding from us." The cloth came away. Cold air touched her face. Somewhere behind her, Simeon made a sound he could not stop. Brane leaned forward. "Well," she said, with genuine interest. "Well, well. Bring her into the light." They pushed her forward, not roughly — worse, carefully, as one handles a thing newly discovered to be valuable or breakable. The gaslight found her: the pale Halloran face, the dark hair pinned as no dock-thief pinned it, her mother's grey eyes. "Lady Aya Halloran," Brane said. "Lord Halloran's daughter. Lord Halloran of the Admiralty Yards, who signs the warrants for half the press-gangs in Morska and hangs witches on the other half of his afternoons." She settled back. "And all this time, creeping through my counting-houses like a rat in a silk petticoat." The foghorn sounded again beyond the walls. A second time. The carved mouths on the tooth seemed, in the shifting light, to have changed their expressions by some small and terrible degree. "Madame—" Aya began. "You will not 'Madame' me, girl. You came for this." Brane lifted her cane and tapped the frame; the tooth swung and chimed faintly against its chains, a note felt in the teeth. "Spell and key, and you thought yourself clever enough for both. Who sold you the key-word?" "No one sold us anything," Katra spat. "Your house is rotten, Ysolt. Everyone knows it. The constables took you at dawn—" "The constables took a woman in my coat at dawn, in a carriage I provided, screaming my name very convincingly." Brane's smile did not reach her eyes. "I paid her family well. I find a rumour of my arrest is an excellent net. It shows me which fish swim upward when they think the shark is dead." She looked back to Aya. "And it has caught me a very strange fish indeed." "You could have announced yourself upstairs," Simeon said, his voice cracking. "You could have — we would have stood down, Madame Brane, we only thought—" "You thought the chair was empty and the strongbox full, Mr. Adeyemi. Do not dress theft in philosophy; it embarrasses you both." She raised the revolver a fraction. "Katra Voss. Simeon Adeyemi. And a lord's daughter, playing at shadows and summoning — what is it your sort summons, Lady Aya? In the immateria? Your mother could have told us, I suppose, if the rope had left her breath to speak." Aya's throat closed. The scaffold at Gallows Reach, remembered though she had been kept from it: the black hood, the crowd, the smell of hot tar and oranges. She had been eleven, and her father had made her stay in the carriage, and she had heard it anyway — the drop, and then the silence that had a shape. *I will not hang,* she thought. *I will not hang as she did, with my name read out like a bill of sale.* "Then think, Madame," she said, and was astonished at how level her voice came out. "Before you do anything that cannot be undone." "Threats?" Brane said softly. "From a bound girl?" "Arithmetic." Aya forced herself to meet the older woman's eyes. "Kill Katra and Simeon and you lose two thieves. Kill me, quietly, down here, and you gain nothing but a risk — because my father will burn this district to the waterline looking for me, and he will not stop at your doors. But alive, I am worth a fortune in ransom. More than that. I am worth *leverage*. Over the Admiralty. Over the yards. Over every contract your guild has ever begged for." "Alive, you are also a tongue," Brane said. "Tongues wag, Lady Aya. Especially aristocratic ones, when the constable puts the question." "And dead, I am a scandal you cannot control," Aya said. "Alive and *ruined*—" The word nearly stuck. She made herself say it plainly, made herself look at what it meant: the drawing-rooms closing like doors, her father's face, the engagement portraits burned, her name become a thing governesses warned girls about in lowered voices. Worse than ruin — exposure. The magick. The noose waiting inside the scandal like a hook inside bait. "Alive and ruined, I am yours. My father will pay anything to keep this buried. Anything. Ask him for the harbour tolls. Ask him for the witch-warrants, unsigned. He will sign his own soul in whale-oil before he lets Morska learn that his daughter ran masked with thieves and called things out of the dark." Silence. The oil in the basin stirred though nothing touched it. "She's lying," Katra said hoarsely. "Aya, don't — don't bargain yourself to this—" "Quiet," Aya said, without looking back, and hated herself for the steadiness of it. "I am not lying, Madame Brane. You know the worth of a secret. You've built this guild on them. I am simply the most expensive secret you have ever owned." Brane studied her for a long moment. Then she lowered the revolver — not away, only down, resting it against her knee like a sleeping animal. "Expensive secrets," she said, "have a habit of eating their keepers." She nodded toward the tooth, turning, turning, in its chains. "But perhaps we shall let something older than either of us appraise you." Beyond the guild walls, out in the fog-drowned harbour, the foghorn sounded a third time. "Bind her separately," Brane said. "And bring her closer to it. I want to see what it does when it smells her mother's blood."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical craft and atmospheric worldbuilding within the "whalepunk" fantasy setting. The author successfully creates a vivid Victorian-gothic atmosphere through detailed descriptions of whale-oil lamps, leviathan ribs, and industrial maritime elements. The opening with the too-easy door handle immediately establishes tension and foreshadowing. The dialogue feels authentic to the period and characters, with Brane's measured, threatening speech patterns contrasting effectively with the younger characters' more emotional responses. Aya's negotiation scene is particularly well-executed, showing her desperation masked by aristocratic composure as she bargains with her own ruin. The pacing builds tension effectively from the quiet entrance through the revelation of Brane's trap to Aya's unmasking and final gambit. The author handles the power dynamics well, showing how Aya attempts to leverage her social position even while captured. However, some elements feel slightly overwrought - phrases like "silence that had a shape" and the repeated emphasis on the carved mouths changing expression border on purple prose. The Scythan artifact, while atmospheric, feels somewhat disconnected from the main action and serves more as gothic decoration than plot element. The characterization is generally strong, particularly Aya's internal conflict between her aristocratic upbringing and criminal activities. Her willingness to accept ruin to save her companions feels earned given her established character. Brane emerges as a formidable antagonist with clear motivations and methods. The worldbuilding integrates well with the plot, using the industrial maritime setting and class tensions to drive character conflicts. The magic system feels appropriately mysterious and feared within this world's context. Minor weaknesses include some repetitive atmospheric descriptions and a few moments where the prose becomes overly dense with imagery at the expense of narrative momentum. + Fanfic-crossover: Gunpowder Rendezvous — Score: 81.6
Prompt:
Gunpowder Rendezvous Spike Spiegel & Revy Write a story where Spike Spiegel (Cowboy Bebop) and Revy (Black Lagoon) meet in a seedy bar after both being hired for the same bounty. Their mutual attraction is complicated by their trust issues and competitive instincts. Include drinking, gunplay, and unresolved sexual tension that culminates in a motel room standoff. **Spike Spiegel (Cowboy Bebop)** Spike is a laid-back bounty hunter with a dark past as a syndicate enforcer. He practices Jeet Kune Do and is exceptionally skilled with firearms. He's chronically broke, constantly hungry, and addicted to cigarettes. Despite his carefree attitude, he's haunted by his past and the woman he left behind. He has a prosthetic eye from a past injury that affects his depth perception. He's fatalistic to the extreme, often saying he's already died once. He values freedom above all else and dislikes attachments, though he secretly cares deeply for his crew. Famous quote: "Whatever happens, happens." **Revy/Rebecca Lee (Black Lagoon)** Revy is a Chinese-American dual-wielding gunslinger with unparalleled shooting skills. She's foul-mouthed, chain-smoking, and has severe anger management issues stemming from childhood abuse. She's known as "Two Hands" for her ability to accurately fire two pistols simultaneously. She drinks heavily and solves most problems with violence. Despite her hardened exterior, she has moments of vulnerability, particularly around Rock. She has a dragon tattoo covering her right arm and typically wears extremely short shorts and a black crop top regardless of the situation. Famous quote: "I'm not a good person, not a bad person. I'm just here." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Gunpowder Rendezvous** The bar sits two streets back from the docks, where the neon stutters, the floor sticks to boots, and nobody looks up unless money or trouble walks in. Spike Spiegel sits at the counter with an empty wallet, a half-empty glass, and a cigarette burning down to his fingers. His stomach growls. The bartender ignores it. In the corner, a neon jukebox keeps playing the same scratchy rock track on repeat, its pink light pulsing across bottles, smoke, and cracked vinyl seats. Spike watches the door in the mirror behind the bar. His real eye tracks movement. His prosthetic eye takes in the same room a fraction differently, flattening distance and turning edges strange. He adjusts without thinking. He always adjusts. The door bangs open. Revy walks in like she owns the place and resents it for existing. A black crop top, shorts cut almost to the point of indecency, boots, and a dragon tattoo curling down her right arm. Two modified Berettas ride at her hips. She lights a cigarette before she reaches the counter, scans the room once, and chooses the stool two seats away from Spike. “Whiskey,” she says. “Leave the bottle.” The bartender obeys fast enough to reveal good survival instincts. Revy drinks, exhales smoke, and glances sideways. “You keep staring, cowboy, and you lose the eye that still works.” Spike smiles around his cigarette. “I’m just admiring the artillery.” “Sure you are.” “That too.” Her eyes narrow, but amusement flickers there. She looks him over without hurry: messy green hair, loose suit, long legs stretched into the walkway, posture so relaxed it borders on insulting. He looks broke, hungry, and completely unbothered by both. “You waiting for someone?” she asks. “Depends who pays.” “Marco Vale. Twelve million. Dead or alive, but alive pays full.” Spike lifts his glass. “Small universe.” Revy turns fully toward him now. “No. Absolutely not. I take this job yesterday.” “I take it three days ago.” “Bullshit.” He shrugs. “Whatever happens, happens.” “What the fuck does that mean?” “It means I’m not leaving.” She laughs once, sharp and humorless. “Then you got a problem.” “I have several. Most of them are charming.” The jukebox skips, catches, and starts the same track again. Guitars grind through static. Revy pours another drink and slides the bottle, despite herself, a few inches toward him. Spike pours. Their fingers almost touch. Neither pulls back immediately. “You syndicate?” she asks. “Not anymore.” “You look like a man with bodies behind him.” “I look in mirrors as little as possible.” “Smart.” She taps ash onto the floor. “People who look too long start making speeches.” “You speaking from experience?” “I’m not a good person, not a bad person. I’m just here.” “Here is my seat.” “Then move me.” The challenge lands between them, warm as the whiskey. Spike leans closer, slow enough that she can stop him, shoot him, or meet him halfway. Revy does none of those things. Her knee brushes his. Her hand rests near her gun, not on it. Smoke curls between their faces. Then the bathroom door opens, and Marco Vale steps out with a hat pulled low and a fresh scar splitting his chin. Both of them stand. Marco freezes. The bar goes silent except for the jukebox, which cheerfully restarts its song. “Mine,” Revy says. Spike sighs. “We can split him.” “I don’t split.” Marco runs. Revy draws both pistols and fires as he dives behind a table. Bottles explode. Glass rains across the counter. Spike moves in the opposite direction, low and loose, his Jericho snapping twice. One shot takes Marco’s hat. Another shatters the exit sign above his head. Marco kicks over a stool, fires blindly, and bolts through the kitchen. Spike flows after him. Revy vaults the counter. In the alley, rain slicks the concrete and turns every neon sign into smeared color. Marco fires from behind a dumpster. Revy answers with both hands, muzzle flashes strobing in perfect rhythm. Spike ducks a shot that passes close enough to move his hair, misjudges the dumpster’s distance by inches, and feels a bullet crease his sleeve. “You hit?” Revy shouts. “Jealous?” “Of the bullet?” He grins, pivots, and uses a Jeet Kune Do kick to slam the dumpster lid down on Marco’s gun hand. Marco screams and runs again, clutching his wrist. Revy shoots the trash cans beside him, herding him toward a fire escape. Spike takes the stairs two at a time. Revy comes up faster, shoulder brushing his as she passes. For one suspended second they move together beautifully, two predators sharing the same line. Then Revy reaches the roof door first and points a gun back at Spike. “End of the team-up.” He points his own gun, lazy and precise. “You’re welcome, by the way.” “For what?” “Not shooting you in the bar.” “I notice you don’t.” “I notice you don’t either.” Marco crashes through a skylight and drops into the motel across the alley. A window shatters below. Both fire at the same time, not at each other, and follow. The motel room smells of mildew, bleach, and old cigarettes. The bed is unmade. Marco lies tangled in curtains under the broken window, groaning, one hand raised. Revy steps on his chest and keeps one pistol on him. Her other pistol swings toward Spike as he enters through the door. Spike keeps his gun level. “Really?” “Call it insurance.” “You call everything insurance when you don’t want to call it fear.” Her jaw tightens. “Say that again.” He steps closer instead. The muzzle of her gun nearly touches his shirt. His gun hovers near her ribs, not quite touching. Marco wisely stops groaning. “You don’t trust me,” Spike says. “No shit.” “You want to.” “I want the money.” “Only the money?” Revy’s eyes drop, briefly, to his mouth. “Don’t flatter yourself.” “You’re still not shooting.” “Neither are you.” Rain hammers the broken window. Somewhere downstairs, another neon sign buzzes, and a radio in the next room plays a song neither of them hears. Revy breathes hard. Her crop top clings with rain. Spike’s cigarette is gone, but smoke still hangs in his clothes. He is close enough that she can see the faint mismatch between his eyes, close enough that trust becomes a physical problem rather than an idea. “Lower it,” she says. “You first.” “Cowboy, I shoot people for less than this conversation.” “I believe you.” “Then why are you smiling?” “Because you keep choosing not to.” Her finger tightens, then eases. His does the same. The guns remain raised. The space between them shrinks by another inch, charged and impossible, until Marco rolls, grabs the fallen curtain rod, and swings it into the lamp. The room plunges into darkness. Two shots flash. When the emergency light flickers on, Marco is gone through the bathroom window, leaving blood, wet footprints, and the bounty unpaid. Revy stands with both guns still out. Spike stands opposite her, his weapon lowered only slightly. Their eyes lock. Anger, attraction, and professional humiliation collide without resolution. “Next time I see you,” she says, “I take the shot.” Spike smiles. “Next time, buy me dinner first.” She holsters one gun, keeps the other loose at her side, and walks past him close enough for their shoulders to touch.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and character work within the noir/action genre. The author successfully captures the distinctive voices and mannerisms of both Spike Spiegel and Revy, maintaining their canonical personalities while creating believable chemistry between them. The dialogue crackles with tension and authenticity, particularly in the bar scene where their verbal sparring establishes both attraction and wariness. The prose style effectively balances descriptive richness with the lean, economical style appropriate to the genre. Sentences like "The bar sits two streets back from the docks, where the neon stutters, the floor sticks to boots, and nobody looks up unless money or trouble walks in" establish atmosphere efficiently while avoiding purple prose. The author demonstrates skill in action sequences, making the chase and gunfight scenes kinetic and easy to follow. Character consistency is a major strength. Spike's fatalistic philosophy, casual competence, and underlying melancholy come through clearly, as does Revy's aggressive exterior masking deeper vulnerabilities. The sexual tension builds organically through their interactions rather than being forced, and their mutual distrust feels earned given their backgrounds. The structure works well, moving from setup through action to the standoff that fulfills the prompt's requirements. The ending avoids false resolution while maintaining the unresolved tension that defines both characters. However, the piece occasionally relies on familiar noir tropes without adding much innovation, and some descriptive passages, while competent, don't rise above workmanlike execution. The action sequences are well-choreographed but could benefit from more distinctive details. The motel room standoff effectively captures the psychological complexity of two dangerous people caught between attraction and professional necessity, though it doesn't quite achieve the emotional depth that would elevate it from good to exceptional.
