+ Young adult drama: Gone South — Score: 86.8
Prompt:
Young adult drama Gone South Taylor is a 16 year old teen with a history of "concerning behavioural patterns" (or that's how the stupid smug school counsellor worded it on the phone call to Mom). It shouldn't be a surprise: When you live in a backwater town in Tennessee, your choices are: a. be mind-fuckingly bored, or b. invent some drama. Two days ago, Taylor came out to their family as trans. This disclosure was *not* in the category of invented drama -- it was, in fact, the real deal, and a long time coming. It didn't go well. The last 48 hours had been pure disaster. In a moment of desperate inspiration, Taylor had decided to get the hell out of dodge. And so an escape plan was hatched and executed within the space of 30 minutes. That was last night. Now Taylor was two states away, having been unceremoniously ejected from their hitched ride in downtown New Orleans. Write the next chapter in Taylor's story as they find their feet in this new environment. Tell the chapter over the course of their first day in New Orleans, in which Taylor meets another runaway with issues and secrets. Taylor navigates this new world, not knowing who to trust or what the dangers are. Write in Taylor's voice, and incorporate their internal monologue as they grapple with intense & conflicting emotions. Also incorporate dialogue with the interesting characters Taylor meets. First person, mixed tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**GONE SOUTH - Chapter Two** My phone is at 12% and my ass is asleep on a bench in Jackson Square, which is how my first morning in New Orleans starts. Not starts, exactly. Last night started it. Last night the guy who picked me up outside Memphis — *nice* guy, church sticker on his dash, kept calling me "buddy" in a way that made my skin crawl less than sir would have — suddenly pulled over on Canal Street at 1 a.m. and said, "This is far as I go." Just like that. Door locks popping. Rain starting. Now it's morning and the rain is gone and everything smells like wet concrete and powdered sugar and piss. My backpack is between my ankles. My binder is damp under my t-shirt and I can't tell if I'm sweating or if I never actually dried off. 12%. Airplane mode ON. Don't be an idiot, Taylor. I have: $43, a toothbrush, two t-shirts, one pair of jeans I'm wearing, a hoodie, my EpiPen (peanuts, because my body couldn't just pick one way to try to kill me), a paperback with the cover ripped off, and Mom's texts unread. 47 notifications. I counted without opening them. That's a talent. *Don't open them. If you open them you'll call. If you call you'll cry. If you cry you'll say where you are.* I open them. **Mom: Taylor please just tell me ur alive** **Mom: Dad didn't mean it like that** **Mom: Mrs Hendricks saw you at the gas station??** **Dad: Get home now.** **Mom: please baby** *Baby.* She hadn't called me that since I was like, ten. Two days ago at the kitchen table I said, "I'm trans, I've known since I was twelve, I'm not doing this for attention," and Dad laughed. Actually laughed. Like I'd told a joke wrong. Then Mom kept saying my old name over and over like if she said it enough it would glue back on. I lock the phone. 11% now. Jesus. Looking at it is eating it. A pigeon walks up to me like it pays rent here. Somewhere a trumpet is playing and it's so good it makes me angry. Everything here is loud and alive on purpose. Back home in Dunlap, the most exciting thing was when the Dollar General got a slushie machine. "You're gonna bake sitting there." I jump so hard my backpack tips. Girl. Maybe seventeen? Black, hair in two puffs, one side shaved, wearing a Saints jersey cut into a crop top and boots with the laces double-knotted. She's holding two paper cups and has a backpack even more beat up than mine, with a little plastic dinosaur keychain hanging off it. She holds out a cup. "Chicory coffee. It's gross until it's not. You look like you slept outside, no offense." "I didn't sleep," I say. "Even more reason." I don't take it. *Rule one of every assembly since sixth grade: don't take stuff from strangers. Rule one of the last 48 hours: strangers are literally the only reason you're not still in Tennessee.* "I'm not gonna poison you in front of the cathedral," she says. "That's like, double illegal. I'm Wren." "Taylor." "I know." My stomach drops. "What?" She grins and sits — not next to me, one bench slat away, which I appreciate more than the coffee. "Nah, I'm kidding. You just look like a Taylor. You got that main-character fleeing-a-small-town thing. Where you from?" "Nowhere." "Cool. I'm from nowhere too. Mine's about twenty minutes that way, but we don't talk about it." She says it light, but her hand tightens around her cup. I notice because I'm doing the same thing. We drink. It's bitter and hot and my hands stop shaking a little, which pisses me off because I don't want to be grateful to a random person yet. "How old are you?" she asks. "Sixteen." *Why did you tell the truth, idiot?* "Almost seventeen." "I'm eighteen," she says, too fast. "Okay." "I am." "I said okay." A cop on a horse goes past. An actual horse. Wren suddenly becomes very interested in her boots. I become very interested in not existing. The cop doesn't even look at us, but my heart is still hammering when he's gone. Wren exhales. "You got a place?" "No." "Plan?" "Working on it." "Money?" I stare at her. "Right, sorry, this is sounding like an interview to rob you. I have forty-three dollars too, probably. Look—" She digs in her pocket and shows me, quick: a crumpled flyer. **ST. JUDE YOUTH DROP-IN. Showers. Food. No ID needed. 12-6.** "They don't call your parents unless you're, like, dying. There's a lady, Miss Dee, she'll let you charge your phone if you don't make it weird." My phone. 11%. Mom. *No charger in sight and this girl just magically has the answer? In movies this is where you get trafficked, Taylor.* "Why are you helping me?" I ask. "Why'd you take the coffee then?" "I didn't say I was smart." That makes her laugh for real. "Maybe you remind me of me in April. I was way worse at this. I cried at a Popeyes for an hour." "Did you go home?" The laugh stops. "No." We walk to Café Du Monde because Wren says if I'm gonna be homeless in New Orleans I legally have to get beignets on day one or they revoke my visa. The line is all tourists in matching shirts. Wren doesn't get in line. She walks around back like she works there, talks to a guy washing dishes — "Hey, Luis, my cousin's first day" — and two minutes later comes back with a bag, powdered sugar already on her chin. "You stole those," I say when we're by the river. "I liberated them. Luis owes me. I helped him jump his car." "Do you actually know him or—" "Taylor. Eat." It's hot and sweet and gets all over my black t-shirt. For like thirty seconds I am not thinking about Dad's face or the bus station bathroom last night where I stood in a stall just trying to breathe flat enough. I'm just a kid eating sugar by the Mississippi, which is browner and faster than I expected. Then a man in a clean white shirt who'd been watching us stands up from his bench. "Y'all need a ride somewhere? My place has AC, y'all can clean up." He smiles at me when he says clean up. Not at Wren. At me. Wren steps — subtle — between us. "We're good, sir. Her dad's meeting us." *Her.* It hits wrong and also, weirdly, it doesn't? Because she guessed wrong but she meant it as a shield? I don't know. My brain is doing that static thing. "We're good," I manage. He holds up his hands, still smiling. "Just being friendly." He walks away. Slow. "You okay?" Wren says. "Yeah. Thanks. For—" I gesture. "Don't thank me yet. That's like, Lesson One. Guys who offer AC at 10 a.m. aren't offering AC." "I know that." "Knowing and freezing are different. I froze the first time too." We spend the afternoon doing nothing in a way that feels like doing something. We watch street performers. We sit in the shade outside the drop-in but don't go in yet because I keep saying "in a minute." Wren doesn't push. She tells me which bathrooms are safest, which corner store won't follow you around, that you should keep your money split — some in your shoe. She has a system for everything. She also keeps checking her own phone, an old cracked Android, and deleting a text before I can see it. Every hour. On the hour. At 3:07 she goes to the bathroom at McDonald's and leaves her backpack with me. "Watch T-Rex," she says, pointing at the dinosaur. "He's the brains." I am not going to look in her bag. I am absolutely not that person. Then her bag buzzes. And buzzes. And a little paper slides halfway out of the front pocket when it falls over. It's a bus ticket. Baton Rouge to New Orleans. Dated three days ago. And underneath it, folded about a hundred times, a MISSING poster printout. Cheap ink. Her face, younger, hair longer, school photo smile. **WREN?? No. ALIYAH BROOKS, 15, LAST SEEN APRIL 9.** Fifteen. Not eighteen. Missing since April. That's — that's almost four months. *Oh. Oh shit.* The bathroom door chimes. I shove the paper back so fast I tear the corner. She comes out, sees my face, and stops. She knows. Of course she knows. Her eyes go to the bag, to me, to the door. "Don't," she says quietly. "I didn't—" "You did. It's fine. Just—" She sits down hard on the curb, all that cool gone. "Don't call. Please don't call. My stepdad put that up. My mom— she knows I'm alive. I text her. She just can't say, because he's—" She presses her palms into her eyes. "I was gonna tell you. I just wanted one day where I was the person who knew shit, you know? Not the poster." Traffic goes by. My phone in my pocket feels like a brick. 9% now. Mom texting a daughter who won't answer. Aliyah's mom texting a daughter who deletes it every hour so someone won't see. "I'm not calling anyone," I say. "I can barely keep my own phone alive." She lets out a breath that shakes. "I'm sorry I lied about—" "Wren. Aliyah. Whatever. You got me beignets." She laughs, wet. "That's a low bar." "It's day one. Bar is on the floor." We finally go into the drop-in at five. Miss Dee is exactly like Wren said — big earrings, no bullshit. She points me to a shower and doesn't say my name wrong because she asks first. Just: "What do I call you, love?" Like it's easy. My throat closes up so fast I have to stare at the tiles. "Taylor," I whisper. "They/them." "You got it, Taylor." In the shower, with real hot water, I cry for like two minutes, hard and ugly, then stop because someone else is waiting. When I come out, Wren is charging both our phones behind the desk and guarding them like a dragon. 8% climbing to 9%. "Miss Dee says there's cots tonight if it storms," she says. "You staying?" I think about Mom's *please baby*. I think about Dad laughing. I think about going back and being deadnamed at school every day until I graduate or explode. I think about not going back and being a poster too. "I don't know," I say honestly. "Yeah," Wren says. "That's Lesson Two. You don't have to know tonight." Outside, thunder rolls over the river. My phone buzzes once on the charger. **Mom: i love you whoever you are. just come home safe** I read it three times. I don't answer. Not yet. But I don't turn it off either.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and authentic voice work within the young adult genre. The author successfully captures Taylor's distinctive narrative voice through a blend of cynical humor, vulnerability, and teenage authenticity. The first-person mixed tense approach works effectively, creating immediacy while allowing for reflection. The characterization is particularly strong. Taylor emerges as a fully realized protagonist whose internal contradictions feel genuine - simultaneously street-smart and naive, guarded yet desperate for connection. The author skillfully weaves Taylor's trans identity into the narrative without making it the sole defining characteristic, showing how it intersects with their broader experience of displacement and family rejection. Wren/Aliyah is equally well-developed, with her own secrets and survival mechanisms that parallel Taylor's journey without feeling repetitive. The dialogue feels natural and age-appropriate, avoiding the common pitfall of adults writing unconvincing teenage speech. Conversations flow organically and reveal character through subtext - particularly effective in the scene where Wren deflects the predatory man, and in the gradual revelation of her true identity and circumstances. The New Orleans setting is rendered with sensory detail that feels authentic rather than touristy. The author captures the city's atmosphere through specific details like chicory coffee, beignets, and the mix of smells, while using the urban environment to highlight both opportunities and dangers for vulnerable youth. The pacing is well-controlled, building tension through small revelations and encounters rather than manufactured drama. The discovery of Wren's missing poster creates genuine stakes without feeling contrived, and the parallel between the two runaways' situations adds thematic depth. However, the piece occasionally relies on convenient plot devices - Wren appearing with exactly the resources Taylor needs, the helpful dishwasher providing free food, the drop-in center being perfectly accommodating. While these serve the narrative, they strain credibility slightly. The emotional complexity is handled with particular skill. The author avoids easy answers while maintaining hope, showing how survival requires both wariness and trust, independence and connection. The ending strikes an appropriate balance - neither falsely optimistic nor gratuitously dark. The prose style is clean and effective, with strong imagery that serves character and mood rather than showing off. The author demonstrates restraint, allowing emotional moments to breathe without over-explaining or manipulating reader response. + Dystopic-comedy: My Apocalypse Buddy — Score: 82.5
Prompt:
My Apocalypse Buddy Write a wry, dry short story of survival and adventure loosely in the style of Terry Pratchett, set in the post-technological collapse world. The story begins with the pair deliberating their predicament and intent for the day's mission, details the ways in which the mission inevitably goes sideways, and returns them to home base in multiple ways, worse for wear. [characters] - the animo-tronic stuffed koala, Chewy, from some long forgotten before time - midas, our hapless protagonist, who has a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# My Apocalypse Buddy "The problem," said Midas, "is that you're dying. Slowly, and with commentary." Chewy considered this from his perch on the dashboard, where he had been charging, or at least thinking very hard about charging. "I am not dying. I am experiencing a managed decline in available power. There's a difference." "Is there?" "Yes. Dying is dramatic. This is merely inevitable." Chewy was a koala, approximately two feet tall, formerly soft and now mostly firm in inconvenient places. He had once lived in a shop in the Before Times, where, according to the faded tag still stitched to his foot, he had been programmed to Teach Your Child About Feelings! This involved singing, hugging, and eyes that changed colour according to his emotional state. The singing had mercifully packed up around the time civilisation did. The hugging remained technically possible but inadvisable. The eyes, unfortunately, worked perfectly. At present they were a thoughtful blue, which meant calm, or possibly that he was saving power by not being annoyed yet. Midas lived with him in a double-decker bus that had come to rest, with a certain finality, halfway up the only hill for miles. It was not a bad home, as homes went after the end of the world. It had a roof, most of a door, and a wood stove made from a filing cabinet. It also had, as of yesterday, a dead battery array, a cracked solar panel, and a koala whose left ear had begun to droop when his charge got low. The apocalypse, it should be noted, had not arrived with fire and trumpets. It had arrived with a series of increasingly urgent software updates, a global shrug, and then a Tuesday when nothing switched back on.* People had adapted, as people do, mostly by complaining and then inventing new religions around supermarkets. "We need a Series Nine cell," said Chewy. "There's one in the drone that crashed behind the old retail park. We go at dawn, avoid the Mire, avoid the Toll Men, retrieve it, and return before dark. A simple plan." "You say that like simple plans have ever met me," said Midas. Midas had a gift. Not a useful one. Where other men found four-leaf clovers, Midas found the one patch of thin ice on an otherwise solid lake, the one loose rung, the one goat with a personal vendetta. His mother had named him Midas in hope. The world, which has a sense of humour and very poor taste, had taken it as a suggestion: everything he touched turned, not to gold, but to a complicated afternoon. They set out at dawn, which in practice meant mid-morning, because Midas had put his boots on the roof to dry and a crow had moved into the left one. They took the Mire anyway, because the Toll Men had raised their prices to two tins and a secret, and Midas was short on both. The Mire was not so much a bog as a rumour of solid ground spread thinly over water. Halfway across, their handcart sank with the quiet resignation of a thing that had seen this coming. Midas lost a shoe, found it again containing a frog, and stepped, with unerring instinct, into the only hole deep enough to require negotiation to get out of. Chewy's eyes flickered amber. Anxiety, or mild alarm. "Don't look at me like that," said Midas, up to his knees. "I am not looking at you like anything. I am conserving—" The amber deepened. "—judgement." They arrived at the retail park by noon, wet, muddy, and accompanied by the frog, which had apparently decided this was a quest now. The delivery drone lay nose-down behind a collapsed shoe shop, half-buried in ivy and old promotional bunting that still insisted EVERYTHING MUST GO, which, in fairness, it had. Midas pried open the compartment with a screwdriver and a certain amount of optimistic violence. Inside, nestled like an egg, was a Series Nine cell, intact and faintly humming. "Oh," he breathed. "Beautiful." Chewy's eyes went bright, unmistakable gold. Excitement. Joy. Greed, possibly, if you were the sort of person who watched a stuffed koala's face for tells. Unfortunately, someone was. "Well," said a voice behind them, "that's interesting." The Toll Men had not, it turned out, stayed on the toll road. Toll Men rarely do; tolls are a philosophy, not a location. There were three of them, led by a woman called Brenda who had once, in the Before, managed a garden centre, and had carried the authority of that position into the new world like a sword. "We'll trade," said Midas quickly. "We found it, but we'd consider—" Chewy's eyes blazed gold. "We'd consider it priceless and irreplaceable," Brenda translated. "Thought so. Hand it over, love." What followed was not exactly a fight. Fights imply a certain symmetry of competence. What followed was Midas attempting to run, discovering his damp boot had other plans, Chewy being grabbed by an ear and objecting in a voice that went squeaky under low power, and the frog achieving, in the confusion, a small but significant victory over Brenda's second-in-command. Midas did the only thing he could reliably do: he made it worse. He kicked the drone. The drone, which had been dead for eleven years, took this personally. Its remaining rotors spasmed into life, it lurched upright shedding ivy and bunting, rose three feet, screamed in a long-forgotten doorbell chime, and flew directly into the shoe shop window. In the ensuing noise, shouting, and brief rain of discounted trainers, they ran. They returned home in several ways, none of them dignified. First on foot, at speed. Then by shopping trolley down the long slope behind the retail park, a mode of transport that relied heavily on screaming as a steering mechanism. Then by river, clinging to a door that Midas insisted was a raft and Chewy insisted was evidence. Then, for the final humiliating mile, towed in a barrow by Brenda's goat, which Brenda lent them, at interest, after Midas — wet, singed, one shoe down, and holding a koala with a torn ear — had offered her the drone's other cell, the one for her hearing aid, which he had pocketed without entirely knowing why. Some things even Midas touched turned out, accidentally, to be useful. He tried not to make a habit of it. The universe noticed habits. By dusk the bus appeared on the hill, lamplit and leaning slightly, like it had been worried. Midas installed the cell by candlelight, with burnt fingers and a great deal of swearing that Chewy pretended, generously, to be too low-powered to hear. Then there was a click, a hum, and Chewy's eyes came up steady and green. Contentment. Or as close as either of them got. "There," said Midas. "Not dying." "No," agreed Chewy. His torn ear flopped. "Merely in several pieces, damp, and in debt to a goat. As is my companion." Midas looked down at himself: mud to the waist, one bare foot, a trainer burn across one arm, and the frog asleep in his pocket. "Tomorrow," he said, "we need food." Chewy's eyes flickered, very faintly, amber. "Of course we do," he said. *The official term was a Cascading Systems Interruption. Most people called it the Great Switching Off, on the grounds that if you were going to lose antibiotics and satellites in the same week, you were entitled to a name that sounded like someone's fault.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates a strong grasp of Terry Pratchett's distinctive style, successfully capturing his dry wit, footnoted observations, and philosophical humor about human nature. The author effectively establishes the post-apocalyptic setting through clever details like the "Great Switching Off" and maintains the requested wry tone throughout. The characterization is particularly well-executed. Midas emerges as a believable hapless protagonist whose "gift" for finding trouble feels authentic rather than forced. Chewy, the animatronic koala, is given genuine personality through his color-changing eyes and dry commentary, avoiding the trap of making him merely a comic relief sidekick. Their relationship feels lived-in and genuine. The dialogue sparkles with Pratchettesque wit, particularly in the opening exchange about "managed decline" versus dying. The banter between characters feels natural while advancing both plot and character development. The prose maintains an elegant balance between humor and genuine pathos. The mission structure follows the prompt perfectly - deliberation, inevitable complications, and return home "worse for wear." The escalating disasters feel organic to Midas's character rather than arbitrary, and each setback builds logically from his established nature. The world-building is economical but effective, painting a believable post-technological landscape without over-explaining. Details like the Toll Men, the Mire, and the bus-home feel authentic to this universe. However, the piece occasionally veers toward being slightly overwrought in its attempts to capture Pratchett's voice, particularly in some of the more elaborate metaphors. A few moments feel like they're trying too hard to be clever rather than letting the humor emerge naturally. The ending, while satisfying, resolves perhaps a bit too neatly given the established pattern of Midas's misfortunes. The writing demonstrates strong technical skill with varied sentence structure and natural flow. The imagery is vivid without being purple, and the emotional beats land effectively. The piece succeeds in being both funny and genuinely engaging, creating investment in these characters' continued survival. + Romance: Love in the Limelight — Score: 81.8
Prompt:
Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write one scene within a larger story set in Wales. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. The scene takes us through the characters meeting in this odd circumstance. Over the course of the scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. Write the actor as somewhat of a rogue with a fragile ego, which needs to be fed by having everyone like him. He is thoroughly charming, but the bookstore owner seems (at least superficially) immune to this; which paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive. The bookstore owner, despite the superficial rebuffs of the actor's charm, is inwardly more than a little charmed and flustered despite themselves. Write primarily in dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The bell over the door of Parry's Books didn't so much ring as scream. Elin Parry looked up from the till. A man had come in backwards, at speed, in the rain — wet coat, wet hair, sunglasses on a wet Tuesday in Pontcanna. "Hide me." "Sorry?" "Hide me. Please. Anywhere. Behind the counter, under a rug, in a coffin if you've got one going spare." "We don't do coffins on Tuesdays." He whipped the sunglasses off. "That's — that's actually funny." "Is it?" Outside, on Cathedral Road, three men with cameras skidded to a halt under the awning. The man ducked. Actually ducked, behind Biography. Elin sighed, walked past him, turned the sign to CLOSED, and shot the bolt. "You," he breathed, "are a heroine." "I'm a bookseller in Cardiff with wet stock by the door. Get up, you're creasing Terry Pratchett." He got up slowly. Very slowly, and with a smile she recognised, because it had been beaming down from her mother's kitchen calendar since January. "Hi. I'm —" "Rory Vaughan." "You know me." "I know of you." "Of me is good. Of me works." He ran a hand through wet hair, which somehow made it look better. Unfair, that. "Filming down at Roath Lock. Press day. I may have... escaped." "Escaped the Bay to Pontcanna? That's a tidy escape, mun. Did you run all the way?" "Taxi, then panic, then your very welcoming doorway." He offered his hand. "Rory." She took it. His hand was warm. Hers, traitorously, was not quite steady. She let go first. "Elin Parry." "Elin Parry of Parry's Books. Lovely shop. Really lovely. Cosy, smells amazing, great light —" "It's raining and a bulb's gone in Poetry." "I meant spiritually great light." "Ah. Right." "You're not —" He tilted his head. That look. The one from *Wexford Hall*, episode six, usually aimed at a governess by a fireplace. "You're not a fan, are you?" "My mother is." "Your mother has excellent taste." "My mother has your calendar." He winced. "January or —" "She keeps it on March. You in a wet shirt by a lake." "That was a very serious drama about land reform." "I'm sure March felt very reformed." He stared at her. "You haven't watched it, have you?" "I watched the first series." "And?" "It was fine." "*Fine?*" "Perfectly fine." He clutched his chest. "Elin Parry. We won a BAFTA." "Well done. Mind that stack." He minded it automatically, catching a pile of hardbacks as she brushed past him with an armful of returns. She was not brushing past him on purpose. She was also not *not* aware of his shoulder, his height, the rain smell on his coat. She put *Persuasion* in Austen. Then took it out. Then put it back in exactly the same place. "So," he said. "What did we do wrong in series one? Hypothetically. For my fragile — for my professional development." "You brooded." "I brood professionally. It's in my contract." "You brooded at windows. At horses. At soup." "The soup had subtext." "It was leek and potato." He laughed. A proper laugh, startled out of him, not the polished interview one. "God. Okay. Nobody on a press tour has ever — sorry. Normally people laugh at the soup line before I say it." "Am I supposed to?" "No! No, that's the — that's refreshing. Terrifying, but refreshing." He followed her down the narrow aisle. "Recommend me something, then. Educate me. A book for a man hiding from photographers behind Terry Pratchett." " *The Invisible Man*." "Too on the nose." "*How to Win Friends and Influence People*." "Now you're being cruel." "*Pride and Prejudice*. Man with too much confidence learns manners." He stopped. "Too much confidence?" "You came in asking a stranger to hide you in a coffin and then reviewed her lighting." "That's not confidence, that's survival instinct and excellent taste in bookshops." He tried the smile again, smaller. "Do you not like me?" "I don't know you." "But your first impression. Gut feeling. One to ten." "I'm not scoring customers, Mr Vaughan." "Rory. And everyone scores customers. I score audiences. Opening night, I can tell by the coughing." "I haven't coughed." "No," he said, more quietly. "You haven't." There was a pause in which the rain got louder on the window and Elin became very interested in a copy of *Under Milk Wood* that did not need straightening. Outside, a camera flashed once, hopelessly, through the glass. Both of them flinched. "They'll go," she said. "They never go. There was a thing this morning, with my co-star. Nothing happened, which apparently is worse than something happening. If something happens they can print it. If nothing happens they have to invent it, and they're very... creative." He rubbed his face. The charm slipped, just for a second. He looked tired. Younger. "Sorry. You didn't ask for the autobiography." "No," she said, gentler despite herself. "I sell them, though." That got her the real smile. Not March. Not episode six. Just — pleased, and a bit relieved, as if she'd passed a test she hadn't agreed to sit. "There," he said. "You do like me." "I said I sell autobiographies." "Your mouth said that. Your tone said, 'poor famous boy in the rain.'" "My tone said no such thing." "Elin." "Rory." He leaned against Welsh History. "Can I stay until they get bored? I'll be quiet. I'll alphabetise. I did a summer at Waterstones in Swansea, I am fully trained." "You were not." "I was! Nineteen. Till two. I was sacked for recommending my own favourite book to everyone regardless of what they asked for." "What was it?" "*The Count of Monte Cristo*. Man escapes, reinvents himself, broods at windows." "At soup?" "At banquets. Much better soup." He nodded at the book still in her hand. "What's that one?" She looked down. She was still holding Dylan Thomas like a shield. "You wouldn't like it. No lakes. No wet shirts. Just a Welsh village, listening." "Try me." She handed it over before she could think better of it. Their fingers brushed. Neither of them moved for half a beat too long. He opened it at random and read, under his breath, *"It is spring, moonless night in the small town, starless and bible-black..."* His Welsh accent, which Hollywood had been sanding down for years, came back all at once on *bible-black*. Elin's stomach did something completely unprofessional. "Okay," he said softly. "I like it." "Tidy." "Was that a compliment?" "That was an acknowledgement." "I'll take it. I'm taking all acknowledgements today, I'm running low." He held onto the book. "They've gone, haven't they?" She looked. The pavement outside was empty, just rain and a woman with a pram hurrying for the arcade. "Looks like." "Right. Right, so I should..." "Probably." "Probably." He didn't move. "If I buy this, and I come back for another recommendation, would that be weird? Stalker-ish? Rogue-ish? My publicist has a chart." "It would be retail." "And if I came back not in the rain? Deliberately?" "Also retail, but drier." He grinned, and this time he looked almost nervous doing it, which was — she thought, furiously — considerably more attractive than March, April, and the lake combined. "Then I'll come back, Elin Parry. For retail." "Diolch," she said. "We close at six." "I'll be here at five fifty-nine. Brooding. At your window." "I'll put the soup on." He bought the book. He left the sunglasses on the counter, remembered them, came back, forgot them again — and when the bell finally screamed him out into Cardiff, Elin stood for a long moment with her hand flat on the till, trying to remember how she'd normally arranged her face. On the counter, he'd left his receipt. On the back, in hurried biro: *Series Two is better. I brood less. — R*
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and adherence to the prompt requirements. The author successfully creates a meet-cute scenario in a Welsh bookstore with two well-defined characters whose personalities emerge clearly through dialogue and action. The characterization is particularly effective. Rory is portrayed as charming yet insecure, genuinely thrown off by Elin's resistance to his usual tactics. His fragile ego shows through his need for validation ("Do you not like me?" and "One to ten") while maintaining his roguish charm. Elin is convincingly portrayed as someone who appears immune to his celebrity status while internally being affected by his presence - shown through subtle physical cues like her unsteady hand and unnecessary book rearranging. The dialogue carries the scene effectively, with distinct voices for each character. Elin's dry Welsh wit ("We don't do coffins on Tuesdays") contrasts well with Rory's more performative speech patterns. The banter feels natural and reveals character while advancing the romantic tension. The Welsh setting is well-integrated through specific location references (Pontcanna, Cathedral Road, Roath Lock) and authentic dialogue touches like "mun" and "tidy." The bookstore environment is convincingly rendered without excessive description. The romantic chemistry builds believably through their verbal sparring, with moments of genuine connection (the Dylan Thomas passage, his nervous grin) that feel earned rather than forced. The pacing allows for natural development of attraction. However, some elements feel slightly predictable - the celebrity hiding from paparazzi trope, the bookish woman immune to fame, the note left behind. While executed well, these don't break new creative ground. The ending, while sweet, borders on being overly neat with the receipt message. The prose is generally clean and effective, though occasionally veers toward being overly polished in a way that can feel slightly artificial. Some descriptions like "His Welsh accent... came back all at once" work well, while others feel more constructed. The emotional complexity is present but not deeply explored - this reads more as skilled romantic comedy than profound character study. The transformations are minimal and appropriate for a single scene, avoiding the trap of unrealistic character changes. + Whalepunk fantasy: The Morska Conspiracy — Score: 83.7
Prompt:
Whalepunk fantasy The Morska Conspiracy The Morska thieves guild experiences a sudden power vacuum as its leader was arrested in a raid in the early hours of the morning. Aya, a young woman born into aristocracy, has a keen interest in both the sciences and the arcane, having inherited her mother's gift for immateria magick (an outlawed practice for which her mother was, regrettably, hanged by the neck). Aya, bored with the world of aristocracy, has been spending her nights moonlighting with this very guild (masked, naturally). Leveraging her latent ability to summon dark entities from the immateria, she quickly rose through the ranks of the guild. Now, recognising the opportunity of the sudden power vacuum, Aya and her close companions Katra and Simeon, make a play for heart of the guild's claim to power: an ancient scythan artifact, under guard of spell and key in the depths of the guild hq. In contrast with the desperate chaos they had navigated thus far, the entrance to the underhold felt suddenly too quiet. Aya braces herself and reaches for the door. Write the next scene as the trio enter the underhold and find themselves confronted by none other than the guild leader herself, decidedly *un*-incarcerated, and in possession of both weapons and bodyguards. Paint a vivid picture of of the confrontation. Story beats: Aya is captured and unmasked. The trio are captured. Aya attempts to stall their demise by negotiating on her value as a hostage -- as she grapples with the inevitable consequences of her role in the guild being brought to light. Incorporate dialogue in the authentic voices of the characters. Do not write a fight scene. Lean into the gritty Victorian aesthetic with the dialogue & worldbuilding, as well as elements of gothic horror. In this world, men trust brass and oil and steel; magicka is feared and barely understood. Write in third person past tense, incorporating both Aya's internal monologue, and a heavy dialogue component. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The underhold door swung inward on oiled hinges, and the silence beyond it swallowed them whole. No alarm bells. No running feet on the wet cobbles above, no Watch whistles shrilling through the Morska dockyards. Only the hiss of gas, the drip of black water through stone, and the low, sweet stink of whale oil and rust. The flickering gas lamps cast long, unsettling shadows across the stone floor, stretching the trio's silhouettes into thin, drowned things against the vaulted brick. Aya paused on the threshold. *Too quiet,* she thought. *A slaughterhouse is quiet, just before.* The vault door at the far end stood open. It should not have stood open. It was iron-banded oak and brass, locked by key and spell and three separate oaths, and behind it — if the old thieves' tales were true — lay the Scythan heart of the guild's power, a thing dredged from a leviathan's belly a hundred years before men learned to burn whale-light instead of tallow. Katra touched her elbow. "Aya. Aya, my love, I have a feeling in my waters, and it ain't a good one." "You always have a feeling," Simeon whispered. He was a big man gone thin from gin and bad luck, an ex-harpooner with trembling hands. "Last week you had a feeling about the races and lost us six crowns." "Last week I didn't feel like the walls was listening." Then a woman's voice came out of the dark beyond the vault, calm as a clerk reading a death warrant. "Close the door behind you, children. You're letting in the weather." Lamps flared — not gas, but spermaceti oil in brass whalebone lanterns, turned up all at once. Men stepped from the alcoves where the guild kept coal and corpse-sacks. Six of them. Then eight. Bodyguards in oilskin coats, faces scarred by rope and frostbite, with cutlasses at their hips and short, ugly revolvers in their hands. Brass and oil and steel. The honest trinity of Morska men. And in the centre, seated upon an upturned strongbox before the open vault, with the Scythan artifact resting in a lead-lined case beside her boot, sat Mistress Varga. Guildmaster of the Morska. Arrested, according to three separate runners, at dawn. Taken in irons by the Watch. Decidedly, presently, and amusedly *un*-incarcerated. "Madam," Aya said. Her mouth had gone dry. Behind her, the door clicked shut. A bolt slid home like a coffin nail. Varga was fifty, perhaps sixty, with iron-grey hair pinned beneath a widow's cap and a face that might have been handsome before the pox and the port took it. She wore black bombazine and a man's waistcoat, and across her knees lay a whalebone cane inlaid with brass. A revolver rested beside the artifact, quite casually, as a lady might set down her teacup. "There was no raid," Aya said. "Oh, there was," Varga replied. "Captain Lyle kicked in the door of a very obliging whore in Cannery Row who happens to share my name and my unfortunate nose. The Watch have her still, I believe. She'll be compensated." Her eyes, pale and wet as oyster flesh, moved from Aya to Katra to Simeon. "I find a rumour of my absence is an excellent net. One learns what fish rise when they think the shark is dead." Simeon made a small, strangled sound. His knife was already lowering. A bodyguard took it from his fingers without hurry and cuffed him once, almost gently, across the ear. "Hands," another said. "Show 'em, pretty." Katra lifted hers. Her grin was all teeth and terror. "Gentlemen, if this is about the silver from St. Cyprian's, I can explain —" "Shut your gob, Kat," one growled. "I was merely —" A pistol cocked. Katra shut her gob. Aya did not raise her hands at once. She was listening, not to them, but *inward* — to that cold pressure at the base of her skull where the immateria pressed its faces against the world. In the underhold the wards were old. Salt in the mortar. Cold iron in the beams. Still, she could feel them scratching. Little dark saints with too many eyes, eager to be invited. *One word,* she thought. *One word and the lamps go out and something comes through wearing my shadow —* Varga smiled. "I wouldn't, dear." "You don't know what I can do." "No. And that frightens my boys, which is why Mr. Hobb has his pistol at Miss Katra's temple." Aya looked. Indeed he did. Katra had gone the colour of tallow. "We are not animals," Varga continued. "Put up your hands. No one need be shot in a place where the blood would spoil the merchandise." *If I summon, they fire. If I don't, they hang us anyway. Mother, you magnificent fool, what did you whisper to when they put the rope on you? Did it come? Did it watch?* Aya raised her hands. They bound them with picture-wire, quick and practised. Simeon was weeping silently now. Katra kept trying to catch Aya's eye. Then Varga rose, leaning on her cane, and crossed the stone floor herself. She stopped before Aya and regarded the black silk mask, the boy's coat, the soot worked into her cuffs. "And now," Varga said, "the mystery of my little night-owl. The one who always knew the Watch rotations. Who could read a manifest and a grimoire with equal ease. Who rose so very fast for a gutter-child." Her gloved fingers hooked the mask. "Madam —" Aya began. Varga pulled. Cold air struck her face. Her hair, unbound from its pins, fell dark and unmistakably well-kept about her shoulders. One of the bodyguards swore. Another, God help him, crossed himself and touched the brass whale-charm at his throat, as men did when magicka was spoken of. "Well," Varga said softly. "Well, well." "Christ on a hook," Hobb breathed. "That's Lord Ashcombe's girl." "Lady Aya Ashcombe," Varga corrected. "Only daughter of Lord Edmund Ashcombe, High Commissioner for Leviathan Duties, scourge of smugglers, and — if memory serves — the very man who signed the warrant that hanged your mother for immaterial congress." Her gaze did not leave Aya's face. "Did he make you watch, dear? They used to make the children watch." Aya felt the room tilt, very slightly. *There it is. Not the rope. Not the river with a stone at my feet. The name. By morning it will be in the broadsheets. Lord Ashcombe's daughter unmasked in a thieves' vault. My father will not weep. He will do arithmetic. A madhouse in the country, perhaps. A marriage to some colonial widower with a taste for damaged stock. Or — cleaner — he will let the law have me, as he let it have her, and stand upon the courthouse steps explaining that corruption is a maternal inheritance.* "Untie my friends," Aya said. Her voice, to her horror, shook. She steadied it with aristocratic contempt, the only armour she had left. "They followed me. Whatever offence you imagine, the design was mine." Katra made a noise of protest. "Aya —" "How noble," Varga said. "And how useless. Simeon picked the lock on the Cannery gate. Katra carried the heart out of two chapels and a counting-house. They hang quite adequately on their own merits." "Then hear my merits," Aya said. She stepped forward until the wire cut her wrists and Varga's cane pressed, warning, against her sternum. "Kill me here and you have a corpse you must feed to the harbour, and corpses have a habit of surfacing at inconvenient tides. But keep me — keep me whole, and unspoiled, and able to write a letter in my own hand — and you have Lord Ashcombe himself by the throat." Silence. Even the gas seemed to hiss quieter. "Go on," Varga said. "You want the northern wharves unmolested. You want Lyle promoted away, or buried. You want your people released from the Black Cells before the assizes. My father can do all of that with a signature, and he will, if the alternative is his daughter's name read aloud in an immateria trial." The words tasted of bile. "I am worth more to you breathing than any Scythan bauble in that box. I am a hostage no gaol can hold for you and no rival can steal." From the lead-lined case beside Varga's empty seat, something inside the artifact made a faint sound — like a fingernail, tapping once against glass. Every bodyguard in the room looked at it. Every bodyguard then pretended he had not. Varga, alone, smiled. "My dear Lady Aya," she said. "At last, you begin to sound like one of mine." She turned the cane in her hand. "Lock them in the lower cell. All three. And bring me pen, paper, and wax. We shall see what Lord Ashcombe's love is worth — weighed, as all things are in Morska, against oil."

[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical craft and atmospheric worldbuilding within the "whalepunk" fantasy setting. The author successfully creates a vivid Victorian-gothic atmosphere through specific details like "spermaceti oil in brass whalebone lanterns," "oilskin coats," and the pervasive imagery of whale oil, brass, and industrial decay. The setting feels authentic and immersive. The dialogue is particularly well-executed, with distinct voices for each character. Varga's calm, calculating menace ("Close the door behind you, children. You're letting in the weather") contrasts effectively with Katra's nervous energy and Simeon's defeated terror. Aya's aristocratic bearing breaking through her thief persona feels genuine and adds layers to her character. The piece adheres closely to the prompt's requirements, hitting all the specified story beats: the trio enters the underhold, confronts the supposedly imprisoned guild leader, Aya is unmasked, they're captured, and she attempts to negotiate using her value as a hostage. The author avoids writing a fight scene as requested and maintains the gritty Victorian aesthetic throughout. Character motivations feel believable and well-grounded. Aya's internal struggle between her magical abilities, aristocratic background, and criminal activities creates compelling tension. Her decision to negotiate rather than use her immateria powers makes tactical sense given the threat to her companions. The prose strikes a good balance between atmospheric description and forward momentum. While occasionally dense, it generally avoids purple prose pitfalls. The author effectively uses Aya's internal monologue to reveal character depth and emotional complexity, particularly her fears about her father's potential reaction and the parallel to her mother's fate. Some minor weaknesses include occasional overwrought passages and a few moments where the period voice feels slightly forced. The pacing is generally strong, though some descriptive sections could be tightened. The ending feels appropriately dark and unresolved, fitting the gothic tone without false optimism. The worldbuilding details about immateria magic, the Scythan artifact, and the industrial-magical setting feel creative and well-integrated. The piece successfully creates tension and maintains reader engagement throughout. Gunpowder Rendezvous Spike Spiegel & Revy Write a story where Spike Spiegel (Cowboy Bebop) and Revy (Black Lagoon) meet in a seedy bar after both being hired for the same bounty. Their mutual attraction is complicated by their trust issues and competitive instincts. Include drinking, gunplay, and unresolved sexual tension that culminates in a motel room standoff. **Spike Spiegel (Cowboy Bebop)** Spike is a laid-back bounty hunter with a dark past as a syndicate enforcer. He practices Jeet Kune Do and is exceptionally skilled with firearms. He's chronically broke, constantly hungry, and addicted to cigarettes. Despite his carefree attitude, he's haunted by his past and the woman he left behind. He has a prosthetic eye from a past injury that affects his depth perception. He's fatalistic to the extreme, often saying he's already died once. He values freedom above all else and dislikes attachments, though he secretly cares deeply for his crew. Famous quote: "Whatever happens, happens." **Revy/Rebecca Lee (Black Lagoon)** Revy is a Chinese-American dual-wielding gunslinger with unparalleled shooting skills. She's foul-mouthed, chain-smoking, and has severe anger management issues stemming from childhood abuse. She's known as "Two Hands" for her ability to accurately fire two pistols simultaneously. She drinks heavily and solves most problems with violence. Despite her hardened exterior, she has moments of vulnerability, particularly around Rock. I'm just here." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
A lazy ceiling fan barely stirs the smoky air inside the bar. The Lost Dog sits three blocks from the Tharsis spaceport, where the neon flickers, the jukebox skips, and nobody asks for a last name. Spike Spiegel slouches at the counter with an empty glass, a lit cigarette, and exactly four Woolongs to his name. He watches the door in the mirror behind the bottles, because his right eye is glass and lies about distance, and mirrors lie more honestly. The bounty sheet burns a hole in his jacket pocket. Marco Vane, ex-Red Dragon accountant, fifty thousand Woolongs alive, thirty dead, last seen drinking here like a man who wants to be found. The door bangs open. Revy walks in like she owns the place and resents it for existing. Black crop top, shorts cut to a suggestion, a dragon tattoo curling down her right arm, and two Beretta 93Rs riding her hips like punctuation. She scans the room once, dismisses everyone, then stops at Spike. Not recognition. Assessment. She takes the stool beside him, too close for strangers, and orders whiskey without looking at the bartender. "You're in my seat, cowboy." Spike exhales smoke toward the fan. "Funny. It doesn't have your name on it." "Give me a minute. I'll carve it." Her glass arrives. She downs it, orders another, and eyes his empty one. "Broke or pacing yourself?" "Philosophically opposed to paying." She snorts, but she signals for two. The whiskey tastes like engine cleaner and bad decisions. He drinks anyway, because he is chronically hungry, perpetually broke, and never stupid enough to refuse free liquor from a beautiful woman with guns. She notices how he sits, loose but balanced, weight ready to move. He notices she keeps both hands visible and her back to the wall even on a barstool. Jeet Kune Do teaches him to read flow. She reads like a riptide. "You here for the view?" she asks. "The view just improved," he says. "Careful. It shoots back." "Wouldn't be fun otherwise." Marco Vane chooses that moment to emerge from the bathroom, pale, sweating, and suddenly very sober. Both hunters see him. Both stand. Vane freezes. Revy grins without warmth. "Well, shit. You're not just pretty. You're competition." Spike stubs out his cigarette. "Whatever happens, happens. But I saw him first." "Bullshit. I tracked him from the port." "And I waited like a gentleman." Vane bolts for the kitchen. Revy draws first, both Cutlasses up, and fires over Spike's shoulder as one of Vane's bodyguards rises from a booth with a shotgun. Her blast takes the shotgun high. Spike is already moving, water finding a crack, one kick folding the second bodyguard at the knee, his Jericho spinning into his hand without seeming to leave the holster. He fires once. A ceiling light explodes. Glass rains. Patrons dive. The bartender vanishes with professional speed. Vane crashes through the kitchen door. Revy vaults the bar. Spike slides after her, and for three seconds they are not rivals but a single violent sentence, her twin pistols clearing corners, his longer stride eating the alley beyond. She fires left-handed while running, shattering a trash bin beside Vane's head. "Alive pays more!" Spike shouts. "Then run faster, asshole!" Vane pulls a compact pistol and fires wildly backward. A round grazes Revy's shorts and tears the edge of her top. Another punches through Spike's sleeve. His depth perception stutters at the muzzle flash, but his body remembers a hundred syndicate rooms before his eye does. He tackles Vane behind a dumpster as Revy's boots hit a crate and she comes down on top of both of them, one knee on Vane's wrist, one pistol under Spike's chin. Silence arrives, ringing. Vane whimpers. Revy breathes hard, smelling of whiskey, cordite, and sweat. Spike looks up the barrel, then at her, and smiles like a man who already dies once and remains unimpressed by the sequel. "Nice landing." "Move and I redecorate." "You'd miss the conversation." "Try me." Her finger does not tighten. His gun, she realizes, rests loosely against her ribs. Neither mentions it. Vane tries to speak. "Shut up," they say together. Revy's eyes flicker with reluctant amusement. "Split?" Spike offers. "Sixty-forty. I bleed more." "You don't bleed." "Emotionally." "Fifty-fifty. I buy dinner." "With my money?" "Our money." She considers, then hauls Vane up and cuffs him to a pipe with his own belt. They stash Vane, bound and gagged, in the trunk of a stolen cab with a parking brake that might hold, and take the motel room across the street to watch, wait for the pickup, and not kill each other. The Blue Hour Motel rents by the hour and cleans by the decade. The room offers one bed, one chair, a shower that drips rust, and a window with a perfect view of the cab. Revy claims the bed. Spike claims the floor, then the chair, then, after she throws him a pillow without comment, the other side of the bed, boots still on. She produces a bottle from somewhere and drinks straight. He bums a cigarette, then another. Smoke curls between them. "I'm not a good person, not a bad person," she says suddenly. "I'm just here." "Here is crowded," he says. "You got someone waiting, cowboy?" Julia's name rises like smoke and ash. "Had. Have. Grammar's tricky with ghosts." Revy looks away first, because Rock's face does something similar to her and she hates owing anyone recognition. Outside, rain starts, ticking the neon sign. She shifts closer under the pretense of reaching the bottle, and her tattooed arm brushes his. Neither moves away. "You aim with that fake eye?" she asks. "I aim with the rest of me." "Show-off." "You're one to talk, Two Hands." A car door slams outside. Both are up instantly, guns drawn, backs to opposite walls, before either consciously decides to move. False alarm. A drunk staggers past. But now Spike's Jericho points at Revy's heart, and both her Cutlasses point at his, and the room shrinks to breath and triggers. Neither lowers a weapon. She steps forward until his muzzle presses her top. He steps in until hers press his shirt. Her eyes drop, briefly, to his mouth. His do the same. The air tastes of rain, whiskey, and gun oil. "Next time," she whispers, "I shoot first." "Next time," he says, "buy dinner." Below them, the cab trunk thumps.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and character understanding. The author captures both Spike and Revy's voices authentically, maintaining their distinct personalities while creating believable chemistry. Spike's fatalistic philosophy and laid-back demeanor contrast effectively with Revy's aggressive, volatile nature, yet both characters feel true to their source material. The prose style is notably sophisticated, employing vivid imagery and metaphorical language that enhances rather than overwhelms the narrative. Phrases like "She reads like a riptide" and "his body remembers a hundred syndicate rooms before his eye does" demonstrate skillful writing that maintains the noir atmosphere appropriate to both source materials. The action sequences are well-choreographed and easy to follow, with the bar fight and chase scene flowing naturally into the motel standoff. The pacing builds tension effectively, moving from initial wariness through partnership to the final confrontation where sexual and violent tension intertwine. Character interactions feel earned rather than forced. The gradual shift from competition to reluctant cooperation to mutual attraction develops organically through shared action and dialogue. Both characters maintain their essential natures while revealing vulnerability - Spike's reference to Julia and Revy's moment of openness about Rock feel authentic to their established personalities. The dialogue captures each character's distinct voice effectively. Revy's crude directness ("Well, shit. You're not just pretty. You're competition.") contrasts with Spike's more philosophical approach, while their banter during the action sequences feels natural and character-appropriate. The ending maintains appropriate ambiguity, avoiding forced resolution while delivering on the promised tension. The final standoff with guns drawn while they're attracted to each other perfectly encapsulates both characters' inability to fully trust or commit. Minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the prose becomes slightly overwrought, and some descriptions that border on purple, though these don't significantly detract from the overall quality. The piece successfully fulfills all prompt requirements while maintaining literary merit. + Folk horror: Útiseta — Score: 85.5
Prompt:
Folk Horror: Útiseta Write a chapter set in rural northern Sweden in the mid-1990s. Linnea, a teenage girl from Stockholm, has reluctantly moved to a small village with her parents after her father's job transfer. She's befriended Astrid, a local girl who claims her grandmother taught her ancient practices passed down through generations. Astrid has been introducing Linnea to "midnight games" that involve old rituals, convincing her they can use them to learn classmates' secrets or influence their behavior. Tonight, Astrid has convinced Linnea to participate in Útiseta—sitting out on an ancient burial mound at midnight to "receive knowledge from beyond." The chapter focuses on this single midnight excursion, the ritualistic preparations, Astrid's matter-of-fact instructions that mix teenage rebellion with eerily specific traditional elements, and the mounting tension as Linnea becomes increasingly uncertain whether they're simply scaring themselves or if something is actually responding to their presence. The narrative should maintain ambiguity about whether the strange occurrences are supernatural or psychological, while establishing the dangerous line they're crossing by treating ancient practices as entertainment. First person, past tense, told as Linnea's recollection of events in the present day (though this device should be largely transparent). 1000 words. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Útiseta I was sixteen the summer we moved north, and for years I told people the worst part was leaving Stockholm. That was easier than telling the truth. It was September 1995. My father had been transferred from an office on Södermalm to a forestry post outside Östersund, and suddenly we lived in a yellow house at the end of a gravel road in a village with one bus stop, one shop, and fields that disappeared into forest. At school I was the girl with the wrong accent and the wrong shoes. Astrid decided on my second day that I would be her friend. She was not like the girls I had known. She wore her grandfather's boots, smoked behind the gym hall, and spoke about her dead grandmother as if she had only gone into the next room. It was her grandmother, she said, who had taught her the old things. Not witchcraft — Astrid hated that word. Just what women here had always known, before the church taught them to pretend otherwise. The midnight games began as jokes. We made a pendulum from Astrid's necklace and held it over class photographs to learn who had stolen money from the changing rooms. We sat in her bathroom with the lights off, whispering into a mirror to see who we would marry. We asked whether Johan Lindqvist had kissed Sara behind the ice rink, whether our maths teacher drank at lunchtime, whether I would ever move back to Stockholm. The pendulum swung yes or no. The mirror showed only our own pale faces, trying not to laugh. I never quite believed it. I also never quite stopped. The útiseta was Astrid's idea, of course. She said it on the bus home, casually, while picking varnish off her nails. "Tonight," she said. "If you actually want to know something, that's how you ask." "Ask who?" "The ones underneath." She meant the burial mound beyond the old church, where the road narrowed between two farms. Everyone knew it was ancient, which in the village meant nobody remembered who was supposed to be buried there, only that you did not plough it, build on it, or let children dig in it. We had cycled past it a hundred times. I asked what we would learn. Astrid shrugged. "Whatever they feel like telling. Johan. The exams. Your dad's job. You have to let them choose first." That night I told my parents I was sleeping at Astrid's. She told hers she was sleeping at mine. It was the sort of lie we had already perfected. I met her by the shop at half past eleven with my father's thick coat over my pyjamas and a torch she immediately made me switch off. "You don't bring electric light," she said. "And no metal against your skin. Take your earrings out." "Mine are plastic." "Then shut up about them." She had brought two hazel staffs cut from behind her barn, a woollen blanket that smelled of smoke, a thermos — not for us, she explained, but to leave — and a small knife wrapped in cloth. She also had a bottle of her father's brännvin with perhaps two mouthfuls missing. That part was teenage rebellion. The rest, I understood even then, was not. We had not eaten since supper. We washed our hands and faces in the ditch by the churchyard, the water so cold it made my teeth ache. Astrid tied her hair up and told me to do the same. "Nothing loose," she said. "Nothing open. Hood up when we sit. If you hear your name, you don't answer. If you hear it three times —" She stopped. "What?" "You still don't answer." She said we must approach from the east, walk around the mound once without speaking, and sit facing north. We could not cross our arms. We could not sleep. We could not look directly at anything that moved at the edge of sight; we had to let it come to us. If we became frightened, we could press the staff into the earth, but we must not run. Running, Astrid said, was an invitation. I laughed, because I thought she expected me to. She didn't laugh back. The mound was larger in darkness. Thick mist clings to the edges of the burial mound, glowing under moonlight. That is how I still see it, even now: not touching the top, where we sat, but circling below, as if kept back by the shape of the hill itself. The grass was wet through the blanket within minutes. Somewhere beyond the fence a horse shifted and blew through its nose. Then the ordinary sounds seemed to withdraw, one by one. Astrid poured a little brännvin onto the ground and set the thermos beside it, unopened. She whispered something I did not catch — not theatrical, not loud. It sounded like greeting someone whose house you had entered without knocking. Then we sat. At first it was boring. My legs cramped. Astrid, beside me, became so still that I could no longer hear her breathe. I thought about Johan, about the exam, about how ridiculous we would look if anyone found us. I thought about saying so. The rule of silence had seemed easy at the road. On the mound, it grew heavier with every minute. The first sound may have been an owl. The second may have been the horse again, though it came from beneath us, a long exhalation through packed earth. I told myself the mound was hollow with rabbit burrows. I told myself mist made sound travel strangely. Then someone said my name from down by the road. Not Astrid's voice. Not a voice I knew. It said, "Linnea," as my mother did when calling me in for supper, with the same slight impatience. My whole body wanted to turn. Astrid's hand found my wrist and held it hard enough to hurt. The voice came again, closer, behind my left shoulder. I could smell ditch water and, faintly, my father's aftershave. That was when I understood the rule was not a game. Or if it was, something else knew how to play it. I did not answer. I swear, now as then, that I did not answer. But I must have made some sound — a breath, a sob — because Astrid whispered, "Don't." At that, everything stopped. The mist below us flattened. Between one heartbeat and the next, the cold ceased to be weather and became pressure, as if the mound itself were listening through us. I had the sudden, absolute conviction that we were not sitting on a grave. We were sitting on a closed mouth. Astrid stood first, which she had forbidden us to do. She left the staff standing upright in the grass and walked backwards down the slope, pulling me with her, her face turned toward the top until we reached the road. Only then did we run for our bikes. We never spoke about the voice. The next morning, cycling to school, we passed the mound in daylight. The thermos was gone. The brännvin had soaked away, of course. Astrid's staff still stood where she had left it, and around it the wet grass was pressed flat in a rough circle, as if several people had been standing there for a long time. Astrid said sheep. There were no sheep in that field. I moved back to Stockholm three years later and did not return for twenty. I still cannot say what happened, only what I have stopped doing. I do not sit out alone after midnight. I do not answer when I hear my name called from another room until I have seen who is calling. And I do not treat old practices as entertainment. Some doors are only doors because generations of people agreed, very carefully, not to open them for fun.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong craft in executing folk horror within the specified parameters. The author successfully captures the voice of an adult Linnea reflecting on teenage events, maintaining the largely transparent framing device while allowing subtle hints of present-day perspective to enhance the narrative's credibility. The characterization is particularly effective. Astrid emerges as a compelling figure who embodies the dangerous intersection of teenage rebellion and genuine occult knowledge. Her matter-of-fact delivery of ritual instructions feels authentic, neither overly dramatic nor dismissive. Linnea's psychology as a displaced city girl seeking belonging while growing increasingly uncomfortable rings true throughout. The prose maintains an appropriate restraint that serves the folk horror genre well. Rather than relying on overwrought descriptions, the author builds tension through specific details: the thermos "not for us, but to leave," the prohibition against metal, the careful approach from the east. These elements feel researched and authentic rather than invented for effect. The ambiguity is skillfully maintained. The voice calling Linnea's name could be supernatural or psychological stress, but the author provides just enough concrete details (the missing thermos, the flattened grass circle) to prevent easy dismissal. The smell of her father's aftershave is a particularly effective touch that suggests either genuine supernatural contact or deep psychological projection. The pacing builds tension effectively, moving from mundane teenage lies through ritual preparation to the climactic sitting. The moment when "everything stopped" and the mound becomes "a closed mouth" represents the story's peak without overplaying the horror. However, some elements feel slightly underdeveloped. The broader context of Linnea's family situation and her relationship with her parents exists mainly as setup. The ending wisdom about "doors" and "old practices" borders on being too neat, though it serves the folk horror tradition well. The dialogue, while limited, feels natural and age-appropriate. Astrid's casual delivery of occult knowledge ("The ones underneath") contrasts effectively with her teenage vernacular. The writing avoids purple prose while maintaining atmospheric richness. The piece succeeds in its primary goal of creating genuine unease while respecting both the folk horror tradition and the psychological realism of teenage experience.
